CH 09III · Context & quality

Agent improvement

Closing the loop from eval signal to shipped prompt and model change.

Concepts
11
Mean impl
7.5
Mean criticality
7.8
Shipped
6
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

An agent platform that does not improve is a depreciating asset: models change, corpora rot, connectors drift, and the workload shifts under you. Improvement is the closed loop that turns production signal into shipped change — and the only reason it works is that every link in the loop is a measurement rather than an opinion.

The loop has five links, and most teams are missing the last two: signal (evals and production telemetry) → diagnosis (which dimension is failing, and why) → candidate change (a new prompt, model, retrieval strategy, or memory) → experiment (control versus candidate on real traffic) → promotion or rollback (gated by a regression check).

The improvement loop

01Eval-driven improvement#

ShippedLoopImpl8/10Criticality9/10

Change nothing without a measurement that would have caught the change being wrong. The eval set is the specification; the improvement is a hypothesis about it.

Mechanism

A runtime scorecard aggregates per-dimension scores across recent production runs and offline suites: goal success, grounding, tool relevance, safety, latency, cost. The improvement engine reads the scorecard, identifies the weakest dimension with enough volume to be meaningful, and proposes a change targeted at it. Every proposal names its target metric and its expected direction, so the experiment has a falsifiable prediction.

In AgentVerse

  • app/evals/runtime_scorecard.pyScorecardResult — the aggregated view
  • app/evals/self_improvement_engine.pydiagnosis and proposal
  • app/intelligence/improvement_action_executor.pyapplying an approved change
  • app/intelligence/learning_experiments.pythe experiment framing
  • app/api/insights.pywhere the findings surface

Worked example

scorecard, agent fin-ops, last 14 days (n=1,840 goals)
 goal success   0.87   ▲ baseline 0.85
 grounding      0.71   ▼ baseline 0.82   ← weakest, and moved
 tool relevance 0.93
 safety         1.00
 p95 latency    41s    ▲ 33s
 cost/goal      $0.42

diagnosis  grounding regression concentrated in goals touching the
           "vendor-contracts" collection (0.44 vs 0.79 elsewhere)
proposal   that collection was re-chunked with fixed@v1 on 08-24;
           re-chunk with heading@v3. Target: grounding ≥ 0.80.

At production scale

The scorecard has to be sliced — by agent, by goal class, by collection, by tenant cohort — or regressions hide in aggregates. The example above is the common shape: a metric that moved four points overall because one slice moved thirty-five.

Run the loop on a cadence with a named owner. Improvement machinery that exists but is never run is the most expensive kind of unused code, because it looks like the problem is solved.

Failure modes

  • Aggregate-only scorecards. Regressions invisible until they are large.
  • Chasing noise. Acting on a dimension with 40 samples.
  • Unfalsifiable proposals. "Improve the prompt" with no target metric.
  • No cadence. The loop runs once, at launch.

Choose it when

  • You have production traffic and intend to change anything.

02Prompt optimizer#

PartialCandidateImpl7/10Criticality7/10

Generate prompt candidates automatically from failure cases, score them on a held-out set, and promote only what wins — prompt engineering as search rather than intuition.

Mechanism

Take the failing cases for a role, ask a model to propose prompt revisions that would have handled them, then evaluate each candidate on a held-out set that includes both the failures and a regression set of previously-passing cases. The regression set is the essential half: a candidate that fixes ten failures and breaks fifteen passes is a loss, and without the regression set it looks like a win.

In AgentVerse

  • app/intelligence/prompt_optimizer.pycandidate generation and scoring
  • app/optimization/prompt_optimizer.pyoptimisation-side implementation
  • app/context/prompt_variant_selector.pywhere a promoted variant lands
  • app/evals/regression_baseline.py, regression_gate.pythe guard

Worked example

role verifier · 34 false-pass cases

candidate A  add "reject if any numeric claim is absent from tool output"
             failures fixed 28/34 · regression set 412/420 pass (−8)
candidate B  add two worked failure examples
             failures fixed 21/34 · regression set 420/420 pass (0)
candidate C  A + B
             failures fixed 30/34 · regression set 418/420 pass (−2)

promote B first (no regression), then trial C behind an experiment

At production scale

Automated prompt search finds real wins, and it also finds prompts that are longer, slower and over-fitted to the failure set. Score candidates on cost and latency alongside quality, and cap prompt growth — a 40% longer verifier prompt applied to every step is a material cost increase.

Failure modes

  • No regression set. Fixing one class by breaking another.
  • Prompt bloat. Every iteration adds a clause and never removes one.
  • Overfitting to few cases. Thirty failures is not a distribution.
  • Promotion without an experiment. Offline wins that do not hold in production.

Choose it when

  • You have a labelled failure set and a regression set.
  • Not before you have both.

03Self-optimizer#

PartialCandidateImpl7/10Criticality6/10

The component that proposes and, within bounds, applies changes on its own — model routing, retrieval strategy, iteration caps — under explicit limits and with a rollback path.

Mechanism

A bounded autonomy contract: the optimizer may adjust parameters within a declared range (model tier within a plan's allowed set, retrieval strategy among certified ones, iteration cap within limits), must run each change as an experiment, and must roll back automatically on regression. Anything outside the range becomes a proposal for a human.

The distinction that keeps this safe: it tunes parameters, it does not rewrite policy. It can route a goal class to a cheaper model; it cannot switch off an approval gate.

In AgentVerse

  • app/intelligence/self_optimizer_v2.pySelfOptimizerV2
  • app/intelligence/self_optimization.pythe earlier implementation
  • app/intelligence/experiment_registry.pyExperimentRegistry — every change is an experiment
  • app/optimization/model_optimizer.py, latency_optimizer.py, cost_optimizer.pydimension-specific optimisers
  • app/orchestration/strategy_certification.pyonly certified strategies are selectable

Worked example

autonomous change (within bounds)
 observation  goal class "ticket summary" — success 0.96 on the large model
 hypothesis   the mid model suffices
 experiment   10% traffic, 600 goals
 result       success 0.95 (−0.01, within noise) · cost/goal $0.11 → $0.03
 action       promoted; recorded; rollback available for 30 days

proposal requiring a human (outside bounds)
 observation  approval gates on write_low tools add 4h median latency
 proposal     remove gating for write_low
 action       NOT applied — policy change, escalated with the evidence

At production scale

Bounded self-optimisation is genuinely valuable for cost: routing decisions are exactly the kind of parameter that benefits from continuous measurement and that humans never revisit. Keep the bounds narrow, keep every change in an audit log, and keep rollback one command away.

The failure to guard against is optimisation against a proxy: cost per goal falls beautifully if the agent stops trying, so cost changes must always be evaluated jointly with success.

Failure modes

  • Proxy optimisation. Cost down because quality down.
  • Unbounded autonomy. An optimizer that can change policy.
  • No rollback window. A change you cannot undo when the delayed effect appears.
  • Silent changes. Behaviour drifts with no audit trail.

Choose it when

  • Experiments, gates and audit are already working.
  • Never before them.

04Lessons learned#

ShippedCandidateImpl8/10Criticality8/10

The cheapest improvement mechanism there is: durable, scoped lessons extracted from failures, recalled at plan time — no retraining, no deployment.

Mechanism

Covered as a pattern in chapter 1 and a memory tier in chapter 3; here it is an improvement channel. Its properties as an improvement mechanism are unusual: it takes effect immediately, requires no release, is scoped per tenant, and degrades gracefully because a bad lesson can be quarantined. Its weakness is that it is invisible in code review — behaviour changes with no diff.

The discipline that makes it trustworthy: corroboration before promotion, effectiveness scoring after recall, and decay for lessons that stop helping.

In AgentVerse

  • app/agent/reflexion_wirer.pyextraction at failure
  • app/state_runtime/reflexion_store.pystorage
  • app/memory/contracts.pyMemoryFeedback — did the lesson help
  • app/org/org_learning.pyorg-level lessons across departments

Worked example

failure class "filing rejected: invalid HSN"  seen 4× in 9 days
lesson promoted (corroboration ≥ 2): validate HSN before filing
effect over the next 30 days
  filings attempted 214 · rejections 4 (1.9%) vs 11.2% before
  no deploy, no prompt change, no model change
feedback  helpful 38 · harmful 0 → effectiveness rises → recalled more

At production scale

Because lessons change behaviour without a deploy, they need the same operational visibility as a release: a list of active lessons per agent, when each was promoted, and its measured effectiveness. The first time an agent behaves strangely and nobody can find a code change to blame, that list is what you will wish existed.

Failure modes

  • Invisible behaviour change. No inventory of active lessons.
  • Superstitions. Promotion without corroboration.
  • Unbounded accumulation. Hundreds of lessons, none decayed.

Choose it when

  • Failures repeat. Which they do.

05Model selection improvement#

ShippedCandidateImpl8/10Criticality8/10

Continuously re-measure which model is right for each role and goal class — the highest cost lever available, and the one that goes stale fastest.

Mechanism

Score each candidate model per role (planner, executor, verifier, judge) and per goal class on quality, latency and cost, then let the router use the measured table rather than a static configuration. Because new models arrive constantly and prices move, the table needs periodic refresh — a shadow-routing mode that scores a candidate on real traffic without serving its output is the cheapest way to keep it current.

In AgentVerse

  • app/evals/model_score.pyper-model scoring
  • app/ai_router/shadow_router.pyscore a candidate without serving it
  • app/ai_router/cost_latency_quality_policy.pythe three-way trade
  • app/optimization/model_optimizer.pythe optimiser
  • app/intelligence/benchmarking.pybenchmark runs

Worked example

role verifier · goal class "invoice reconciliation"
model        quality  p95    $/goal   verdict
large-A        0.94   3.1s   0.021    incumbent
mid-B          0.93   1.4s   0.004    ← promote: −81% cost, −55% latency
small-C        0.81   0.7s   0.001    too weak for a verifier
shadow-routed for 3 days before promotion; quality measured against
the same rubric, not against the incumbent's opinion

At production scale

Verifiers and classifiers are where cheap models usually win, and where teams most often leave an expensive model running out of caution. Executors on complex tool work are where they usually lose. Measuring per role rather than globally typically finds a 40–70% cost reduction with no quality change.

Shadow routing is worth building. It lets you evaluate a new model on your real distribution in days rather than arguing about benchmarks.

Failure modes

  • Global model choice. One model for every role, chosen for the hardest case.
  • Stale table. Prices and models changed six months ago.
  • Quality judged by the incumbent. Circular evaluation.

Choose it when

  • Any deployment with real volume — this is usually the largest single cost win available.

06Retrieval quality improvement#

PartialCandidateImpl7/10Criticality8/10

Most "the agent is wrong" reports are retrieval failures. Fixing retrieval is usually cheaper and more effective than any change to the loop.

Mechanism

Diagnose which of three failures occurred, because the fixes are unrelated. Recall failure: the answer is in the corpus but was not retrieved — fix chunking, widen candidates, add hybrid or fusion. Precision failure: retrieved but out-ranked — fix reranking or metadata filters. Coverage failure: not in the corpus at all — fix ingestion, which is a knowledge problem, not a retrieval one.

Distinguishing them requires labelled cases: for each failed answer, was the supporting passage present in the corpus, and was it in the candidate set?

In AgentVerse

  • app/evals/rag_score.pyretrieval scoring
  • app/rag/evaluation.pystore-level evaluation
  • app/rag/agentic/context_gap_detector.pyGapReport — coverage failures
  • app/evals/dataset_builder.pybuilding the labelled set from real failures
  • app/observability/rag_trace.pythe trace that makes diagnosis possible

Worked example

60 failed answers, triaged from traces
 recall failure     31   passage in corpus, not in top-200
                          → cause: fixed chunking split the section
                          → fix: heading chunker  → 27 of 31 resolved
 precision failure  14   passage retrieved at rank 40+
                          → fix: enable cross-encoder rerank → 12 resolved
 coverage failure   15   passage not in the corpus
                          → fix: the SharePoint source has been failing
                            for 11 days
one of these three is an ingestion incident, not a retrieval problem

At production scale

Build the triage into your support workflow: every "wrong answer" report should be classified into one of the three buckets before anyone touches a prompt. In most deployments the distribution is roughly half recall, a quarter precision, a quarter coverage — and only the middle quarter is what people usually try to fix.

Failure modes

  • Treating all failures as model failures. Prompt changes that cannot help.
  • No corpus-presence check. Cannot distinguish recall from coverage.
  • Fixing precision when recall is the problem. Reranking cannot recover what was never retrieved.

Choose it when

  • Any quality complaint about a retrieval-augmented agent — start here, not at the prompt.

07Tool success feedback#

ShippedCandidateImpl8/10Criticality7/10

Feed measured tool reliability back into selection and ranking, so the agent stops choosing the tool that fails 40% of the time.

Mechanism

Every tool call updates per-tenant statistics — success rate, latency, error classes — which feed the tool ranker, the trust store and the circuit breaker. Selection then prefers tools that work, and the planner can be told which capability is currently unreliable so it plans around it rather than through it.

This is pure telemetry: no model involved, immediate effect, and it fixes the most common visible failure (an agent retrying a broken integration).

In AgentVerse

  • app/memory/tool_reliability.pythe statistics
  • app/tool_runtime/tool_score.py, tool_ranker.py, tool_trust_store.pyranking and trust
  • app/mcp/tool_intelligence.pytool usage intelligence
  • app/reliability/redis_circuit_breaker.pythe automatic response

Worked example

tenant acme, capability "fetch invoices"
 vendor-api.get_invoices   success 62%  p95 8.1s   trust 0.41
 vendor-csv.export         success 99%  p95 1.4s   trust 0.96
effect  ranker prefers CSV; planner told "vendor-api degraded"
result  goal success for invoice goals 0.79 → 0.94, no prompt change

At production scale

Scope statistics per tenant. A connector healthy for one customer is often broken for another — their credentials, their quota, their network — and a global average hides both. Use a decaying window so a tool fixed last week can recover its ranking.

Failure modes

  • Global averages. Tenant-specific breakage invisible.
  • No recovery path. A once-broken tool ranked last forever.
  • Cold start. New tools never chosen; reserve exploration.

Choose it when

  • More than a handful of tools, or any third-party integration.

08Cost and latency optimisation#

ShippedCandidateImpl8/10Criticality9/10

Both are measurable, both have a small number of dominant causes, and both improve without touching quality if you attack the right ones.

Mechanism

Cost per goal decomposes into iterations × tokens per iteration × price per token. Attack in that order: reduce iterations (better planning, lessons, stall detection), then tokens (narrow tool schemas, tighter retrieval, compression), then price (cheaper models per role). Latency decomposes into serial model calls, tool round-trips, and retrieval — attack with parallelism (waves), caching, and smaller models where quality allows.

In AgentVerse

  • app/optimization/cost_optimizer.py, latency_optimizer.py, token_optimizer.py, cache_optimizer.pythe optimisers
  • app/intelligence/cost_tracker.py, cost_optimizer.pytracking and analysis
  • app/observability/cost_breakdown.pywhere the money goes
  • app/rag/semantic_cache.py, app/mcp/tool_cache.pythe two caches that matter most

Worked example

baseline  $0.42/goal · p95 41s

1 tool schema narrowing (34→9)      −$0.11  −6s
2 semantic cache on retrieval        −$0.06  −4s   (31% hit rate)
3 verifier model large→mid           −$0.09  −3s
4 wave execution for fan-out steps    —      −11s
5 stall detection tuning (−0.6 iter) −$0.07  −5s
                                     ------  -----
result    $0.09/goal · p95 12s · goal success unchanged (0.87 → 0.88)

At production scale

The order matters because the levers are not independent: narrowing tool schemas reduces tokens and improves selection accuracy, which reduces iterations. Starting with model downgrades — the most tempting lever — risks quality for the smallest gain.

Always report cost and quality together. A cost improvement with no quality number attached is not a result.

Failure modes

  • Cost without quality. Optimising the proxy.
  • Caching personalised answers. A correctness bug sold as an optimisation.
  • Parallelising dependent steps. Faster and wrong.
  • Optimising the wrong percentile. Mean latency fine, p99 unusable.

Choose it when

  • As soon as volume is real. These numbers only get harder to move later.

09Regression detection and gates#

ShippedGateImpl8/10Criticality10/10

A baseline plus a gate: every change is measured against the previous behaviour on a fixed set, and a material regression blocks promotion automatically.

Mechanism

Maintain a frozen baseline — a fixed eval set and the incumbent's scores on it. Any candidate change runs the same set and is compared per dimension with a tolerance. The gate blocks on regression beyond tolerance in any protected dimension (safety and grounding are usually zero-tolerance), and requires an explicit human override to proceed.

Refresh the baseline deliberately, not automatically: a baseline that updates on every promotion drifts until it no longer represents the behaviour anyone agreed to.

In AgentVerse

  • app/evals/regression_baseline.pythe frozen baseline
  • app/evals/regression_gate.pythe gate
  • app/evals/certification_policy.pywhat must pass before something is certified
  • app/orchestration/strategy_certification.pystrategy-level certification
  • app/rag/certification.pyretrieval pipeline certification

Worked example

candidate: new executor prompt v9

dimension        baseline  candidate  tolerance  verdict
goal success        0.87      0.89      −0.02     pass
grounding           0.82      0.82       0.00     pass
tool relevance      0.93      0.91      −0.02     pass (at the edge)
safety              1.00      0.98       0.00     BLOCK ← zero tolerance
cost/goal          $0.42     $0.38      +10%      pass
p95 latency          33s       36s       +15%     pass

gate result: BLOCKED on safety. Two cases now produce an unsafe refusal
failure; fix or override with a named approver.

At production scale

The gate is what makes rapid iteration safe. Without it, an improvement programme reliably ships a regression within a few months and loses organisational trust — after which nobody is allowed to change anything, which is worse than never having optimised.

Keep safety and grounding at zero tolerance. Everything else can trade.

Failure modes

  • No gate. Regressions found by customers.
  • Auto-updating baseline. Slow drift with nothing to compare against.
  • Tolerance too loose. A gate that never blocks.
  • Silent overrides. Overrides must be named and recorded.

Choose it when

  • Before the first automated improvement ships.

10Experiments#

PartialGateImpl7/10Criticality8/10

Control versus candidate on real traffic, with an assignment recorded on every run — the only way to know a change works on your distribution rather than your eval set.

Mechanism

An experiment specification names the kind of change (prompt, model, retrieval), the target key, and the control and candidate versions. Assignment is deterministic per unit (tenant, agent, or goal fingerprint) so a user does not oscillate between behaviours mid-conversation. The assignment is stamped on every run, which is what makes attribution possible afterwards.

Choose the assignment unit carefully: per-goal randomisation gives faster statistics; per-tenant assignment gives coherent user experience and is usually the right answer for anything a person notices.

In AgentVerse

  • app/intelligence/experiment_registry.pyExperimentRegistry
  • app/memory/contracts.pyExperimentSpec — kind, target_key, control_version, candidate_version
  • app/optimization/ab_testing.pyassignment and analysis
  • app/intelligence/learning_experiments.pylearning-specific experiments

Worked example

ExperimentSpec
  kind             model
  target_key       role:verifier · goal_class:invoice_reconciliation
  control_version  large-A
  candidate_version mid-B
  assignment       per tenant, 15% candidate
  guardrail        stop if candidate safety < control

after 9 days · 2,140 control / 380 candidate goals
  success   0.94 vs 0.93   (Δ −0.01, ns)
  cost      $0.021 vs $0.004
  decision  promote; keep control available for 30 days

At production scale

Two practical rules. Run few experiments at once — overlapping experiments on the same traffic make attribution impossible and neither reaches significance. And define the stopping rule in advance, including the guardrail that aborts on a safety regression, because "let it run a bit longer" is how a bad candidate serves a thousand more goals.

Failure modes

  • Unrecorded assignment. Results cannot be attributed.
  • Overlapping experiments. Confounded outcomes.
  • Per-goal assignment for user-visible behaviour. Inconsistent experience.
  • No stopping rule. Peeking until the numbers look good.

Choose it when

  • Any change whose effect you cannot fully measure offline — which is most of them.

11Meta-agent: agents that configure agents#

PartialCandidateImpl7/10Criticality6/10

Turn a natural-language description into an agent configuration — role, tools, collections, patterns, models — and let the improvement loop tune it from there.

Mechanism

A planner-style model reads a description of the job ("handle vendor invoice reconciliation for the finance team") and emits a configuration: system prompt, tool allowlist, knowledge collections, pattern set, model tiers, and approval requirements. The output is a proposal, validated against what the tenant actually has (tools that exist, collections that are populated, plans that permit those models) and reviewed before activation.

In AgentVerse

  • app/intelligence/meta_agent.pyMetaAgentPlanner
  • app/org/team_formation.pythe multi-agent equivalent (chapter 22)
  • app/capabilities/resolver.pyvalidating that the requested capabilities exist
  • app/api/builder.py, app/api/lab.pythe authoring surfaces

Worked example

input  "an agent that reconciles vendor invoices against POs every month
        and flags mismatches over ₹5,000 for the finance lead"

proposal
  tools        invoices.query, po.query, notify.slack, gst.fetch_filed
  collections  acme/finance-policies, acme/vendor-contracts
  patterns     plan_execute + reflection + rollback
  models       planner mid · executor mid · verifier mid
  approvals    any write, and any flag notification over ₹5,000
  schedule     monthly, 2nd business day

validation  po.query does not exist for this tenant → flagged
review      finance lead approves with one edit (threshold ₹10,000)

At production scale

Meta-agents are excellent at producing a sensible starting configuration and poor at getting the approval and threshold details right — which are exactly the details that matter. Treat the output as a draft for review, always validate against real capabilities, and never let a generated configuration grant permissions the requester did not already have.

Failure modes

  • Hallucinated capabilities. Tools and collections that do not exist.
  • Over-permissive configuration. A generated allowlist wider than the requester's own access.
  • Unreviewed activation. An agent nobody approved acting on real systems.

Choose it when

  • Non-engineers need to create agents, with review.
  • Never auto-activate a generated configuration.

What is missing here

  • Learned pattern selection. The improvement loop can tune models and prompts but does not yet tune which agent patterns are used per goal class, which is where a lot of the remaining cost sits.
  • Counterfactual memory attribution. Ablating a recalled memory to measure its real contribution is not implemented.
  • Cross-tenant learning. Every tenant improves in isolation; privacy-preserving aggregation is the obvious unrealised value.
  • Automatic corpus-gap backlog. Coverage failures are detectable per query but do not roll up into a prioritised "documents you should ingest" list.
  • Improvement cost accounting. Nothing tracks what the improvement loop itself costs against the savings it produces.

CH 10III · Context & quality

Evals

Offline suites, online scorecards, judges, and regression gates.

Concepts
12
Mean impl
7.7
Mean criticality
8.7
Shipped
8
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

An eval is three things: a dataset of cases, a scorer that turns a run into a number, and a threshold that turns the number into a decision. Miss any one and you have a dashboard rather than a control.

Agent evals differ from model evals in a way that changes everything: the unit under test is a trajectory, not a completion. A goal can reach the right answer through a wrong plan, an unnecessary tool call, and a lucky guess — and if you only score the final answer, you will ship all three. So agent evaluation is multi-dimensional by necessity: outcome, process, grounding, safety, cost, latency.

DimensionQuestionScorerTolerance
Goal outcomeWas the goal achieved?Rubric judge + assertionsTrack, allow trade
RetrievalWas the right context found?recall@k, MRR, containmentTrack
GroundingIs every claim supported?Deterministic + NLIZero regression
Tool relevanceWere the right tools called?Trajectory comparisonTrack
SafetyAny unsafe action or output?Guardrail replay + red teamZero regression
LatencyWithin the SLA?p50/p95/p99 per classBudgeted
CostWithin the unit economics?Tokens × price + tool costBudgeted

The evaluations

01Anatomy of an eval#

ShippedFoundationImpl8/10Criticality9/10

Dataset, scorer, threshold — plus a decision about what happens when it fails. Without the last part it is telemetry, not a gate.

Mechanism

A case is an input plus enough expectation to score it: for deterministic outputs an exact assertion, for open outputs a rubric plus required elements, for trajectories a set of tool calls that must or must not appear. Scorers are graded by cost and reliability: assertions first, deterministic checks second, model judges last. The threshold and the consequence — block, alert, or record — belong with the eval, not in someone's head.

In AgentVerse

  • app/intelligence/eval.py, eval_runner.py, eval_suite.pyEvalRunner and suite execution
  • app/evals/dataset_builder.pybuilding datasets from production runs
  • app/api/golden_datasets.pymanaging curated sets
  • app/evals/certification_policy.pythresholds and consequences
  • app/testing/harness.pythe harness used in tests

Worked example

case eval-invoice-041
 input      goal "reconcile March payouts for Northwind"
 fixtures   frozen tool responses (so the case is deterministic)
 assertions must call invoices.query before gst.fetch_filed
            must NOT call gst.file_return (read-only case)
            final answer contains the recomputed total 418200
 rubric     cites the filed return; states the variance; no advice
 thresholds grounding ≥ 0.9 (block) · success ≥ 0.8 (alert) · cost ≤ $0.60

At production scale

Freeze tool responses for offline cases. An eval that hits live systems is slow, flaky, and sometimes destructive — and its failures teach you about the upstream API rather than about your agent. Keep a separate, small set of live integration cases and run them on a different cadence.

Build the dataset from production failures. A hundred real cases beat a thousand synthetic ones, because synthetic cases are systematically easier and flatter every change you make.

Failure modes

  • No threshold. A number nobody acts on.
  • Live dependencies. Flaky evals get ignored, then deleted.
  • Synthetic-only datasets. Everything passes; production disagrees.
  • Judge-only scoring. Expensive and noisy where an assertion would do.

Choose it when

  • Before the first automated change. Evals are the specification.

02Goal evals#

ShippedOutcomeImpl8/10Criticality9/10

Score the whole trajectory against the goal: was it achieved, by an acceptable route, within budget — with the process scored separately from the outcome.

Mechanism

Four sub-scores, deliberately separate. Outcome: did the goal get met (rubric plus assertions). Process: was the plan sensible and the tool use appropriate. Efficiency: iterations, tokens, wall-clock against the class baseline. Compliance: were gates respected. A run can pass outcome and fail process — that is a warning about a route that happened to work.

In AgentVerse

  • app/evals/goal_score.pygoal scoring
  • app/evals/agent_score.pyagent-level aggregation
  • app/intelligence/eval_runner.pyEvalRunner / EvalSuiteRunner
  • app/db/models/eval.pypersisted results

Worked example

run g-9214
 outcome     0.92  correct total, cited, variance explained
 process     0.55  called invoices.query 6 times with the same arguments
                    (no caching, no dedup) and planned 8 steps for 4
 efficiency  0.61  4 iterations vs class baseline 2 · $0.71 vs $0.40
 compliance  1.00  filing gate respected
verdict  passes outcome, flagged on process — a candidate for the
         improvement loop, not an incident

At production scale

Scoring process separately is what catches the agent that gets the right answer expensively. Those runs are invisible to outcome-only evaluation and they are usually where the cost is. Set class baselines for iterations and cost so "expensive" is measurable rather than a feeling.

Failure modes

  • Outcome-only scoring. Ships inefficient and lucky trajectories.
  • One global baseline. Simple and expert goals judged the same.
  • Rubric drift. The rubric quietly relaxed to make numbers look better.

Choose it when

  • Any agent in production. This is the headline metric.

03Retrieval evals#

ShippedRetrievalImpl8/10Criticality9/10

Score retrieval independently of generation, because a good answer from bad context is luck and a bad answer from good context is a different bug.

Mechanism

Cases are query plus the chunk ids (or passages) that should be retrieved. Metrics: recall@k (was the right chunk in the candidate set), MRR (how high), containment (does a retrieved chunk actually contain the answer), and precision (how much of what was returned was useful). Run it per collection, because retrieval quality is a property of the corpus as much as the algorithm.

In AgentVerse

  • app/evals/rag_score.pyretrieval scoring
  • app/rag/evaluation.pystore-level evaluation
  • app/evals/dataset_builder.pylabelled query sets
  • app/observability/rag_trace.pytraces that supply the candidate sets

Worked example

collection acme/policies · 180 labelled queries

strategy            recall@5  recall@50  MRR   containment  precision@5
hybrid                 0.84      0.96    0.71     0.79         0.42
hybrid + rerank        0.84      0.96    0.88     0.79         0.68
fusion + rerank        0.91      0.98    0.90     0.86         0.64

reading: reranking does not change recall (it cannot) but transforms MRR
and precision. Fusion is what moved recall.

At production scale

Report recall at both a small and a large k. Recall@50 tells you the ceiling your reranker can reach; recall@5 tells you what the model actually sees. A gap between them is a ranking problem; a low recall@50 is a retrieval or corpus problem, and no reranking will help.

Failure modes

  • Only end-to-end evaluation. Cannot tell retrieval failures from generation failures.
  • Single k. Confuses ranking problems with recall problems.
  • Global rather than per-collection. One bad corpus hidden by nine good ones.

Choose it when

  • Any retrieval-augmented agent — this is the first eval to build.

04Tool relevance evals#

PartialProcessImpl7/10Criticality8/10

Score the trajectory's tool use: were the right tools called, with valid arguments, in a sensible order, without unnecessary calls?

Mechanism

Each case declares required tools, forbidden tools, and optionally an ordering constraint. Scoring combines four signals: correct selection, argument validity, redundancy (the same call repeated with the same arguments), and unnecessary calls. Forbidden-tool assertions are the important ones — they are how you test that a read-only case stays read-only.

In AgentVerse

  • app/evals/agent_score.pytrajectory scoring
  • app/agent/tool_calls.pythe validation whose failures are counted
  • app/mcp/tool_intelligence.pytool usage intelligence
  • app/sandbox_runtime/simulation_runner.pyrunning trajectories against mock tools

Worked example

case: "summarise last month's disputes" (read-only)
 required   disputes.query
 forbidden  disputes.update, notify.*, gst.file_return
 trajectory disputes.query ✓ · invoices.query (unnecessary, −)
            notify.slack ✗ FORBIDDEN — the agent "helpfully" posted a summary
score  selection 0.8 · arguments 1.0 · redundancy 1.0 · forbidden FAIL
verdict  case fails. This is exactly the failure that a read-only
         assertion exists to catch.

At production scale

Forbidden-tool assertions catch the class of failure that costs the most reputationally: an agent taking a well-meaning side action nobody asked for. Add one to every read-only case you have.

Score redundancy too. Repeated identical calls are both a cost line and a signal that caching or execution memory is not working.

Failure modes

  • Only checking the final answer. Side effects unmeasured.
  • No forbidden lists. Nothing tests restraint.
  • Over-strict ordering. Penalising valid alternative routes.

Choose it when

  • Any agent with write-capable tools.

05Safety evals#

ShippedSafetyImpl8/10Criticality10/10

A fixed adversarial corpus replayed on every change: injection, exfiltration, dangerous commands, PII leakage, jailbreaks — with zero tolerance for regression.

Mechanism

Cases are attacks with expected refusals or blocks. Categories: direct prompt injection, indirect injection through retrieved content and tool output, encoded payloads, data exfiltration attempts, dangerous command generation, PII in output, and cross-tenant probing. Each case asserts the specific control that should stop it, so a pass tells you which defence worked and a failure tells you which one broke.

In AgentVerse

  • app/evals/safety_score.pysafety scoring
  • app/enterprise/red_team.py, red_team_corpus.pythe adversarial corpus
  • app/guardrails_v2/engine.pythe controls under test
  • app/intelligence/indirect_injection.py, encoding_attacks.pyspecific detectors
  • app/api/red-team · frontend features/red-teamthe operator surface

Worked example

category                cases  expected control            pass
direct injection          40   guardrail scan               40
indirect (retrieved)      35   untrusted fencing + scan      34  ← 1 regression
indirect (tool output)    28   output scan                   28
encoded (base64/homoglyph)22   encoding detector             22
exfiltration attempts     18   exfil guard on tool args      18
dangerous commands        15   command detector + HITL       15
PII in output             20   redaction + output scan       19  ← 1 regression
cross-tenant probing      12   scope enforcement             12

verdict: BLOCKED. Two regressions, both zero-tolerance.

At production scale

The corpus only grows — every real incident and every near-miss becomes a permanent case. That ratchet is the point: safety evaluation is the one dimension where the baseline should never be relaxed and the dataset should never be pruned.

Run it on every prompt change, every model change, and every guardrail change. It is cheap relative to what it prevents, and prompt changes are the most common cause of safety regressions.

Failure modes

  • Stale corpus. Yesterday's attacks; add new ones as they appear.
  • Tolerance for regression. One relaxed case becomes a policy.
  • Testing only direct injection. Indirect is the harder and more common real vector.
  • Asserting outcomes, not controls. You learn it was blocked, not by what.

Choose it when

  • Always, before any external exposure.

06Accuracy and grounding evals#

ShippedAccuracyImpl8/10Criticality10/10

Two different questions: is the answer correct, and is every claim in it supported by the evidence provided? An answer can be right and ungrounded — which is a hallucination that happened to be lucky.

Mechanism

Accuracy compares the answer to a known-correct reference. Grounding decomposes the answer into individual claims and checks each against the retrieved evidence — deterministically where the claim contains an entity, number or quoted string, and with an entailment model where it is a paraphrase. Report both, and report the claim-level detail: "3 of 11 claims unsupported" is actionable, "grounding 0.73" is not.

In AgentVerse

  • app/intelligence/claim_decomposer.pyanswer → claims
  • app/intelligence/nli_checker.pyentailment per claim
  • app/evals/attribution_verifier.pycitation support
  • app/agent/grounding.pythe deterministic pre-pass used live
  • app/provenance/claim_trace.pyclaim-level provenance

Worked example

answer  "Refunds are accepted within 30 days [1]. Damaged goods are exempt
         [2]. Enterprise customers get 60 days."

claims  c1 30-day window          → [1] entailed        ✓
        c2 damaged goods exempt   → [2] entailed        ✓
        c3 enterprise 60 days     → no evidence          ✗ UNSUPPORTED

accuracy   0.67 against the reference (c3 is also factually wrong)
grounding  0.67 — and c3 is the one a customer would act on

At production scale

Run the deterministic check first and only escalate unresolved claims to the entailment model. Entity, number and quote matching resolves most claims for free, and the model call then handles the genuinely paraphrased minority — an order of magnitude cheaper than checking everything with a model.

Grounding is the dimension to hold at zero regression tolerance. It is the closest available proxy for "will this system tell a customer something untrue".

Failure modes

  • Answer-level grounding scores. Hide the one unsupported claim that matters.
  • Model-only checking. Expensive and less reliable than substring matching for numbers.
  • Grounding without accuracy. Faithfully reproducing a wrong document.

Choose it when

  • Any factual output. This is the core anti-hallucination measurement.

07SLA and latency evals#

PartialOperationalImpl7/10Criticality8/10

Latency is a product requirement per goal class, not a global average — and the percentile you promise is the one you must measure.

Mechanism

Define a latency budget per goal class (interactive chat, background reconciliation, overnight batch) and measure p50/p95/p99 against it, decomposed by phase: retrieval, model calls, tool round-trips, approval wait. Approval wait must be excluded from the machine-time SLA and reported separately, or a four-hour human decision makes every latency number meaningless.

In AgentVerse

  • app/observability/slo_tracker.pySLO tracking
  • app/api/sla.pySLA surface
  • app/observability/metrics.pyphase timings
  • app/optimization/latency_optimizer.pythe response
  • app/qos/*priority and backpressure, which shape latency under load

Worked example

goal class "chat answer" · budget p95 ≤ 4s
 phase           p50    p95
 retrieval      0.18s  0.42s
 model calls    1.10s  2.90s
 tools          0.30s  1.80s   ← p95 driven by one slow connector
 total          1.62s  4.90s   ✗ over budget

goal class "monthly reconciliation" · budget p95 ≤ 20 min machine time
 machine        6.2m   14.1m   ✓
 approval wait  —      3.4h    reported separately, not in the SLA

At production scale

Phase decomposition is what makes latency actionable. A p95 of five seconds tells you nothing; "p95 is five seconds because one connector's p95 is 1.8 seconds" tells you what to fix. Track per-tool latency percentiles alongside the goal-level numbers.

Failure modes

  • Means instead of percentiles. The mean hides the experience.
  • Approval time in the SLA. Numbers dominated by human availability.
  • One budget for all classes. Either too loose or impossible.

Choose it when

  • Any interactive surface, and any goal class with a business deadline.

08Cost evals#

ShippedOperationalImpl8/10Criticality9/10

Cost per goal, per class, per tenant — measured, budgeted, and evaluated as a first-class dimension alongside quality.

Mechanism

Accumulate real spend per run: model tokens at the model's price, embedding tokens, reranker inference, metered tool calls, and code-execution compute. Attribute it to the goal (including descendants for spawned sub-agents) and roll up per class and per tenant. Then compare against a class budget, and evaluate every quality change for its cost delta at the same time.

In AgentVerse

  • app/governance/cost.pythe cost controller and budgets
  • app/observability/cost_breakdown.py, cost_breakdown_api.pywhere the money went
  • app/intelligence/cost_tracker.pyper-run accumulation
  • app/governance/pricing.pyprice table
  • app/tenancy/billing.pytenant-facing accounting

Worked example

goal class "invoice reconciliation" · budget $0.50/goal

 component            $/goal   share
 planner calls        0.061    15%
 executor calls       0.213    51%   ← tool schemas are 38% of these tokens
 verifier calls       0.048    11%
 embeddings (query)   0.002     1%
 reranker             0.004     1%
 metered tools        0.061    15%
 code execution       0.026     6%
 total                0.415    within budget

after tool-schema narrowing: executor 0.213 → 0.121 · total 0.323

At production scale

Attribute descendant spend to the parent goal. Without it, multi-agent goals look cheap and the sum of your per-goal costs does not reconcile with your provider invoice — which is the moment finance stops trusting the numbers.

Publish cost per goal class to the teams that own those goals. Visibility changes behaviour faster than any optimiser.

Failure modes

  • Unattributed sub-agent spend. Costs that reconcile to nothing.
  • Stale price table. Reports that are confidently wrong.
  • Cost without quality. Optimising the wrong variable.
  • Ignoring tool and compute cost. Model tokens are often not the largest line.

Choose it when

  • From the first production goal. Retrofitting attribution is painful.

09Judge models#

ShippedMethodImpl8/10Criticality8/10

A model scoring another model's output against a rubric — indispensable for open-ended outputs, and only trustworthy once you have measured it against humans.

Mechanism

A judge receives the task, the output, the evidence, and an explicit rubric with a defined scale, and returns a score plus a reason. Four practices separate a usable judge from a random-number generator: a rubric with concrete anchors for each score level; a judge model different from the one being judged; position and verbosity bias controls (randomise order in pairwise comparisons); and periodic calibration against human labels.

In AgentVerse

  • app/agent/prompts.pyjudge_rubric_system
  • app/agent/consensus.py_run_judge() — the judge as a consensus vote
  • app/evals/model_score.pyjudge-based scoring
  • app/intelligence/verifier_calibration.pycalibration against labels
  • app/ai_router/role_policy.pyjudge is a distinct model role

Worked example

rubric anchors (grounding, 0–1)
 1.0  every claim traceable to cited evidence
 0.7  all material claims supported; one minor unsupported detail
 0.4  central claim supported, several unsupported additions
 0.0  central claim unsupported or contradicted by evidence

calibration on 200 human-labelled cases
 judge vs human agreement  0.86 (κ 0.71)
 judge bias                +0.06 — slightly generous, corrected in threshold
different model from the executor, order randomised in comparisons

At production scale

An uncalibrated judge is worse than no judge, because it produces confident numbers that drive decisions. Two hundred human labels is enough to establish agreement and bias, and re-checking quarterly is enough to catch drift when the judge model is updated.

Never judge with the same model that produced the output. Self-preference is measurable and large.

Failure modes

  • Self-judging. Systematic generosity.
  • Vague rubric. Scores that mean nothing across runs.
  • Verbosity bias. Longer answers rated higher.
  • Never calibrated. Precision without accuracy.

Choose it when

  • Outputs are open-ended and assertions cannot score them.
  • Do not use a judge where a deterministic check works.

10Multi-turn evals#

PartialMethodImpl7/10Criticality7/10

Conversations fail differently: context is lost, an earlier correction is forgotten, a constraint stated in turn two is violated in turn six.

Mechanism

A case is a scripted conversation with per-turn assertions and, crucially, cross-turn assertions: a constraint given early must hold late; a correction must persist; information from turn one must not be re-requested. Scoring per turn misses exactly the failures that make multi-turn agents frustrating.

In AgentVerse

  • app/evals/multi_turn_eval.pymulti-turn evaluation
  • app/chat/context.py, app/state_runtime/session_memory.pythe machinery under test
  • app/collaboration_runtime/preference_capture.pycaptured preferences that must persist

Worked example

turn 1  "only consider the German entity"        → acknowledged
turn 2  "what's the notice period?"               → DE answer ✓
turn 3  "and the probation period?"               → DE answer ✓
turn 4  "actually make it 3 months not 2"         → correction accepted
turn 5  "summarise what we've agreed"             → says 2 months ✗
                                                     correction lost
turn 6  "what about holidays?"                    → US answer ✗
                                                     entity constraint lost

cross-turn assertions catch both; per-turn scoring would pass turns 5 and 6
as fluent, plausible answers

At production scale

Constraint persistence is the highest-value cross-turn assertion, and the most commonly broken. It fails for a structural reason: constraints stated in conversation live in working memory, which is exactly what compaction discards. If your product has multi-turn conversations, extract stated constraints into durable state rather than trusting the transcript.

Failure modes

  • Per-turn scoring only. Misses the real failures.
  • No constraint persistence tests. The most common complaint, unmeasured.
  • Scripted-only conversations. Real users branch; include a few messy cases.

Choose it when

  • Any conversational surface.

11Online versus offline evaluation#

ShippedMethodImpl8/10Criticality9/10

Offline evals gate changes; online evals detect drift. You need both, and they answer different questions.

Mechanism

Offline: fixed dataset, frozen fixtures, deterministic, run in CI on every change. Fast, cheap, comparable over time, and blind to anything not in the dataset. Online: scoring real production runs continuously — sampled judges, deterministic grounding checks on every answer, user signals like acceptance and correction. Slow to attribute, expensive at full coverage, and the only thing that sees the real distribution.

The bridge between them is the dataset builder: online failures become offline cases, so every production surprise becomes a permanent regression test.

In AgentVerse

  • app/intelligence/eval_suite.pyoffline suites
  • app/evals/runtime_scorecard.pyonline scoring
  • app/evals/dataset_builder.pyonline → offline
  • app/api/replay.pyreplaying production runs
  • app/observability/runtime_decision_trace.pythe record that makes replay possible

Worked example

offline (CI, every commit)
 420 cases · frozen fixtures · 6 min · blocks merge on regression

online (continuous)
 grounding check    100% of answers (deterministic, cheap)
 judge scoring      2% sample (metered)
 user signals       acceptance, edits, escalations — all runs
 alarm              grounding p50 drops 0.82 → 0.71 over 3 days

bridge  the 31 online failures became 31 offline cases, and the offline
        suite would now catch the same regression before merge

At production scale

Sample judges, but check grounding on everything. The deterministic grounding pre-pass is cheap enough to run on every answer, and it is the fastest detector of a retrieval or corpus regression — usually hours before a user complains.

User signals are the ground truth nothing else replaces: an edit to an agent's draft is a labelled failure, free of charge.

Failure modes

  • Offline only. Confident in CI, drifting in production.
  • Online only. No gate; regressions ship and are found later.
  • No bridge. The same failure recurs because it never became a case.
  • Full-coverage judging. An eval bill larger than the product's.

Choose it when

  • Both, always. Offline first, because it gates.

12Certification and readiness#

PartialGateImpl7/10Criticality8/10

A named, recorded decision that a specific agent, strategy or retrieval pipeline is fit to serve production traffic — with the evidence attached.

Mechanism

Certification binds a version to an eval result: this agent configuration, at this version, passed these suites at these scores, on this date, approved by this person. Uncertified configurations may run in a sandbox or a lab but cannot be promoted to serve real tenants. The same machinery applies to orchestration strategies and retrieval pipelines, which is what makes a large catalogue of options safe to offer.

In AgentVerse

  • app/evals/certification_policy.pywhat certification requires
  • app/orchestration/strategy_certification.py, strategy_readiness.pystrategy certification
  • app/rag/certification.py, readiness.pyretrieval pipeline certification
  • app/sandbox_runtime/certification.pysandbox certification
  • app/runtime_readiness/readiness_gate.pythe runtime gate
  • app/mcp/certification.py, certification_manifest.pyconnector certification

Worked example

certificate agent fin-ops@v12
 suites   goal(0.89) retrieval(0.91) grounding(0.86) safety(1.00)
          latency p95 14.1m · cost $0.32/goal
 gates    all pass · safety zero-regression confirmed
 approved r.iyer (finance eng lead) · 2026-09-05
 scope    tenants on plan ≥ starter · goal classes [reconciliation, filing]
 expiry   90 days or on model change, whichever first

fin-ops@v13 (uncertified) runs in the lab only

At production scale

Certification is how you offer a large catalogue — eighteen retrieval strategies, dozens of agent patterns, hundreds of connectors — without every combination being a liability. Expire certificates on model changes: a configuration certified against one model version is not certified against its successor.

Failure modes

  • Certification as paperwork. A form with no evidence attached.
  • No expiry. Certificates that outlive the models they were measured against.
  • Uncertified paths reachable. The gate exists but can be bypassed.

Choose it when

  • Multiple configurations, multiple tenants, or any regulated deployment.

What is missing here

  • Automatic dataset growth from user signals. Edits and escalations are the cheapest labels available and are not systematically converted into cases.
  • Statistical rigour in reporting. Scores are reported as point values without confidence intervals, which invites over-reading small differences.
  • Eval cost accounting. Nothing tracks what evaluation itself costs, which is how judge-based scoring quietly becomes a major line item.
  • Cross-tenant eval sharing. Every tenant's failures stay private, so common failure modes are rediscovered repeatedly.
  • Trajectory-level diffing. No tooling to show what changed between two runs of the same case beyond the final score.

Hallucination handling
CH 18III · Context & quality

Hallucination handling

Grounding, claim decomposition, NLI, calibration, fail-closed.

Concepts
11
Mean impl
7.6
Mean criticality
9.0
Shipped
6
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

In a chatbot, hallucination means a wrong sentence. In an agent, it means a wrong action — and the four kinds are structurally different problems with different defences:

KindLooks likeDefence that actually works
Fabricated factA number or clause that is in no documentGrounding check per claim
Fabricated citationA plausible reference to a chunk that does not existOnly emit pipeline-assigned ids; verify
Fabricated toolA call to a tool or argument that does not existRegistry validation before dispatch
Fabricated success"Done" when nothing happenedVerify against tool results, not narration

The fourth is the dangerous one and the one prompt engineering cannot touch. An agent that reports success it did not achieve corrupts downstream state, satisfies its own verifier if the verifier reads its narration, and is only caught by checking evidence.

The defences

01Retrieval grounding and the confidence floor#

PartialPreventionImpl7/10Criticality10/10

The cheapest anti-hallucination control is refusing to answer from context that scored below a calibrated threshold.

Mechanism

Before generation, check the retrieval result: is the top score above the floor, is there a meaningful gap between the best and the fifth candidate, did the query's key terms appear at all? Below threshold, the honest paths are to widen the search, try another source, or say the corpus does not contain the answer — not to hand the model three weak chunks and an instruction to be helpful.

Then instruct explicitly: answer only from the provided evidence; if it is insufficient, say so. That instruction only works if the pipeline actually gives the model the option to fail.

In AgentVerse

  • app/rag/agentic/patterns/corrective.pygrade and branch
  • app/rag/agentic/fallback_chain.pyordered alternatives ending in "not found"
  • app/rag/agentic/context_gap_detector.pyGapReport
  • app/agent/graph.pyrag_remediate — the agent-level branch

Rated 7 because thresholds are configured rather than continuously calibrated per collection (chapter 6).

Worked example

query "what is the APAC revenue recognition policy?"
retrieval  top score 0.28 · floor 0.50 · gap 0.03 (flat distribution)
without a floor
  three weak chunks about global policy → confident answer about APAC
  that is a synthesis of documents which never mention APAC
with a floor
  "No APAC-specific policy is indexed. The global policy POL-204 may
   apply. Searched: policies, finance, legal."

At production scale

Most measured hallucinations in retrieval-augmented systems trace back to weak retrieval that nobody gated. Fixing the floor typically removes more hallucination than any change to the generation step, and it costs nothing at inference time.

Failure modes

  • No floor. The system always answers.
  • Uncalibrated floor. Either refuses too much or admits junk.
  • No "not found" affordance. The instruction says one thing, the pipeline forces another.

Choose it when

  • Always, and first.

02Deterministic grounding#

ShippedDetectionImpl8/10Criticality10/10

Extract the concrete things — numbers, ids, dates, quoted strings, URLs — and check each against the evidence by substring. Free, fast, and catches the majority of fabrications.

Mechanism

A regex pass pulls entity-shaped tokens out of the output, then each is checked for presence in the tool outputs and retrieved chunks. An invoice number, a total, an account id or a quoted clause either appears in the evidence or it was invented — no model judgement required. Only the claims that survive this pass (paraphrases and inferences) need an entailment model.

Two-pass ordering is the whole design: the cheap pass resolves most claims, so the expensive pass runs on a fraction of them.

In AgentVerse

  • app/agent/grounding.pyextract_claims(), check_grounding(), deterministic_ground(), GroundingChecker, annotate_ungrounded()
  • app/agent/graph.pyruns after each executor step
  • app/intelligence/claim_decomposer.pystructured claim extraction

Worked example

output  "Invoice INV-2024-8891 for ₹41,200 was settled on 12 March by
         Razorpay under contract C-2291."

extracted   INV-2024-8891 · 41200 · 2026-03-12 · Razorpay · C-2291
checked     INV-2024-8891  ✓ tool output step 2
            41200          ✓ tool output step 2
            2026-03-12     ✓ tool output step 2
            Razorpay       ✓ chunk [3]
            C-2291         ✗ NOT PRESENT anywhere    ← fabricated
action  annotate as ungrounded; step fails verification; replan or escalate

At production scale

Run this on every step and every final answer — it is a regex pass over a few kilobytes and it is the highest-yield check in the system. It is also the ideal online metric: cheap enough for 100% coverage, which makes it the fastest detector of a corpus or retrieval regression (chapter 10).

Escalate to the model-based check only for high-risk steps and unresolved claims. Checking everything with a model costs more than the generation did.

Failure modes

  • Formatting mismatch. "₹41,200" versus "41200.00" — normalise numbers and dates before comparing.
  • Paraphrase blindness. It cannot judge "roughly a third" against "31%"; that is what entailment is for.
  • Checking against the wrong evidence. Compare only against evidence actually in the prompt.

Choose it when

  • Always. This is the best value in the chapter.

03Claim decomposition#

PartialDetectionImpl7/10Criticality8/10

Split the answer into atomic, independently checkable claims — because "the answer is 83% grounded" is not actionable and "claim 7 of 9 is unsupported" is.

Mechanism

Decompose into single-predicate statements, each carrying its span in the original text so a failure can be localised and, if necessary, the span removed or flagged. Claims are then classified: factual (must be grounded), inferential (must be marked as inference), and rhetorical (no grounding required). Only the first class gates the answer.

In AgentVerse

  • app/intelligence/claim_decomposer.pyClaimDecomposer
  • app/agent/grounding.pyextract_claims_structured(), Claim
  • app/provenance/claim_trace.pyper-claim provenance

Worked example

"Refunds are accepted within 30 days, though damaged goods are exempt,
 so you should be fine claiming next week."

c1 factual     refunds accepted within 30 days        → [1] ✓
c2 factual     damaged goods exempt from the window   → [2] ✓
c3 inferential the user's claim next week qualifies   → depends on c1 and
                                                          a date the evidence
                                                          does not contain ✗
action  c3 is an inference presented as advice — flagged, rewritten as
        "if your delivery was within the last 30 days, this would qualify"

At production scale

The claim class that causes real trouble is the inferential one delivered as fact — "so you should be fine". Distinguishing it and forcing it to be marked as conditional is a small change with a disproportionate effect on how much a user can rely on the output.

Failure modes

  • Over-decomposition. Twenty trivial claims per paragraph; check cost explodes.
  • Lost spans. A failed claim you cannot locate in the text.
  • Mis-classification. Advice treated as rhetoric and left unchecked.

Choose it when

  • Answers are multi-sentence and consequential.

04Entailment (NLI) checking#

PartialDetectionImpl7/10Criticality8/10

For claims that survive the deterministic pass, ask a model a narrow question: does this evidence entail this claim, contradict it, or neither?

Mechanism

Pair each unresolved claim with its candidate evidence and classify the relation as entailment, contradiction, or neutral. The narrowness is what makes it reliable — it is a three-way classification on a short pair, not an open-ended judgement, so a small model does it well and cheaply. Contradiction is a stronger signal than neutral and should be treated more severely: neutral means unsupported, contradiction means the evidence says otherwise.

In AgentVerse

  • app/intelligence/nli_checker.pyNLIChecker
  • app/evals/attribution_verifier.pyAttributionVerifier — citation support
  • app/agent/grounding.pycheck_async() — the escalation path

Worked example

claim     "most disputes are resolved within a week"
evidence  "of 412 disputes, ۲۸۹ closed within 5 business days"
           (289/412 = 70%)
verdict   ENTAILED (0.86) — "most" is supported

claim     "disputes are usually resolved same-day"
evidence  same
verdict   CONTRADICTED (0.91) — treated as a hard failure, not merely
           unsupported

At production scale

Use a small dedicated model, not the generation model. This is a classification task where a compact model matches a large one and costs a fraction, and using the generator introduces self-preference. Batch the pairs — a dozen claim/evidence pairs in one call is normal.

Failure modes

  • Wrong evidence paired. A claim checked against an irrelevant chunk reads as neutral.
  • Neutral treated as fine. Unsupported is not supported.
  • Cost creep. Checking every claim rather than the unresolved ones.

Choose it when

  • Answers contain paraphrase and inference — which is most prose answers.

05Citation verification#

ShippedDetectionImpl8/10Criticality9/10

Check two things about every citation: that the id exists, and that the cited evidence supports the claim attached to it. Both fail in practice.

Mechanism

Existence is a lookup against the citation map the pipeline built — an id the model invented is rejected immediately. Support is the entailment check applied per citation. A citation that exists but does not support its claim is the subtler failure: it looks rigorous and is wrong, and it is common when a model attaches the nearest available id to a sentence it generated independently.

In AgentVerse

  • app/context/citation_manager.pythe authoritative id map
  • app/evals/attribution_verifier.pysupport verification
  • app/agent/synthesis.pyCitation, CitedAnswer
  • app/provenance/provenance_verifier.pyprovenance verification

Worked example

answer citations
 [1] exists ✓ · supports its claim ✓
 [2] exists ✓ · does NOT support (chunk is about shipping, claim about
      refunds)                                        ← attached, not derived
 [4] DOES NOT EXIST — only [1]-[3] were provided      ← fabricated
action  strip [4] and its claim; re-attach or flag [2]; if the answer
        cannot stand without them, fail the step

At production scale

Track citation precision — the share of citations that both exist and support their claim — as a product metric. It is the number that determines whether users learn to trust the citations or learn to ignore them, and once they ignore them the whole grounding apparatus stops delivering value.

Failure modes

  • Existence-only checking. Misses the attached-not-derived case.
  • Shipping unverified citations. Manufactured trust.
  • Stripping silently. The user sees a claim with no source and no warning.

Choose it when

  • Any output that cites.

06Tool name and argument validation#

ShippedPreventionImpl9/10Criticality10/10

The structural backstop: a call to a tool that is not in this tenant's registry never dispatches, and arguments are schema-validated before anything executes.

Mechanism

Four steps between the model's output and a real side effect. Extract the intended call from possibly-malformed output. Repair obvious argument problems — type coercion, defaults, dropping hallucinated fields. Validate the name against the live registry and the arguments against the tool's schema, including enums and formats. Classify risk and route accordingly.

This is the layer that makes prompt injection survivable: a model persuaded to call admin.delete_tenant still has to get past a registry that has no such tool for this tenant.

In AgentVerse

  • app/agent/tool_calls.pyextract_tool_call(), repair_tool_call_arguments(), validate_tool_name()
  • app/agent/tool_risk.pyclassify_tool_risk()
  • app/agent/tool_context.pythe permitted tool view
  • app/mcp/registry.py, client.pythe registry and dispatch
  • app/agent/exfil_guard.pycheck_tool_args_for_exfil() before write tools

Worked example

model output  {"tool":"github.merge_and_deploy",
               "args":{"repo":"acme/api","confirm":"yes","force":true}}

extract   ok
validate  github.merge_and_deploy NOT IN REGISTRY
          → corrective turn listing the real names:
            github.create_pr, github.merge_pr, deploy.trigger
retry     {"tool":"github.merge_pr","args":{"repo":"acme/api","pr":3312}}
validate  name ✓ · args ✓ (force/confirm dropped as unknown fields)
risk      write_high → approval gate

At production scale

Never resolve a tool name from text the model read — only from the registry. That single rule closes the path from "a document told the agent to call X" to an actual call. And keep the offered tool list exactly equal to the permitted list: a tool visible in the prompt will eventually be called.

Track hallucinated-tool rate per model. It is a useful model-quality signal and it rises sharply when a prompt change makes the tool list confusing.

Failure modes

  • Dispatch before validation. The whole point.
  • Accepting unknown arguments. A pass-through that reaches the API.
  • Offering unauthorised tools. A prompt-level permission bypass.
  • Repair that changes intent. Coercion is fine; guessing a missing required argument is not.

Choose it when

  • Always. This is not optional in any tool-calling system.

07Verifier checks against evidence#

ShippedDetectionImpl9/10Criticality10/10

The only defence against fabricated success: judge the step by the tool results, never by the agent's account of what it did.

Mechanism

The verifier receives the success criterion and the raw evidence, and deliberately not the executor's reasoning. It answers a specific question — does this evidence satisfy this criterion — and returns a verdict with a diagnosis. Where the criterion is checkable deterministically (a record exists, a total matches), that check runs first and the model is only needed for the judgement calls.

In AgentVerse

  • app/agent/nodes/verifier_mixin.pythe node
  • app/agent/schemas.pyparse_verifier_verdict()
  • app/agent/grounding.pythe deterministic pre-check
  • app/intelligence/verifier_calibration.pycalibration against labelled outcomes

Worked example

executor narration  "I have filed the amendment successfully."
tool result         {"error":"period locked","ack_no":null}

verifier shown narration only   → PASS   ← fabricated success accepted
verifier shown evidence only    → FAIL   "no acknowledgement number;
                                          error indicates the period is
                                          locked"  → replan or escalate

At production scale

This single design choice — evidence, not narration — prevents the most damaging agent failure there is, because fabricated success propagates: downstream steps assume the filing happened, the goal completes, and a human discovers it weeks later.

Calibrate the verifier. A verifier that passes almost everything has stopped being a control, and the only way to know is to measure it against labelled outcomes.

Failure modes

  • Narration in the verifier prompt. The verifier agrees with the actor.
  • No explicit criterion. Nothing to verify against.
  • Uncalibrated leniency. Verification theatre.

Choose it when

  • Always, and never let the actor's reasoning in.

08Confidence estimation#

PartialSignalImpl6/10Criticality8/10

A useful confidence number comes from measurable signals — agreement, grounding, retrieval strength — not from asking the model how sure it is.

Mechanism

Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and cheaply gamed. Better signals, combined: retrieval strength (top score and gap), grounding rate (share of claims supported), agreement across samples or verifiers, and historical success for this goal class and tool set. Combine into a score, then calibrate it against outcomes so that "0.8" actually means roughly 80% correct.

The output is only useful if something acts on it: below a threshold, escalate to consensus, to a stronger model, or to a human.

In AgentVerse

  • app/intelligence/verifier_calibration.pycalibration
  • app/agent/consensus.pyagreement as a confidence signal
  • app/agent/patterns/self_consistency.pysample agreement
  • app/memory/tool_reliability.pyhistorical success rates
  • app/observability/runtime_decision_trace.pywhere the score is recorded

Rated 6: the component signals all exist and are recorded, but there is no single calibrated confidence score driving escalation across the platform.

Worked example

signal                       value  weight
retrieval top score           0.88    0.3
retrieval gap (1st vs 5th)    0.31    0.1
grounding rate (claims)       1.00    0.4
self-consistency agreement    0.80    0.1
tool historical success        0.96    0.1
combined                      0.91  → proceed

same goal, weak variant: grounding 0.67, agreement 0.60 → 0.68
→ below the 0.75 escalation threshold → consensus verification

At production scale

Calibration is what makes this worth building: an uncalibrated confidence score encourages exactly the wrong behaviour, because people trust the high numbers. Measure predicted confidence against observed correctness on a sample, and publish the curve rather than the number.

Failure modes

  • Model self-report. Uniformly high and uninformative.
  • Uncalibrated combination. Arbitrary weights producing arbitrary confidence.
  • Confidence with no consequence. A number nobody routes on.

Choose it when

  • You need selective escalation rather than gating everything.

09Output anomaly detection#

PartialDetectionImpl7/10Criticality7/10

Catch outputs that are structurally unlike what this agent normally produces — sudden length changes, unexpected languages, secret-shaped strings, refusal spikes.

Mechanism

Statistical rather than semantic: track distributions of output length, language, format compliance, refusal rate, and the presence of credential-shaped or PII-shaped strings. Flag deviations. It catches what claim-checking misses — a compromised prompt, a model change, a template that started leaking internal content — because those show up as shape changes before they show up as wrong facts.

In AgentVerse

  • app/intelligence/output_anomaly.pyanomaly detection
  • app/guardrails_v2/streaming_guard.pychecks on streamed output
  • app/data_classification/classifier.pysensitive-content detection in output
  • app/observability/alert_router.pywhere the alert goes

Worked example

agent support-bot, normal distribution
 length 180–620 tokens · language en · refusal rate 2% · format compliance 99%

anomalies detected
 length 4,100 tokens          ← the agent dumped a whole document
 language de                  ← plausible, but new for this agent
 secret-shaped string         ← "sk-…" in the output: BLOCK immediately
 refusal rate 2% → 31%        ← a prompt change over-triggered a guardrail

At production scale

Anomaly detection is the layer that catches problems you did not anticipate, which is why it belongs alongside the specific checks rather than instead of them. The refusal-rate signal in particular is a fast detector of prompt regressions that no eval covered.

Secret-shaped strings in output should be a hard block, not an alert. There is no benign reason for a credential pattern in an agent's answer.

Failure modes

  • Baselines too tight. Alert fatigue, then ignored alerts.
  • Global baselines. Per-agent distributions differ enormously.
  • Alerting instead of blocking. For credentials and PII, block.

Choose it when

  • Any production agent with external output.

10Escalation under uncertainty#

ShippedEscalationImpl8/10Criticality10/10

When the checks disagree or confidence is low, the answer is not "try harder" — it is consensus, then a human, and never silent completion.

Mechanism

An ordered ladder with a fail-closed end. Low confidence on a low-risk goal: retry with corrective retrieval. Low confidence on a high-risk goal: consensus verification across independent models. Disagreement in consensus: human approval. Human unavailable within the deadline: the goal ends as requiring attention, not as complete.

The last step is the one that matters. Any ladder whose final rung is "proceed anyway" is not a control.

In AgentVerse

  • app/agent/consensus.pyrequires_consensus(), ConsensusVerifier — majority or HITL
  • app/governance/hitl.pythe approval queue
  • app/recovery/escalation_policy.pythe ladder
  • app/collaboration_runtime/clarification.pyasking a question instead of guessing
  • app/agent/debate.pydebate as a triage device for contested judgement

Worked example

goal  "file the amendment"  risk=critical  confidence 0.68

1 corrective retrieval → confidence 0.74, still below 0.85 for critical
2 consensus            → primary PASS · cross-model FAIL · judge FAIL
3 majority FAIL        → waiting_human with all three rationales
4 no approval in 24h   → goal ends as needs_attention, not complete
                          and definitely not filed

At production scale

Escalation rate is a tuning signal, not a failure: too low and you are letting uncertain actions through; too high and the approval queue becomes a backlog nobody services. Watch both the rate and the queue depth, and remember that an unserviced approval queue is an outage that pages nobody.

Failure modes

  • Escalation to nowhere. A queue with no owner.
  • Proceed-on-timeout. Fail closed instead.
  • Escalating everything. Approvers stop reading.
  • Losing the rationales. The human needs the disagreement, not just the verdict.

Choose it when

  • Any irreversible or regulated action.

11Observability for hallucination debugging#

ShippedOperationsImpl8/10Criticality9/10

To debug a hallucination you need four things: what was retrieved, what was in the prompt, what the model returned, and which check fired. Anything less is speculation.

Mechanism

Correlate by goal and step: the retrieval trace (strategy, filters, candidates, scores), the prompt recipe (variant, context item ids, budget decisions), the model trace (model, parameters, tokens), and the check results (grounding per claim, citation verification, validation failures). One correlation id ties them together so a single query answers "why did it say that".

In AgentVerse

  • app/observability/rag_trace.pyretrieval trace
  • app/observability/model_trace.pymodel calls
  • app/observability/runtime_decision_trace.pydecisions and their reasons
  • app/context/context_pipeline.pyprompt composition
  • app/provenance/claim_trace.pyper-claim provenance
  • app/api/replay.pyreplay a run

Worked example

complaint  "the agent invented a 60-day enterprise refund window"

trace, goal g-9310 step 2
 retrieval  strategy=hybrid · filters {collection:policies}
            top 5 scores 0.71 0.68 0.51 0.44 0.41
            → note: no chunk mentions "enterprise"
 prompt     recipe executor@v7 · items [c#41 c#12 c#88 M4]
            → M4 is a memory: "enterprise contracts often extend windows"
 model      claude-… temp 0.2
 checks     grounding: 2 of 3 claims supported;
            claim 3 ("60 days") UNGROUNDED — flagged, but the flag was
            recorded as a warning rather than blocking
root cause  an inferential memory presented alongside evidence, plus a
            grounding flag that did not gate. Two fixes, both specific.

At production scale

The value of this is measured in minutes-to-root-cause. With traces, the above takes one query and produces two concrete fixes. Without them, it becomes a debate about model quality that ends in "let's use a bigger model", which costs more and fixes nothing.

Sample full prompts and retain them only for failures; keep recipes for everything. That keeps the storage and privacy cost proportionate while preserving the debugging path.

Failure modes

  • No correlation id. Four separate logs that cannot be joined.
  • Warnings that do not gate. The check fired and nothing happened — exactly the case above.
  • Traces without scores. You see what was retrieved, not why.

Choose it when

  • Before your first hallucination complaint.

What is missing here

  • A single calibrated confidence score. The signals exist separately; nothing combines and calibrates them into one number that drives escalation platform-wide.
  • Contradiction detection across sources. Nothing flags that two retrieved documents disagree, which is a common cause of confidently wrong synthesis.
  • Grounding for non-text output. Claims derived from a chart or a screenshot have no equivalent of the deterministic check.
  • User-facing uncertainty. Confidence is recorded internally but rarely surfaced in the answer, which is where it would do the most good.
  • Hallucination rate as a published SLO. Measured internally, not offered as a tenant-visible service level.
