CH 11IV · Safety & control

Observability

Logs, metrics, traces, decision traces, and the incident playbook.

Concepts
9
Mean impl
8.0
Mean criticality
8.6
Shipped
7
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

An agent is a distributed system that also makes non-deterministic decisions, which means it needs everything ordinary observability provides — logs, metrics, traces — plus a layer ordinary systems lack: a record of why the agent decided what it decided. When a goal costs $14 or takes an unexpected action, the question is never "which service was slow" but "why did the planner choose that, what did it retrieve, what did the verifier see". That is a decision trace, and it is the difference between debugging an agent and guessing about one.

The organising principle is one correlation id, many linked traces: a goal id ties together its logs, its metrics, its decision trace, its RAG traces, its cost breakdown, and its audit entries, so any one question is one query rather than a cross-reference across six systems.

The signals

01Structured logging#

ShippedSignalImpl9/10Criticality9/10

Every log line is a queryable event with the goal id, tenant, and step — never a free-text string — so "show me everything that happened in goal g-8891" is one filter.

Mechanism

A logger produces structured records with consistent fields: correlation id, tenant, agent, goal, step, level, and event-specific data. Sensitive values are redacted at the logging boundary, not hoped to be absent. The logger is one of the most-connected nodes in the whole system precisely because everything logs through it.

In AgentVerse

  • app/observability/logging.pyget_logger() — the structured logger (a top hub node, 575 edges)
  • app/tenancy/context.pycontext fields injected into every line
  • app/data_classification/redaction.pyredaction at the log boundary

Worked example

{"ts":"...", "level":"info", "corr":"g-8891", "tenant":"acme",
 "agent":"fin-ops", "step":3, "event":"tool_call",
 "tool":"gst.fetch_filed", "risk":"read", "ms":180}
query: corr="g-8891" → the whole goal's timeline, ordered, in one view

At production scale

Structured-first is not optional at scale: grepping free text across a fleet does not work, and the redaction-at-the-boundary discipline is what keeps customer data out of a log that a hundred engineers can read. Sample verbose events; keep errors and decisions at full fidelity.

Failure modes

  • Free-text logs. Ungreppable at scale.
  • PII in logs. Redact at the boundary, not by convention.
  • Missing correlation id. Events that cannot be joined.

Choose it when

  • Always.

02Metrics#

ShippedSignalImpl8/10Criticality9/10

The numbers that go on a dashboard and drive alerts: goals per minute, success rate, iterations, cost, latency percentiles, tool success — labelled by tenant, agent, and goal class.

Mechanism

Counters, gauges and histograms emitted at every meaningful event, with labels that let you slice by the dimensions that matter. The agent-specific metrics — iterations per goal, stall-detection rate, pattern set used, delegation rate — are as important as the infrastructure ones, because they are the leading indicators of cost and quality regressions.

In AgentVerse

  • app/observability/metrics.pymetric definitions and emission
  • app/observability/health.pyhealth metrics
  • app/scaling/tasks.pyper-stage counters

Worked example

agent_goals_total{tenant,agent,status}
agent_iterations{quantile="0.99"}          → cost regression detector
rag_strategy_delegations_total{from,to}    → a capability broke
ingestion_quality_drops_total{reason}      → a parser regressed
approval_queue_depth{tenant}               → an unserviced backlog

At production scale

The three agent metrics that belong on the main dashboard: p99 iterations (cost), stall-detection rate (broken retrieval or tools), and approval queue depth (an outage that pages nobody). Slice everything by goal class — aggregates hide the regression in one slice that moved thirty points.

Failure modes

  • Aggregate-only. Regressions hidden in slices.
  • Missing agent metrics. Infra green, agents misbehaving.
  • Label explosion. Per-goal-id labels blowing up cardinality.

Choose it when

  • Always.

03Distributed tracing#

ShippedSignalImpl8/10Criticality8/10

Spans across the whole request — API, queue, worker, model calls, tool calls, database — so latency is attributable to a stage rather than guessed.

Mechanism

OpenTelemetry spans propagate the trace context from the API through the queue into the worker and down each model and tool call. The trace shows where wall-clock actually went — usually a tool round-trip or a serial chain of model calls, rarely the place people assume — and exports to a backend like Jaeger.

In AgentVerse

  • app/observability/tracing.pyOTel setup and propagation
  • app/workflow/otel.pyworkflow-step spans
  • app/observability/model_trace.pyper-model-call spans
  • app/ingestion/pipeline.pya span per ingestion stage

Worked example

trace for goal g-8891 (total 41s)
 api.submit            12ms
 queue wait            1.2s   ← queue depth on the enterprise queue
 worker.plan           2.9s
 worker.execute
   tool gst.fetch      8.1s   ← the real cost, one slow connector
   tool invoices.query 0.3s
 worker.verify         1.8s
attributes the 41s precisely; the fix is the connector, not the model

At production scale

Trace context must survive the queue hop, or the worker's spans float detached from the request — the single most common tracing gap in agent systems, because the Celery boundary is where propagation is easy to drop. Sample traces (1–5%) plus all errors keeps the backend affordable.

Failure modes

  • Context lost at the queue. Detached worker spans.
  • Model/tool calls not spanned. The interesting part invisible.

Choose it when

  • Any multi-service or async execution — so all of them.

04Runtime decision traces#

ShippedSignalImpl8/10Criticality10/10

The agent-specific signal: a record of every decision the runtime made — which pattern, which model, which tools, which policy constraints — with the reason for each.

Mechanism

Each decision point records its inputs, its choice, and its reason: the classifier's output, the assembled pattern set and why, the model selected per role, the policy constraints applied, the routing decision. This is what turns "the agent did something weird" into "the classifier scored this expert, so the assembler added ToT and self-consistency, which is why it cost $4". Without it, agent behaviour is a black box that invites the useless conclusion "use a bigger model".

In AgentVerse

  • app/observability/runtime_decision_trace.pythe decision trace
  • app/orchestration/decision_trace.pySelectionDecision — orchestration choices
  • app/observability/pattern_trace.pywhich patterns ran
  • app/policy_runtime/policy_trace.pyPolicyTrace — policy decisions
  • app/explainability_runtime/decision_explainer.pyhuman-readable explanation

Worked example

decision trace g-8891
 classify   complexity=expert domain=analytical risk=high conf=0.88
 assemble   +CoT +reflection +self_refine +self_consistency +ToT +hitl
            reason: expert(HIGH) + analytical(HIGH) + risk=high(CRITICAL)
 models     planner=large executor=large verifier=mid
 policy     denied admin.*, gated write_high, cost ceiling $8
 route      agent fin-ops (connector match + 96% history)
"why did this cost $4?" → the six reasoning patterns, and here is the rule
for each

At production scale

The decision trace is the highest-value observability investment specific to agents. It converts cost and behaviour investigations from speculation into lookups, and it is what the explainability surface reads to answer an operator's or a regulator's "why". Make every decision record its reason — an unexplained choice is a debugging dead end.

Failure modes

  • Choices without reasons. You see what, not why.
  • Decisions not recorded. The black box returns.

Choose it when

  • Any agent whose behaviour or cost you will ever need to explain.

05RAG traces and cost breakdown#

ShippedSignalImpl8/10Criticality8/10

Two specialised traces: retrieval (strategy, filters, candidates, scores, delegation) and cost (tokens and spend per model, tool, and phase) — the two questions asked most after "why is it wrong" and "why is it expensive".

Mechanism

The RAG trace records each retrieval leg with its scores and any delegation, so a retrieval failure is diagnosable as recall, precision, or coverage (chapter 6). The cost breakdown attributes every token and every metered call to a component, so a cost spike points at a section — usually tool schemas or an expensive reasoning pattern — rather than at a vague "the model".

In AgentVerse

  • app/observability/rag_trace.pyretrieval trace
  • app/rag/agentic/rag_trace.pyagentic retrieval trace
  • app/observability/cost_breakdown.py, cost_breakdown_api.pycost attribution
  • app/observability/model_trace.pyper-call model usage

Worked example

RAG trace  strategy=hybrid→rerank · filters{policies} · 312→50→8 · scores
           0.94..0.41 · no delegation
cost break planner $0.06 · executor $0.21 (schemas 38%) · verifier $0.05
           embeddings $0.002 · tools $0.06 · total $0.38
two lookups answer "why wrong" (recall/precision/coverage) and "why
expensive" (which component)

At production scale

These two traces close most agent investigations. The cost breakdown in particular ends the recurring argument about model choice by showing that tool schemas, not the model, are 38% of the executor spend — a fixable, non-model problem. Surface both to tenants for their own goals; cost transparency changes behaviour.

Failure modes

  • Traces without scores. What was retrieved, not why.
  • Cost without attribution. A total nobody can act on.

Choose it when

  • Any retrieval-augmented or cost-sensitive agent.

06Goal events, SSE, and worker events#

ShippedDeliveryImpl9/10Criticality8/10

The live view: every step of a goal streams to the frontend as it happens, over Redis pub/sub and Server-Sent Events, so an operator watches execution rather than polling for a result.

Mechanism

The agent emits events at every transition — planned, executing, tool called, verified, waiting on approval, completed. These publish to a per-goal Redis channel; a subscriber bridges Celery workers to the API process, and the API streams them to the browser over SSE. The same events feed observability, so the live view and the historical record are the same data.

In AgentVerse

  • app/services/goal_service.pysubmit_goal, subscribe_events, the Celery→pub/sub bridge
  • app/services/goal_events.py, event_store.pyevent definitions and store
  • app/scaling/tasks.pyappend_submitted_goal_event, run_goal
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/lib/sse/useGoalStream.tsthe browser subscriber

Worked example

browser subscribes to goal g-8891
 ← {type:"planned", steps:5}
 ← {type:"executing", step:1}
 ← {type:"tool_call", tool:"gst.fetch_filed"}
 ← {type:"waiting_human", step:4, reason:"filing approval"}
 [hours later, after approval]
 ← {type:"completed", result:...}
the worker died and resumed between step 1 and step 4; the stream is
continuous because events flow through Redis, not the worker's memory

At production scale

Routing events through Redis pub/sub rather than a direct worker-to-browser connection is what makes the live view survive worker restarts and work across replicas — the browser is connected to the API, not to the worker that happens to be running the goal. This is the same mechanism that makes durable HITL possible.

Failure modes

  • Events tied to worker lifetime. The stream dies when the worker does.
  • No replay from the store. A reconnecting client missing what it did not see live.

Choose it when

  • Any goal a human wants to watch.

07SLOs and alerting#

PartialOperationsImpl7/10Criticality8/10

Define what "healthy" means per goal class and alert on the deviations that matter — including the agent-specific ones that infrastructure monitoring will never catch.

Mechanism

An SLO tracker measures against targets — success rate, latency percentile, grounding rate, cost per goal — and an alert router sends deviations to the right channel with the right severity. The alerts that matter most are agent-specific: a grounding-rate drop (a corpus regression), a stall-rate spike (broken retrieval or tools), an approval backlog (a silent outage), a delegation-rate jump (a broken capability).

In AgentVerse

  • app/observability/slo_tracker.pySLO tracking
  • app/observability/alert_router.pyrouting and severity
  • app/api/sla.py, public_status.pySLA and status surfaces
  • app/voice/alerts.pyvoice alerting

Worked example

SLOs (goal class "chat answer")
 success ≥ 0.95 · grounding ≥ 0.85 · p95 ≤ 4s · cost ≤ $0.05
alert  grounding 0.85 → 0.71 over 3 days
       → severity high → #agent-oncall
       → decision trace shows the "vendor-contracts" collection re-chunked
         with fixed@v1 → root cause in minutes

At production scale

Grounding rate is the best early-warning signal an agent platform has: it is cheap to compute on every answer (chapter 18) and it drops hours before users complain when a corpus or retrieval path regresses. Alert on it. And watch the approval queue — a backlog there is an outage that no infrastructure alert will ever fire on.

Failure modes

  • Infra-only SLOs. Green dashboards, unhappy users.
  • Alert fatigue. Thresholds so tight nobody reads them.
  • No grounding alert. The fastest signal, unused.

Choose it when

  • Any production deployment with users who notice.

08Audit correlation and replay#

ShippedOperationsImpl8/10Criticality8/10

Tie the observability signals to the audit trail by the same id, and be able to replay a goal from its recorded events — so an incident investigation is reconstruction, not archaeology.

Mechanism

The goal id links the decision trace, the RAG traces, the cost breakdown, and the audit entries, so an investigation moves seamlessly from "what was approved" (audit) to "why was it proposed" (decision trace) to "what did it retrieve" (RAG trace). Replay reconstructs a goal from its event stream and prompt recipes, letting you re-run it against a fix or step through exactly what happened.

In AgentVerse

  • app/api/replay.pygoal replay
  • app/coordination/replay.pycoordination replay
  • app/governance/audit_v3.pythe audit entries keyed by goal
  • app/provenance/claim_trace.pyclaim-level provenance

Worked example

investigation: "why was a ₹418k filing submitted?"
 audit       approved by j.iyer at 16:41, argument hash matches execution
 decision    plan proposed the filing; verifier passed against the filed
             return; consensus required (risk=critical) and reached
 RAG trace   the recomputed total came from chunk [2], filed record
 replay      re-run the goal with the same fixtures to confirm
one id, four signals, a complete answer

At production scale

The correlation is what makes incident response fast. Without it, an investigation is a manual join across systems that takes hours and often ends inconclusively. Store prompt recipes rather than full prompts (chapter 8) so replay is possible without a storage or privacy problem.

Failure modes

  • Different ids per system. No join.
  • Mutable sources. A re-chunked collection making replay impossible.

Choose it when

  • Before your first incident.

09Debugging and incident workflows#

PartialOperationsImpl7/10Criticality9/10

A repeatable playbook: from symptom to signal to root cause to fix, using the traces rather than reasoning about the model — because "use a bigger model" is the answer you reach when you cannot see.

Mechanism

The workflow follows the signals. A quality complaint → RAG trace (recall/precision/coverage) → the right fix (chunking, reranking, or ingestion). A cost spike → cost breakdown → the component (tool schemas, a reasoning pattern, iterations). A wrong action → decision trace + audit → the rule or the missed gate. A latency regression → distributed trace → the slow stage. Each symptom has a signal that localises it, and the discipline is to look before theorising.

In AgentVerse

  • app/observability/*the signals the playbook uses
  • app/api/observability.py, insights.pythe operator surfaces
  • app/explainability_runtime/*decision, profile, and source explainers
  • RUNBOOK.mdthe operational runbook

Incident playbook

SymptomFirst signalLikely root cause
Wrong answers risingRAG trace + groundingCorpus/chunking regression, or a broken sync
Cost spikeCost breakdownTool schemas, a pattern, or iteration blowout
Latency regressionDistributed traceA slow connector or serial model chain
Unexpected actionDecision trace + auditMisclassification or a missed gate
Goals stuckApproval queue depthUnserviced HITL backlog
Stall-rate spikeMetrics + RAG traceRetrieval returning nothing, or a dead tool

At production scale

The playbook exists to prevent the two worst incident outcomes: a fix aimed at the wrong layer (changing the prompt for a retrieval failure) and the reflexive "use a bigger model" that costs more and fixes nothing. Every symptom in the table has a signal that localises it in minutes — the investment is having built the signals before you needed them.

Failure modes

  • Theorising before looking. Fixes aimed at the wrong layer.
  • No playbook. Every incident debugged from scratch.
  • Signals that do not exist yet. Building observability during the incident.

Choose it when

  • Any production system that gets paged.

What is missing here

  • Automated root-cause suggestion. The signals exist; nothing correlates a symptom to a likely cause automatically the way the playbook does manually.
  • Trajectory diffing. No tool to show what changed between a working and a failing run of the same goal beyond the final result.
  • Tenant-facing observability. Rich internal signals; a thinner story for letting a tenant debug their own agents' behaviour and cost.
  • Cost-anomaly detection. Cost is attributed but a per-tenant spend anomaly detector is not wired to alerting.

Multimodal
CH 15V · Modality & models

Multimodal

Text, PDF, image, screenshot, audio, video, tables, DOM.

Concepts
9
Mean impl
7.2
Mean criticality
7.1
Shipped
2
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

Multimodal is not one capability — it is the discipline of turning every non-text modality into something the rest of the platform can retrieve, reason over, and cite. The recurring move is extract to text plus keep the original by reference: a screenshot becomes a description plus OCR plus a stored image; audio becomes a timestamped transcript; a table becomes a structure plus a summary. Text is the lingua franca, and the original is the evidence.

The chapter is organised by modality because each has a different extraction path, a different cost profile, and a different privacy risk — images and screenshots being the most likely to carry personal data, video the most expensive per minute, tables the most likely to produce confidently wrong numbers.

The modalities

01Text — the baseline#

ShippedModalityImpl9/10Criticality9/10

Everything reduces to text, so the text path is the one every other modality is measured against: chunk, embed, retrieve, cite.

Mechanism

The native path (chapters 4–8): parse to structured text, chunk by strategy, embed, index in vector and lexical form, retrieve, and cite by stable chunk id. Other modalities succeed to the extent they produce text of comparable quality — a good caption or transcript is one that retrieves and cites as well as authored prose.

In AgentVerse

  • app/ingestion/pipeline.pythe shared pipeline
  • app/rag/store.pythe shared index
  • app/multimodal/pipeline.pyrouting modalities into it

Worked example

a PDF report yields native text (body) + OCR text (scanned appendix) +
captions (diagrams) + table structures — all four become chunks in the
same collection, retrievable together

At production scale

Keeping every modality's output in one text index is what lets a single query span a diagram, a table, and a paragraph. The alternative — a separate store per modality — makes cross-modal retrieval a join nobody wants to maintain.

Failure modes

  • Modality silos. Separate indexes that cannot be searched together.

Choose it when

  • Always. It is the target every extractor aims at.

02PDF and document layout#

ShippedModalityImpl8/10Criticality9/10

The multimodal workhorse: digital text, scanned images, and hybrids in one format, each needing a different path, with layout reconstruction deciding whether the output is usable.

Mechanism

Detect the sub-case per page (chapter 5), reconstruct reading order from geometry, route scanned pages to OCR, extract tables as structures, and keep page numbers for citation. A single report often exercises all three sub-cases at once, which is why per-page handling matters.

In AgentVerse

  • app/ingestion/parsers/pdf_parser.py, chunkers/pdf_layout.pyextraction and layout chunking
  • app/ocr/engine.pythe scanned-page path
  • app/multimodal/pipeline.pyper-page routing

Worked example

84-page report: prose (columns reordered) + financial tables (structured)
+ a scanned appendix (OCR) → one document, correct reading order, tables
intact, citations to page numbers

At production scale

PDFs are the majority of enterprise multimodal volume and the majority of the bugs. Measure extracted-characters-per-page as a health signal; a drop means a parser or upstream change. Full treatment in chapter 5.

Failure modes

  • Column interleaving. Unusable text.
  • Missed scanned pages. Silent content loss.

Choose it when

  • Any enterprise corpus.

03Images#

PartialModalityImpl7/10Criticality6/10

Three extractions — OCR for embedded text, a vision caption for what it depicts, and the surrounding context — with the original stored and classified as sensitive by default.

Mechanism

Route by content: photos and diagrams get a vision caption, screenshots and scans get OCR, charts benefit from both. The text (caption plus OCR) is embedded; the image is stored by reference and linked to the chunk. Cache by image hash — the same logo appears in thousands of documents.

In AgentVerse

  • app/ingestion/parsers/vision_parser.pyvision captioning
  • app/perception/multimodal.pyperception-side analysis
  • app/multimodal/models.pymultimodal asset model
  • app/ocr/engine.pythe OCR path

Worked example

architecture diagram → OCR labels [API GW, auth, payments, pgbouncer]
                     + caption "request flow: gateway → auth/payments → DB"
                     + surrounding section text
"what sits between payments and the DB?" → answerable from the caption+OCR

At production scale

Vision captioning is metered per image, so gate it: caption images users query, skip decorative assets, cache by hash. Images hide personal data — classify originals as sensitive and never put a raw screenshot in a prompt without redaction. Full treatment in chapter 5.

Failure modes

  • Captioning everything. 4,000 copies of the letterhead.
  • OCR on photos. Garbage text.

Choose it when

  • Documents carry meaning in images.

04Screenshots and browser DOM#

PartialModalityImpl7/10Criticality6/10

For agents that operate a UI, prefer the DOM (structured, cheap) and fall back to screenshots (vision, expensive) — and never carry either forward across steps unnecessarily.

Mechanism

The page analyzer extracts an accessibility/DOM summary first; only when that is opaque (a canvas app, an image-based UI) does it escalate to a vision description or the raw screenshot. Successful selectors are remembered (visual memory, chapter 3), so subsequent runs replay cheaply. Screenshots are redacted before any prompt use and stored with short retention.

In AgentVerse

  • app/perception/page_analyzer.pyDOM + visual analysis
  • app/perception/browser_agent.pythe browsing agent
  • app/rpa/artifacts.pyscreenshots by reference
  • app/rpa/session.pyremembered selectors

Worked example

step "submit the form"
 DOM summary → form#filing with named inputs → act on structure (420 tok)
 only if opaque → vision description (900 tok) → screenshot (1,400 tok)
escalate on failure, not by default

At production scale

DOM-first is the cost story for RPA: it turns most steps into cheap deterministic actions and reserves vision for genuinely visual pages. Carrying screenshots across steps is the most common way RPA cost per goal triples. Full treatment in chapters 8 (visual injection) and the RPA sections of chapter 5.

Failure modes

  • Pixels first. Expensive and less reliable than the DOM.
  • Screenshot accumulation. Cost blowout.

Choose it when

  • UI automation where the DOM is insufficient.

05Audio and video#

PartialModalityImpl7/10Criticality6/10

Transcribe to timestamped text; for video, add sampled keyframes and scene boundaries — the timestamps are the feature, because they let a citation point at a moment.

Mechanism

Audio: STT produces text plus word/segment timing and speaker labels; chunk on time windows with overlap. Video: transcribe the audio, detect scenes, sample a keyframe per scene, caption or OCR those frames, and chunk by scene so each chunk has words and visual context aligned on one timeline.

In AgentVerse

  • app/ingestion/parsers/audio_parser.py, video_parser.pyextraction
  • app/ingestion/chunkers/timestamp.py, scene.pychunking
  • app/voice/stt_engine.pytranscription

Worked example

demo video → scene 4 (3:40–5:10): speech "configure the retry policy" +
frame OCR "Retry: 3, Backoff: exponential" → chunk answers "default backoff?"
from the frame the audio never stated

At production scale

Transcription is priced per minute and video per frame; gate both by value and sample frames sparsely (one per scene). Recordings are among the most regulated data you hold — consent, retention, residency all apply. Full treatment in chapters 5 and 26.

Failure modes

  • No timestamps. A wall of text, uncitable.
  • Frame flood. One per second is 1,800 vision calls per 30 min.

Choose it when

  • Calls, meetings, and recordings hold knowledge.

06Tables#

PartialModalityImpl7/10Criticality8/10

Structure, not prose: every chunk of a table carries its header, and large tables are summarised and queried rather than embedded row by row.

Mechanism

Small tables serialise to one chunk with the header; large tables split into row groups with the header repeated, plus a summary chunk; very large tables are indexed as schema plus sample and answered with code execution (chapter 25). A header separated from its values is the cause of most confidently wrong numeric answers.

In AgentVerse

  • app/ingestion/chunkers/table.pytable chunking
  • app/ingestion/parsers/excel_parser.py, csv_parser.pyextraction
  • app/tools/code_interpreter.pythe query path for large tables

Worked example

revenue table → each row group keeps "Region | Q1 | Q2 | Q3" header
+ summary "FY24 revenue by region, INR lakhs, 12 regions"
large transactions.csv → schema + sample, then code execution for
"failed over ₹10k in March"

At production scale

Header preservation is an invariant to test. For anything above a few hundred rows, schema-plus-execution is cheaper and more accurate than embedding rows. Full treatment in chapters 5 and 17.

Failure modes

  • Headers dropped. Numbers without labels.
  • Row-per-vector. Expensive and useless.

Choose it when

  • Documents or data with tables that matter.

07Extracted spans and visual context in planning#

PartialStructureImpl7/10Criticality7/10

Extraction produces not just text but located spans — a field on an invoice, a label in a diagram, a moment in a call — which the agent can reason over and, when planning, see visually.

Mechanism

An extracted span carries its value, its type, and its location (bounding box, page, timestamp, DOM path), so a downstream step can act on a specific field rather than searching prose. In planning, a vision-capable model can be given the visual context directly — a screenshot of the page it is about to operate, or the diagram it is reasoning about — turning "describe then act" into "see then act" where the DOM is insufficient.

In AgentVerse

  • app/multimodal/models.pyextracted span model
  • app/ocr/models.pyOCR spans with locations
  • app/perception/multimodal.pyvisual context for the agent
  • app/perception/page_analyzer.pylocated page elements

Worked example

invoice OCR → spans {invoice_no@(x,y,p1), total@(x,y,p1), due_date@(x,y,p1)}
the agent acts on span.total directly, and the location lets a human
verify by opening the original at that box

At production scale

Located spans are what make multimodal output verifiable: a human can jump from the extracted value to its exact position in the original, which is essential for document AI that has to be right (chapter 21). Visual context in planning is powerful but expensive — reserve it for the cases the DOM cannot cover.

Failure modes

  • Spans without locations. Values you cannot verify against the original.
  • Vision in planning by default. Cost without need.

Choose it when

  • Field-level extraction or UI operation where verification matters.

08Asset ingestion jobs#

PartialInfrastructureImpl7/10Criticality7/10

Multimodal extraction is heavy, bursty, and separately scaled — large files, GPU-ish workloads, per-asset metering — so it runs as its own job class, not inline with the agent loop.

Mechanism

Asset processing (OCR, transcription, captioning, frame sampling) is dispatched as background jobs with their own queue, concurrency limits, and retry/DLQ handling. Originals are stored in object storage by reference; extracted text and spans flow into the standard pipeline. The separation matters because asset work is CPU/GPU-bound and bursty while the agent loop is IO-bound — mixing them makes both scale badly.

In AgentVerse

  • app/multimodal/pipeline.pyasset processing pipeline
  • app/ingestion/modality_pipeline.pymodality routing
  • app/rpa/artifacts.py, app/services/result_artifacts.pyartifact storage
  • app/scaling/tasks.pythe job runners

Worked example

tenant uploads 400 scanned PDFs
 → asset queue (separate from goal queue)
 → OCR jobs, bounded concurrency, per-asset metering, DLQ on failure
 → extracted text → standard ingestion pipeline → searchable
the agent workload is unaffected by the backfill

At production scale

Give asset processing its own queue and its own scaling. A batch of video transcriptions must not starve interactive goals of workers, and asset work's cost profile (per-minute, per-frame, per-page) is different enough that it needs its own budget and its own alarms.

Failure modes

  • Inline extraction. A large upload stalling the agent loop.
  • Shared queue. Backfill starving interactive work.

Choose it when

  • Any real volume of non-text assets.

09Multimodal limitations and future work#

PartialRealityImpl6/10Criticality6/10

The honest boundary: extraction loses information, cross-modal reasoning is shallow, and some modalities (native audio understanding, video reasoning) are still caption-and-transcribe rather than true multimodal inference.

Mechanism

The extract-to-text approach is pragmatic and lossy. A caption cannot capture everything in an image; a transcript loses tone; a table summary loses the long tail. True multimodal models that reason over pixels and audio directly would close some of this gap, but they are more expensive, harder to cite, and harder to govern — so the platform's production path is text extraction, with native multimodal reserved for the narrow cases where it clearly wins.

In AgentVerse

  • app/perception/multimodal.pywhere native vision is used when available
  • app/multimodal/pipeline.pythe extraction-based production path
  • app/embedding/router.pythe multimodal-embedding seam (rated thin, chapter 7)

Worked example

what works well   OCR, transcription, document layout, table structure
what is shallow   cross-modal reasoning ("does this chart match this text?")
what is future    native audio understanding, video reasoning, joint
                  multimodal embeddings (caption-then-embed today)

At production scale

The extraction approach is the right default because it is cheap, citable, and governable. Native multimodal is worth adopting only where the extraction loses something the use case depends on — visual search, document-understanding tasks where layout is the meaning. Name the limitation to users rather than implying capability the system does not have.

Failure modes

  • Overclaiming. Implying visual reasoning the system does by captioning.
  • Extraction loss unmeasured. No sense of what the caption dropped.

Choose it when

  • Set expectations honestly; adopt native multimodal only where extraction demonstrably falls short.

What is missing here

  • Native joint multimodal embeddings. The production path is caption-then-embed; true image/text joint retrieval is a thin seam (chapter 7).
  • Image-region chunking. Images are handled whole rather than split into semantically distinct regions.
  • Cross-modal grounding. No equivalent of the deterministic grounding check for claims derived from a chart or a screenshot (chapter 18).
  • Extraction-loss measurement. Nothing quantifies what a caption or summary dropped relative to the original.

OCR
CH 21V · Modality & models

OCR

Classify, extract, validate — document AI that has to be right.

Concepts
5
Mean impl
7.8
Mean criticality
8.0
Shipped
4
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

OCR in an agent platform is not "turn an image into text" — it is document understanding that has to be right, because the output feeds a filing, a payment, or a compliance decision. The difference from generic image captioning is that OCR here is structured extraction with validation: classify the document, extract typed fields with their locations, and validate each field against rules before anything downstream trusts it.

The three-stage shape — classify, extract, validate — is what separates document AI from a demo. A caption that is 90% right is useful; an invoice total that is 90% right is a liability, so the third stage exists to catch the 10%.

The OCR subsystem

01The OCR engine#

ShippedEngineImpl8/10Criticality8/10

Orchestrates the pipeline: OCR each page, classify the document, dispatch to the right extractor, and fall back to LLM vision OCR where classic OCR is weak.

Mechanism

The engine runs page-level OCR to get raw text and layout, classifies the document kind, and selects a kind-specific extractor via a factory. For low-quality scans or complex layouts where character-level OCR struggles, it escalates to LLM vision OCR — a vision model reading the image directly — which is more robust but more expensive, so it is a fallback rather than the default. The result is a typed OcrResult with fields and confidences.

In AgentVerse

  • app/ocr/engine.pyOcrEngine: extract(), _ocr_page(), _llm_vision_ocr(), the get_extractor factory + DocumentClassifier
  • app/ocr/models.pyOcrResult and field models
  • app/tools/ocr_tool.pyOCR exposed to agents as a tool
  • app/api/ocr.pythe API surface

Worked example

scan-invoice.pdf
 _ocr_page   raw text + word boxes, mean confidence 0.94
 classify    → invoice
 extractor   financial extractor → {vendor, invoice_no, total, tax, due}
 low-conf    "total" box confidence 0.61 → _llm_vision_ocr on that region
             → resolved to ₹41,200 at 0.97
 result      OcrResult with typed fields, each with a box and a confidence

At production scale

Reserve LLM vision OCR for the fields and pages classic OCR flags as low-confidence — running it on everything is expensive and usually unnecessary. The per-field confidence is what makes selective escalation possible: extract cheaply, escalate the uncertain 10%, and only then involve a human.

Failure modes

  • Vision OCR on everything. Cost with little marginal accuracy.
  • No per-field confidence. Cannot escalate selectively.
  • Silent low-confidence acceptance. A guessed total in a filing.

Choose it when

  • Any scanned or image-based document that feeds a decision.

02Document classification#

ShippedStageImpl8/10Criticality7/10

Decide what kind of document this is — invoice, ID, bank statement, contract — so the right extractor and the right validation rules apply.

Mechanism

Distinct from the content-type classifier of chapter 5 (which decides file format), this classifier decides business kind from the OCR'd content and layout. The kind determines everything downstream: which fields to extract, which rules to validate against, which retention and residency policy applies. A misread kind sends the document to the wrong extractor and produces confidently wrong fields.

In AgentVerse

  • app/ocr/classifier.pyDocumentClassifier — business kind
  • app/ocr/engine.pyuses it to select the extractor

Worked example

uploaded document
 layout + keywords → "invoice" (0.91) vs "purchase order" (0.06)
 → financial extractor, invoice validation rules, 7-year retention
misread as a receipt → wrong fields, wrong rules → wrong total downstream

At production scale

Kind classification errors are silent and expensive because everything downstream trusts the kind. Where confidence is low, route to a generic extractor plus human confirmation rather than committing to a wrong kind. Track the kind distribution — a shift signals a new document type nobody built an extractor for.

Failure modes

  • Confident misclassification. Wrong extractor, wrong fields.
  • No fallback for unknown kinds. New document types failing silently.

Choose it when

  • You process more than one kind of document.

03Kind-specific extractors#

ShippedStageImpl8/10Criticality8/10

Each document kind has an extractor that knows its fields: a financial extractor knows totals and tax, an ID extractor knows names and numbers, a general extractor handles the rest.

Mechanism

Extractors share an interface but encode kind-specific knowledge: the fields to look for, where they typically appear, and their expected types. A factory resolves the extractor from the classified kind. This specialisation is what makes extraction reliable — a general extractor guesses, a financial extractor knows an invoice has a total, a tax amount, and a due date, and where to find them.

In AgentVerse

  • app/ocr/extractors/base.pythe interface + get_extractor factory
  • app/ocr/extractors/financial.pyinvoices, statements, receipts
  • app/ocr/extractors/id_docs.pyidentity documents
  • app/ocr/extractors/general.pythe fallback extractor

Worked example

financial extractor on an invoice
 knows to find: vendor, invoice_no, line_items[], subtotal, tax, total, due
 locates each by layout + keyword + type → typed fields with boxes
 cross-field: subtotal + tax should equal total (a validation hook)

id_docs extractor on a passport
 knows: name, number, DOB, expiry, MRZ → and can checksum the MRZ

At production scale

Kind-specific extractors are where accuracy comes from, and they are worth building for the document kinds you process in volume. The general extractor is the honest fallback for the long tail — it extracts what it can and flags low confidence rather than pretending to understand a form it has no template for.

Failure modes

  • General extractor for everything. Guessed fields.
  • No cross-field checks. A total that does not match its line items, accepted.

Choose it when

  • You process specific document kinds in volume.

04Validation#

ShippedStageImpl8/10Criticality10/10

The stage that makes OCR trustworthy: check each field against format rules, checksums, and cross-field consistency, and escalate anything that fails rather than passing it downstream.

Mechanism

Validators apply deterministic rules: format (a date looks like a date, a GSTIN has 15 characters), checksums (Luhn for cards, MRZ check digits, GSTIN checksum), and cross-field consistency (subtotal + tax = total). A field that fails validation is not silently corrected — it is flagged for LLM vision re-read or human review. This is the difference between "we extracted a total" and "we extracted a total that is internally consistent and correctly formatted".

In AgentVerse

  • app/ocr/validators.pyformat, checksum, cross-field validation
  • app/ocr/engine.pyescalation on validation failure
  • app/governance/hitl.pyhuman review for unresolvable fields

Worked example

extracted invoice
 subtotal 38,200 · tax 3,000 · total 41,200 → 38,200+3,000=41,200 ✓
 GSTIN "27AAAPZ1234C1Z5" → checksum valid ✓
 due_date "31/13/2026" → invalid month → FLAG → re-read → "31/12/2026"
 total confidence 0.61 → below threshold → human confirms against the box
nothing with a failed check reaches the filing step

At production scale

Validation is the stage that lets you automate document workflows that touch money and compliance. The checksum and cross-field checks catch the errors that matter most — a transposed digit in a total passes an eyeball and fails arithmetic. Set confidence thresholds by field consequence: a total needs a higher bar than a memo line.

Failure modes

  • Silent correction. "Fixing" a field to what the validator expected, hiding an error.
  • No cross-field checks. Individually-plausible fields that do not add up.
  • Uniform confidence threshold. A memo line gated as strictly as a total.

Choose it when

  • Any OCR output that feeds an action that must be correct.

05OCR in the platform: ingestion, agents, and privacy#

PartialIntegrationImpl7/10Criticality7/10

OCR is both an ingestion stage (scanned documents become searchable) and an agent tool (extract fields on demand) — and its output is among the most sensitive data the platform handles.

Mechanism

In ingestion, scanned pages route to OCR at the parse stage and the extracted text joins the index (chapter 5). As a tool, an agent calls OCR to extract fields from a document mid-goal — "read this invoice and file it". Either way, the output is classified as sensitive by default: OCR'd documents are exactly the kind that contain personal and financial data, so redaction, retention, and residency all apply.

In AgentVerse

  • app/tools/ocr_tool.pyOCR as an agent tool
  • app/ingestion/parsers/pdf_parser.pythe ingestion path to OCR
  • app/data_classification/classifier.pyclassifying OCR output as sensitive
  • app/lifecycle/retention_policy.pyretention for extracted documents
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/ocrthe operator surface (a JARVIS page)

Worked example

agent goal "file the attached invoice"
 ocr_tool.extract(invoice.pdf) → validated fields
 → data classified confidential (contains vendor bank details)
 → PII redacted before any external tool call
 → original + extraction retained per the tenant's retention policy
 → filing step gated (write_high) with the extracted total hashed

At production scale

OCR sits at the intersection of the platform's most valuable and most sensitive workflows — automating invoice, ID, and statement processing — which is exactly why its output needs the full governance treatment. Classify originals as sensitive, apply short retention to raw scans, and keep the located spans so every extracted value can be audited against the source.

Failure modes

  • OCR output not classified. Financial data flowing without redaction.
  • Raw scans retained indefinitely. A compliance liability.
  • Extraction without verifiable spans. No audit path to the original.

Choose it when

  • Any document-processing workflow, especially financial or identity documents.

What is missing here

  • Handwriting and low-resource scripts. The extractors target printed documents in common scripts; handwriting and rare scripts are weaker.
  • Table extraction within documents. Field extraction is strong; complex nested tables inside scanned documents lean on the general path.
  • Confidence calibration per field type. Thresholds are set but not continuously calibrated against human-corrected outcomes.
  • Active-learning from corrections. Human corrections are not systematically fed back to improve extractor accuracy over time.

CH 16V · Modality & models

Multi-model router

Per-role model selection under cost, latency, plan, and health.

Concepts
6
Mean impl
7.7
Mean criticality
8.2
Shipped
4
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

A production agent uses many models, not one — a planner, an executor, a verifier, a judge, an embedder, sometimes a vision or audio or reranker model — and the right choice for each is a different point on the cost/latency/quality surface. The model router is the component that makes that choice per role, per goal, under constraints, and reroutes when a provider fails.

Two ideas organise it. Role-based selection: the model that plans well is not necessarily the model that verifies cheaply, so choose per role. Constraint-aware routing: the choice is bounded by the tenant's plan, the goal's latency budget, and each provider's current health — so the same role can get different models on different goals.

Routing

01The model orchestrator#

ShippedCoreImpl8/10Criticality9/10

The component that binds a goal's pattern config to concrete models per role and hands the agent loop a set of ready, health-checked model clients.

Mechanism

At goal start, the orchestrator reads the pattern config (which named a model per role) and the routing signals, resolves each role to an actual model and provider, and constructs the clients — wrapped in circuit breakers and cost guards. It is where "the planner should be a strong model" becomes "the planner is this provider's this model, and here is the client".

In AgentVerse

  • app/ai_router/model_orchestrator.pyModelOrchestrator
  • app/ai_router/router.pyAIRouter — the routing decision
  • app/services/goal_service.py_make_agent_loop_for_tenant() constructs it per goal
  • app/agent/model_router.pyagent-side model routing

Worked example

pattern config  planner=large executor=large verifier=mid classifier=mini
goal signals    plan=enterprise · latency budget=relaxed · all providers ok
orchestrator    planner → anthropic/large · executor → anthropic/large
                verifier → openai/mid (cross-provider, for consensus)
                classifier → mini
                each client wrapped in a breaker + cost guard

At production scale

Constructing model clients per goal rather than globally is what lets routing be goal-specific and plan-aware. It is also where cross-provider verification is arranged — deliberately choosing a different provider for the verifier than the executor, so consensus is not two instances of the same blind spots (chapter 1).

Failure modes

  • Global model config. One model for every goal, chosen for the hardest case.
  • Same provider for actor and verifier. Correlated errors in consensus.

Choose it when

  • Any agent using more than one model role.

02Per-role model selection#

ShippedSelectionImpl8/10Criticality8/10

Planner, executor, verifier, judge — each has different requirements, and choosing per role is the largest cost lever in the platform without touching quality.

Mechanism

Each role is scored independently on quality, latency and cost against a measured table (chapter 9). The patterns that recur: verifiers and classifiers usually run well on cheaper models; executors on complex tool work usually need stronger ones; planners sit in between; judges must differ from the model they judge. The role policy encodes these and the router applies them per goal.

In AgentVerse

  • app/ai_router/role_policy.pyper-role selection policy
  • app/ai_router/complexity_scorer.pyscoring the goal's difficulty
  • app/evals/model_score.pythe measured per-role table
  • app/agent/pattern_config.pymodel_planner/executor/verifier/classifier fields

Worked example

role       requirement                     typical choice   cost share
planner    decomposition, judgement         strong           medium
executor   tool selection, reasoning        strong           high
verifier   check against a rubric            mid              low
judge      independent scoring              mid (diff vendor) low
classifier fast keyword+LLM tiebreak        mini             tiny
embedder   semantic quality                 small/medium     tiny
measuring per role typically finds 40-70% cost savings vs one global model

At production scale

The most common waste is a strong model on the verifier "to be safe". Verification is a rubric check — a task where a mid model matches a large one — and it runs on every step, so downgrading it is a large, quality-neutral saving. Measure per role rather than assuming; the answer shifts as models change.

Failure modes

  • One model for all roles. Overpaying on the cheap roles.
  • Judge = executor model. Self-preference in scoring.

Choose it when

  • Any multi-role agent — which is any production agent.

03Cost-, latency-, and plan-aware routing#

ShippedPolicyImpl8/10Criticality9/10

The same role gets a different model depending on what the goal can afford, how fast it must be, and what the tenant's plan permits.

Mechanism

A three-way policy: cost (route to a cheaper model when the budget is tight or the goal class does not justify the spend), latency (route to a faster model for interactive goals), and plan (a free tier gets the economy models, enterprise gets the frontier ones). These interact — an interactive enterprise goal optimises for latency within the enterprise model set — and the policy resolves the trade with a recorded reason.

In AgentVerse

  • app/ai_router/cost_latency_quality_policy.pythe three-way trade
  • app/tenancy/entitlements.py, limits.pyplan constraints
  • app/optimization/model_optimizer.py, latency_optimizer.py, cost_optimizer.pythe optimisers that tune it
  • app/routing_runtime/optimizer.py, model_router.pyruntime routing

Worked example

same role (executor), three goals
 interactive chat, enterprise  → fast enterprise model (latency wins)
 overnight batch, enterprise   → strong model (quality wins, latency free)
 chat, free tier               → economy model (plan caps the set)
each decision recorded: "executor=fast-enterprise, reason=latency<4s budget"

At production scale

Plan-aware routing is both a cost control and a product feature — it is how tiers are differentiated. The subtlety is not to optimise cost against a proxy: routing to a cheaper model that fails more often raises cost through extra iterations. Always evaluate a routing change on success and cost together (chapter 9).

Failure modes

  • Cost optimisation ignoring success. Cheaper model, more retries, higher net cost.
  • Plan not enforced in routing. Free tier reaching frontier models.
  • Latency ignored on interactive goals. A strong slow model on a chat path.

Choose it when

  • Multiple plans, or mixed interactive and batch workloads.

04Specialised model roles: embedding, vision, audio, reranker#

PartialSelectionImpl7/10Criticality7/10

Beyond the text roles, the platform routes to specialised models — an embedder per content type, a vision model for images, STT/TTS for voice, a cross-encoder for reranking — each selected on its own axis.

Mechanism

Each specialised role has its own selection logic. The embedding router chooses by content type and dimension compatibility (chapter 7). Vision routing picks a model that can read the image at acceptable cost. Voice routes to STT and TTS providers by language and latency (chapter 26). The reranker is selected by the retrieval pipeline (chapter 6). They share the router's constraint-awareness — plan, cost, health — but differ in what "quality" means for each.

In AgentVerse

  • app/embedding/router.py, app/routing_runtime/embedding_router.pyembedding selection
  • app/perception/multimodal.pyvision model use
  • app/voice/router.py, stt_engine.py, tts_engine.pyvoice model routing
  • app/rag_platform/reranker.pyreranker selection
  • app/routing_runtime/skill_router.py, tool_router.pythe same idea for skills and tools

Worked example

one goal touches four specialised roles
 embedder   code chunk → code model (1024) · prose → text model (3072)
 vision     invoice image → vision model for OCR fallback
 reranker   retrieval → cross-encoder, top 50
 (voice)    if voice channel → STT by language, TTS by latency
each selected on its own axis, all under the same plan/health constraints

At production scale

The specialised roles are where model diversity is highest and where a single hardcoded choice hurts most — an English STT model on German audio, a prose embedder on code. Route each by its own signal, and keep the selection recorded so a quality problem in one modality is traceable to the model that produced it.

Failure modes

  • One embedder for all content. Code and prose degrading each other.
  • Language-blind voice routing. Poor transcription on non-default languages.

Choose it when

  • Any workload spanning content types or modalities.

05Provider fallback and circuit breakers#

ShippedReliabilityImpl8/10Criticality10/10

Providers fail. A circuit breaker detects it, stops hammering the dead provider, and reroutes to a fallback — turning an outage into a degraded mode rather than a failure.

Mechanism

Each provider is fronted by a circuit breaker: after a threshold of failures the breaker opens and calls short-circuit to a fallback provider instead of timing out repeatedly. Fallback must respect constraints — a fallback model must be capable of the role, and for embedding it must match the index dimension (chapter 7). Provider health feeds back into routing so an unhealthy provider is deprioritised before the breaker even trips. When the breaker half-opens, a probe checks whether the provider has recovered.

In AgentVerse

  • app/providers/circuit_breaker.pyProviderCircuitBreaker, call_with_circuit_breaker()
  • app/ai_router/provider_health_policy.pyhealth feeds routing
  • app/providers/registry.pyresolve_provider(), fallback resolution
  • app/providers/fake.pythe ultimate fallback for tests/no-key
  • app/reliability/redis_circuit_breaker.pythe cross-replica breaker state

Worked example

primary provider returns 503s
 breaker after 5 failures → OPEN → calls short-circuit
 router reroutes executor to fallback provider (capable of the role)
 embedding role: fallback must match index dim → if none, queue, not reroute
 90s later → breaker HALF-OPEN → probe → recovered → CLOSE
users saw degraded latency for 90s, not an outage

At production scale

Cross-replica breaker state (in Redis) matters: without it, each replica discovers the provider is down independently, so the fleet keeps hammering a dead provider from every node. The breaker is also what makes cross-provider verification robust — if the verifier's provider is down, the system knows before it tries. Multi-provider capability is the whole reason the provider abstraction (chapter 20) must be genuinely vendor-neutral.

Failure modes

  • No breaker. A provider outage becoming your outage via retry storms.
  • Dimension-incompatible embedding fallback. Index corruption dressed as resilience.
  • Per-replica breaker state. The fleet not learning collectively.

Choose it when

  • Any dependency on an external model provider — so always.

06Shadow routing#

PartialImprovementImpl7/10Criticality6/10

Score a candidate model on real traffic without serving its output — the cheapest way to evaluate a new or cheaper model on your actual distribution before promoting it.

Mechanism

For a sampled fraction of goals, run both the incumbent (whose output is served) and a candidate (whose output is scored but discarded). Compare quality, latency and cost on identical inputs. Because the candidate never affects the user, shadow routing is safe to run on production traffic, and it answers the question benchmarks cannot: how does this model do on our goals?

In AgentVerse

  • app/ai_router/shadow_router.pyshadow routing
  • app/intelligence/experiment_registry.pyexperiment framing
  • app/evals/model_score.pyscoring both
  • app/optimization/ab_testing.pypromotion decision

Worked example

candidate: a new cheaper verifier model, shadowed on 5% of goals
 incumbent served, candidate scored on the same inputs
 over 3 days: candidate quality 0.93 vs 0.94, cost 0.004 vs 0.021
 → promote candidate; no user ever saw its output during evaluation

At production scale

Shadow routing is how you keep the per-role model table current as models and prices change (chapter 9). It de-risks model migration: you learn a candidate's real-world behaviour before it serves a single user, which is the difference between a confident promotion and a hopeful one. Budget the shadow cost — you are paying for a second inference on the sampled fraction.

Failure modes

  • Shadow output leaking to users. The one thing that must never happen.
  • Unbudgeted shadow cost. Doubling inference on the sample without accounting.

Choose it when

  • Evaluating a model change on real traffic before committing.

What is missing here

  • Learned routing. Selection uses hand-tuned policies over a measured table; a bandit over models per goal class would optimise success-per-dollar continuously.
  • Predictive complexity scoring. The complexity scorer runs before the goal; it cannot yet learn from how goals of a given shape actually turned out.
  • Cross-provider consensus automation. Consensus picks a second provider manually; routing does not automatically ensure verifier and executor providers differ.
  • Speculative multi-model execution. No support for racing two providers and taking the first acceptable answer under a tight latency budget.

Core platform workflows

Startup to SSE: the twenty-two steps a goal actually takes.

Concepts

Orientation

This chapter is the spine that the rest of the book hangs on: the twenty-two steps a goal actually takes, from an HTTP request to a streamed result. Every subsystem you have met — retrieval, memory, guardrails, routing, audit — appears here as a station on one line. If you understand this flow, you understand how the pieces compose; if you are debugging, this is the map that tells you where to look.

The one structural idea to hold onto is the two-phase service wiring: the app is built once with in-memory services, then a lifespan upgrades them to DB- and Redis-backed versions. Most "works in tests but not in prod" bugs live in the gap between those two phases.

The twenty-two steps

01App startup and two-phase service wiring#

ShippedLifecycleImpl9/10Criticality10/10

The app is assembled once with in-memory services, then a lifespan swaps them for DB- and Redis-backed versions and re-hydrates state — the single most important thing to understand about the platform's behaviour.

Mechanism

create_app() constructs every service (tenant, goal, knowledge, MCP, cost, rate limiter…) in an in-memory form and binds them to app.state, then includes ~25 routers. When manage_pools=True, the FastAPI lifespan starts connection pools, swaps the in-memory services for DB/Redis-backed ones, re-hydrates state from Postgres, and re-wires auth, SSE, cost control, and the MCP client. Dependency resolution reads from app.state dynamically, so the swap takes effect without breaking already-registered middleware.

In AgentVerse

  • app/main.pycreate_app() (a hub node, 183 edges) and the lifespan
  • app/bootstrap/services.py, routers.pyservice and router assembly
  • app/core/pools.pyConnectionPools
  • app/db/session.pyget_session_factory()

Worked example

tests            create_app(manage_pools=False)
                 → in-memory services, no DB, deterministic FakeProvider
production       create_app() + lifespan(manage_pools=True)
                 → in-memory services built first
                 → pools start → services swapped to DB/Redis-backed
                 → sync_from_db() re-hydrates tenants, agents, schedules
                 → real providers resolved from env keys
the swap is why a bug can be invisible in tests and appear only in prod

At production scale

When something works in tests but not in production (or vice versa), this swap is the first suspect: the in-memory path and the DB-backed path are different implementations of the same interface, and behaviour that depends on persistence, cross-replica state, or real providers only exists on one side. Knowing the two phases exist turns a baffling bug into a targeted one.

Failure modes

  • State not re-hydrated. A service swapped but its data not loaded.
  • Middleware bound to the old service. The swap not taking effect.
  • Test-only behaviour. Relying on the in-memory path's quirks.

Choose it when

  • Understanding, debugging, or extending the platform — always start here.

02Steps 1–2: submission and tenant authentication#

ShippedStepImpl9/10Criticality10/10

A goal arrives over HTTP; middleware authenticates it, establishes the immutable tenant context, and sets the RLS boundary before any business logic runs.

Mechanism

The request hits POST /goals. Tenant middleware authenticates (API key or JWT), resolves the tenant, checks the key's scope and IP allowlist, and constructs the TenantContext. The database session sets app.tenant_id so RLS applies to everything that follows. Only then does the request reach the goal endpoint.

In AgentVerse

  • app/api/goals.pythe submit endpoint
  • app/tenancy/middleware.pyTenantMiddleware
  • app/tenancy/context.pyTenantContext
  • app/auth/scope_enforcement.py, ip_allowlist.pykey checks
  • app/db/rls.pythe boundary set per request

Worked example

POST /goals {goal:"reconcile March payouts"}  Authorization: Bearer ak_...
 middleware  key valid, scope goals:submit ok, IP in allowlist
             → TenantContext(acme, plan=enterprise)
 session     SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = 'acme'
 endpoint    now runs, everything it touches is tenant-scoped

At production scale

Authentication and scope establish the outermost two scopes (chapter 14) before the goal exists as a record — so an unauthorised or out-of-scope request never creates state. The RLS boundary being set here, at the session level, is what makes every downstream query safe by default. Full treatment in chapters 13–14.

Failure modes

  • Context not propagated to the worker. The goal runs without its tenant.
  • Scope checked after record creation. State for a request that should have been rejected.

Choose it when

  • Always — this is the front door.

03Steps 3–5: record, budget, queue, worker#

ShippedStepImpl9/10Criticality9/10

GoalService creates the record and checks the budget, enqueues the goal on the tenant's plan queue, and a Celery worker acquires a lock and builds the agent graph.

Mechanism

GoalService writes a GoalRecord, checks the tenant and goal budget, and enqueues onto a per-plan queue (goals.free … goals.enterprise) so an enterprise tenant is not stuck behind a free tenant's backlog. A worker picks it up, acquires a distributed lock (one worker per goal), and constructs the AgentGraph with the goal's runtime profile and model clients.

In AgentVerse

  • app/services/goal_service.pysubmit_goal, GoalRecord
  • app/services/goal_queue.pyenqueue_goal
  • app/scaling/celery_app.pyPLAN_QUEUE_MAP — per-plan routing
  • app/scaling/tasks.pyrun_goal, append_submitted_goal_event
  • app/reliability/distributed_lock.pyone worker per goal

Worked example

GoalService  record g-8891 · tenant budget ok · goal budget $8
enqueue      → goals.enterprise queue
worker-4     acquires lock lock:goal:g-8891 (worker-7 would skip)
             builds AgentGraph(runtime_profile, model clients, checkpointer)

At production scale

Per-plan queues are how the platform avoids noisy-neighbour effects — the single most important scaling decision for a multi-tenant agent system, because one tenant's batch of 10,000 goals must not delay another's interactive one. The lock prevents the duplicate-execution bug that otherwise appears under retries and rebalancing. Full treatment in chapters 20 and 32.

Failure modes

  • Shared queue. Noisy-neighbour delays.
  • No lock. A goal running twice on two workers.
  • Budget checked after enqueue. Work scheduled that cannot be paid for.

Choose it when

  • Any multi-tenant async execution.

04Steps 6–11: the agent loop#

ShippedStepImpl9/10Criticality10/10

Initialize, retrieve, plan, execute, verify — the LangGraph state machine from chapter 1, running with real tools, real credentials, and real approval gates, looping to replan or completing.

Mechanism

The graph runs the loop: initialize loads context and checks budget; retrieve runs RAG before planning; plan produces a validated plan; execute calls tools through MCP with vault credentials, guardrails, and HITL gates; verify checks against evidence and routes to complete, replan, max-iter, waiting-human, or rag-remediate. State is checkpointed after each node, so the goal survives a worker restart mid-loop.

In AgentVerse

  • app/agent/graph.pyAgentGraph — the state machine
  • app/agent/nodes/*.pyone mixin per node
  • app/mcp/client.pyMCPClient.call_tool — tool dispatch
  • app/providers/vault.pycredential resolution at call time
  • app/governance/hitl.pyapproval gates

Worked example

6 initialize  tenant ctx, agent config, budget check
7 retrieve    4 chunks from the runbook collection (chapters 2, 6)
8 plan        [fetch filed, recompute, diff, file*, notify]  (*gated)
9 execute     step 1 → MCP call, vault resolves the GST credential
              step 4 → write_high → HITL → waiting_human (checkpointed)
              [resume after approval]
10 verify     totals match the filed return → complete
11 (or replan on failure, bounded by max_iterations)

At production scale

This is the product. Every earlier chapter — patterns, retrieval, memory, prompts, guardrails, routing — converges here into the running loop. The checkpointing is what makes it operable: workers are cattle, a deploy mid-goal is not an outage, and a HITL pause costs nothing because the worker is released. Full treatment in chapter 1.

Failure modes

  • Non-serializable state. Checkpointing fails, resume impossible.
  • Credentials in state. A secret in the checkpoint.
  • Unbounded loop. No iteration cap (chapter 1).

Choose it when

  • Always. This is the core.

05Tool discovery and execution through MCP#

ShippedStepImpl9/10Criticality9/10

Tools live behind the Model Context Protocol: the registry lists what a tenant has, the client executes calls with circuit breaking and stale-cache fallback, and credentials are resolved from the vault so the model never sees them.

Mechanism

The MCP registry holds per-tenant connectors; tools/list discovers available tools; call_tool executes one, delegating to an inner implementation wrapped in a circuit breaker. On an open circuit it can serve a stale cached result before raising. Credentials are resolved from the vault at call time and injected into the request, never placed in the prompt. Results are sanitized and wrapped as untrusted before returning to the loop.

In AgentVerse

  • app/mcp/registry.pyper-tenant connector registry
  • app/mcp/client.pycall_tool, _call_tool_impl, CircuitBreakerOpenError, stale-cache fallback
  • app/mcp/tool_cache.pyToolResultCache
  • app/mcp/oauth.pyPKCE OAuth for connectors
  • app/providers/vault.pycredential resolution
  • app/mcp/servers/325 built-in server modules

Worked example

execute step "fetch filed GSTR-1"
 registry     gst connector present for acme
 vault        resolves the GST API token (model never sees it)
 call_tool    gst.fetch_filed(period, gstin)
              breaker closed → _call_tool_impl → result
              [if breaker open] → serve stale cached result or raise
 result       sanitized, wrapped untrusted, returned to the loop

At production scale

MCP is the architecture decision that makes tools safe and per-tenant: each connector is its own process, so a misbehaving integration cannot take the agent down, and the tool surface is configuration rather than compiled in. The stale-cache fallback is a thoughtful touch — a read tool whose provider is down can still answer from cache rather than failing the goal. Full treatment in chapter 20.

Failure modes

  • Credentials in the prompt. Exfiltration surface.
  • No breaker on the connector. A dead tool taking down goals.
  • Unsanitized tool output. Injection vector.

Choose it when

  • Any agent that calls external tools.

06Steps 12–14: memory, eval, and event emission#

ShippedStepImpl9/10Criticality9/10

On completion (or failure), the platform writes memory, scores the goal, and emits the final events — the closing stations that turn a finished run into learning, measurement, and a delivered result.

Mechanism

Goal completion fans out into memory writes — episodic, procedural, execution, long-term, and on failure reflexion (chapter 3). The eval layer scores the run across dimensions (chapter 10). Throughout and at the end, events publish to the goal's Redis channel, bridged to the API and streamed to the browser over SSE (chapter 11). The outcome persists to Postgres and the LangGraph checkpoint.

In AgentVerse

  • app/memory/*the tier writes on completion
  • app/agent/reflexion_wirer.pylesson extraction on failure
  • app/evals/runtime_scorecard.py, goal_score.pyscoring
  • app/services/goal_service.pyevent emission, Celery→pub/sub bridge
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/lib/sse/useGoalStream.tsthe browser receiver

Worked example

goal g-8891 completes
 memory   execution (all steps), episodic (this run), procedural (if a
          stable method emerged), long-term (durable facts learned)
 eval     goal 0.91 · grounding 0.88 · cost $0.42 · latency 41s
 events   {type:"completed", result, citations} → Redis → SSE → browser
 persist  outcome to Postgres, final checkpoint retained

At production scale

The closing steps are what make the platform improve rather than merely run: memory turns this goal into context for the next, eval turns it into a measurement, and events turn it into a live experience. Skipping any of them leaves a platform that works today and does not get better — or one whose users cannot see what it is doing.

Failure modes

  • Memory write failure swallowed. Learning silently lost.
  • Events tied to worker lifetime. The stream dying with the worker.
  • Eval skipped on failure. The most informative runs unmeasured.

Choose it when

  • Any goal you want to learn from, measure, or show.

07The frontend SSE/WebSocket path and the SDK/Action boundary#

ShippedBoundaryImpl8/10Criticality7/10

The same events reach a browser over SSE, a collaboration client over WebSocket, and CI over the SDK and GitHub Action — one backend, several front doors, one event model.

Mechanism

The React frontend subscribes to a goal's SSE stream for live execution and to a WebSocket for collaboration. The Python and TypeScript SDKs submit a goal and poll or stream its result. The GitHub Action wraps the SDK to submit a goal from CI and await it. All of them speak the same OpenAPI contract published by the backend, so the backend is the single source of truth and the clients are thin.

In AgentVerse

  • agent-verse-frontend/src/lib/sse/useGoalStream.tsSSE
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/lib/ws/useCollabSocket.tscollaboration WebSocket
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/lib/api/client.tsHTTP client
  • app/api/goals.pythe endpoints all clients consume
  • scripts/export_openapi.pythe contract the clients are generated against

Worked example

same goal, three front doors
 browser   POST /goals → SSE stream → live step-by-step view
 CI        GitHub Action → SDK → submit → await → pass/fail the build
 script    SDK client → submit → poll → result
all consume the same OpenAPI contract; the backend does not know or care
which client called

At production scale

A single backend contract with thin clients is what keeps five deployable projects in sync: the backend publishes OpenAPI, the SDKs are generated or checked against it, and a backend change that breaks a client is caught at contract level. The Action is just the SDK in a Docker entrypoint — the smallest possible front door, which is the right size for CI. (The SDKs themselves are out of scope for this manual, per the brief; here they matter only as consumers of the same event model.)

Failure modes

  • Contract drift. Clients and backend disagreeing after a change.
  • SSE without reconnect. A dropped stream losing the live view.

Choose it when

  • Any platform with more than one kind of client.

What is missing here

  • A single end-to-end trace view. The signals exist per station; a one-screen "here is the whole goal from submit to SSE" view would speed onboarding and debugging.
  • Warm-start for the two-phase swap. The in-memory-then-DB swap re-hydrates on every start; a faster warm path would cut cold-start latency.
  • Backpressure from loop to queue. The queue routes by plan but does not yet shed load based on downstream worker saturation (chapter 28).

Other core platform concepts

MCP, providers, bulkheads, breakers, dedup, rollback, Redis, RLS.
