Voice & realtime agents

STT, barge-in, intent routing, TTS, and the latency budget.

Concepts
4
Mean impl
7.0
Mean criticality
6.0
Shipped
0
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

Voice turns an agent into something you can talk to, and it changes one thing above all: the latency budget. A user tolerates seconds of silence from a chat box and none from a voice that has started to reply. Every design decision in a voice agent — streaming, barge-in, model choice — is downstream of the fact that a person is listening in real time.

The pipeline is speech-to-text → intent → agent → text-to-speech, and the art is making it feel continuous: streaming transcription so the agent starts thinking before you finish, streaming synthesis so it starts speaking before it finishes thinking, and barge-in so you can interrupt.

The voice pipeline

01The streaming voice session#

PartialPipelineImpl7/10Criticality7/10

A session that streams audio in, transcribes, routes, runs the agent, and streams speech back — orchestrated so the pieces overlap rather than run strictly in sequence.

Mechanism

The session runs a pipeline: incoming audio is converted and streamed to STT, the transcript routes to an intent handler that invokes the agent, and the response streams to TTS and back as audio. The overlap is the point — transcription runs while the user is still speaking, and synthesis starts on the first words of the response — so perceived latency is far below the sum of the stages.

In AgentVerse

  • app/voice/streaming.pyVoiceStreamingSession: run_pipeline(), _to_wav(), _send()
  • app/voice/schemas.pysession contracts
  • app/gateway/channels/voice_webhook.pythe voice channel entry
  • app/voice/greeting.pythe opening interaction

Worked example

user: "what's the status of my invoice reconciliation?"
 STT streams the transcript as they speak → routes at end of utterance
 agent runs → first sentence ready → TTS streams it → user hears it
 while the agent is still forming the rest
perceived latency ≈ time to the first spoken word, not the full turn

At production scale

The streaming overlap is the whole game — a non-streamed voice pipeline (transcribe fully, think fully, synthesise fully) feels broken because the silences are unbearable. Measure time-to-first-audio, not total turn time. Voice sessions are also long-lived connections, which is a different scaling profile from request/response goals (chapter 32).

Failure modes

  • No streaming. Unbearable silences.
  • Measuring total turn time. Missing what the user actually feels.

Choose it when

  • Any real-time voice interaction.

02Speech-to-text#

PartialComponentImpl7/10Criticality6/10

Transcription with provider choice by language and latency — a fast local model for real-time, a cloud model for accuracy, selected like any other model role.

Mechanism

An STT engine abstracts multiple providers (Whisper API, faster-whisper for local low-latency, AssemblyAI), selected by language and latency needs (chapter 16). Streaming STT emits partial transcripts as audio arrives. Domain vocabulary hints improve accuracy on jargon where the provider supports them.

In AgentVerse

  • app/voice/stt_engine.pythe STT abstraction
  • app/voice/providers/stt/whisper_api.py, faster_whisper.py, assemblyai.pyproviders
  • app/voice/providers/base.pythe provider interface
  • app/voice/router.pyprovider selection

Worked example

real-time call, German audio
 router → faster-whisper (local, low-latency) with a German model
 streaming partials: "wie ist der..." → "wie ist der Status..."
 domain hint: ["GSTR-1", "Razorpay"] improves jargon accuracy

At production scale

STT is the accuracy foundation — a mis-transcription propagates to a wrong action. Route by language (an English model on German audio is poor) and by latency (local for real-time, cloud for batch accuracy). Full provider-routing treatment in chapter 16; the ingestion side (transcribing recordings) is chapter 5.

Failure modes

  • Language-blind routing. Poor transcription on non-default languages.
  • No streaming. Latency the user feels.
  • Jargon errors. Domain terms mangled without hints.

Choose it when

  • Any voice input.

03Intent routing and barge-in#

PartialComponentImpl7/10Criticality6/10

Turn an utterance into an action — a command, a question, or a goal — and let the user interrupt the agent mid-sentence, which is what makes voice feel conversational.

Mechanism

An intent router classifies the transcript: a direct command (execute), a question (answer), or a goal (submit to the agent loop). Barge-in detects the user speaking while the agent is talking and cancels the TTS immediately — cooperative cancellation of the output stream — so the user can interrupt naturally rather than waiting for the agent to finish.

In AgentVerse

  • app/voice/intent_router.pyroute_voice_command()
  • app/voice/streaming.pybarge-in via stream cancellation
  • app/voice/alerts.pyvoice alerting

Worked example

agent (speaking): "The reconciliation found three discrepancies. The first—"
user (interrupts): "just tell me the total"
 barge-in detected → TTS cancelled immediately
 intent router: question → answer directly → "The total variance is ₹4,120."
without barge-in, the user would have to wait through the whole explanation

At production scale

Barge-in is the feature that separates a voice agent from a voice menu. It requires the output stream to be cancellable at any point (chapter 1's cooperative cancellation applied to audio) — a TTS that cannot be interrupted makes every interaction feel like waiting on hold. Intent routing keeps cheap requests (a question) off the full agent loop.

Failure modes

  • No barge-in. The user waits through everything.
  • Everything routed to the full loop. A simple question taking a full goal.

Choose it when

  • Any conversational voice agent.

04Text-to-speech#

PartialComponentImpl7/10Criticality5/10

Streaming synthesis with provider choice by quality, latency, and voice — from a fast local voice for real-time to a premium cloud voice where quality matters, with a browser fallback.

Mechanism

A TTS engine abstracts providers (ElevenLabs, OpenAI, Azure, Kokoro, macOS say, a browser fallback, and others), streaming synthesis so audio starts on the first sentence. Selection trades quality against latency and cost (chapter 16): a premium voice for a customer-facing line, a fast local voice for internal tools, a browser fallback when nothing else is available.

In AgentVerse

  • app/voice/tts_engine.pysynthesize_streaming
  • app/voice/providers/tts/elevenlabs.py, openai_tts.py, azure_tts.py, kokoro.py, macos_say.py, omnivoice.py, browser_fallback.pyproviders
  • app/voice/router.pyselection

Worked example

customer-facing line → ElevenLabs (premium voice), streamed
internal tool       → Kokoro (fast local), streamed
provider down       → browser_fallback (Web Speech API)
first sentence synthesised and playing while the rest is generated

At production scale

Streaming TTS is what lets the agent start speaking before it finishes thinking — the second half of the low-latency story. The provider spread (premium to local to browser fallback) is the same reliability pattern as the model router: quality where it matters, cheap where it does not, and a fallback that always works. Full routing treatment in chapter 16.

Failure modes

  • Non-streaming synthesis. A pause before the agent speaks.
  • No fallback. Silence when the provider is down.

Choose it when

  • Any voice output.

What is missing here

  • Native speech-to-speech models. The pipeline is STT→LLM→TTS; end-to-end speech models would cut latency further but are harder to govern and cite.
  • Emotion and prosody control. Synthesis is largely neutral; conveying appropriate tone is future work.
  • Voice-specific guardrails. The text guardrails apply to the transcript, but audio-specific concerns (voice cloning, spoofing) are not addressed.
  • Full HITL over voice. Approving a gated action mid-call is thinner than the text/console approval flow (chapter 23).

Triggers & event-driven agents
CH 27VII · Not on the list

Triggers & event-driven agents

Cron, webhooks, IoT, data change — agents nobody typed a prompt into.

Concepts
4
Mean impl
7.8
Mean criticality
7.5
Shipped
3
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

Every goal so far started because a human asked. Triggers are the other half of an agent platform: goals that start because the world changed — a schedule fired, a webhook arrived, a metric crossed a threshold, a sensor reported, a row was inserted. This is what turns a request/response tool into an autonomous operator that watches and acts.

And it is where autonomy's risks concentrate. A trigger acts on behalf of someone who is not present, so the discipline is every trigger fires a normal, fully-governed goal — same auth, budget, approval gates, and audit — plus the trigger-specific controls (verification, rate-limiting, dedup, stale authorisation checks) that a request from a live user does not need.

Event-driven agents

01Natural-language scheduling#

ShippedSchedulingImpl8/10Criticality7/10

"Every weekday at 9am, summarise overnight incidents" becomes a trigger spec — cron and goal template parsed from plain language.

Mechanism

An NL scheduler parses a natural-language schedule into a TriggerSpec: a cron expression (via croniter), a goal template, and any parameters. It is the meta-agent idea (chapter 9) for schedules — a human describes what and when, the parser produces a governed, editable spec. The spec is stored and fired by beat.

In AgentVerse

  • app/triggers/nl_scheduler.pyparse() — NL → TriggerSpec
  • app/triggers/models.pyTriggerSpec, TriggerType
  • app/triggers/store.pyScheduleStore
  • app/scaling/tasks.pyfire_due_schedules, run_scheduled_goal

Worked example

"every weekday at 9am, summarise overnight incidents and post to #ops"
 → TriggerSpec(cron="0 9 * * 1-5", template="incident-summary", channel="#ops")
 stored → beat fires it at 9am on weekdays → submits a governed goal
editable and reviewable, not code

At production scale

NL scheduling makes autonomous work authorable by non-engineers, which is the point — but the resulting spec must be reviewable and editable, because "every weekday at 9am" parsed wrong is a goal firing at the wrong time indefinitely. Jitter scheduled goals (chapter 5) so a fleet of 9am triggers does not stampede.

Failure modes

  • Misparsed schedule. A trigger firing at the wrong time forever.
  • Unjittered fleet. A stampede at the top of the hour.

Choose it when

  • Recurring autonomous work authored by humans.

02Webhook triggers#

ShippedSourceImpl8/10Criticality8/10

An external event (a payment failed, a PR opened) submits a goal — with signature verification, secret rotation, and rate-limiting, because a webhook endpoint is an attacker-reachable front door.

Mechanism

A webhook arrives; the platform verifies its signature against the source's secret (which is rotated), parses the payload, and — if valid — submits a goal. Because the endpoint is public, it needs the full defence: signature verification (reject forgeries), rate-limiting (absorb floods), dedup (webhooks are often delivered more than once), and treating the payload as untrusted input (chapter 12).

In AgentVerse

  • app/triggers/webhooks/verifier.py, rotation.py, parsers.pyverification, secret rotation, parsing
  • app/triggers/dedup.py, rate_limiter.py, bulkhead.pydedup, rate-limit, bulkhead
  • app/triggers/dispatcher.pydispatch to a goal
  • app/gateway/channels/webhook.py, app/gateway/webhook_delivery.pythe channel

Worked example

Stripe webhook: payment.failed
 verify signature against the rotated secret → valid
 dedup: this event id seen before? no → proceed (webhooks retry)
 rate-limit: within bounds → dispatch a "triage failed payment" goal
 forged webhook → signature fails → rejected, logged

At production scale

The webhook endpoint is one of the few genuinely public, attacker-reachable surfaces. Signature verification is non-negotiable — without it, anyone can submit goals as any tenant. Dedup matters because webhook providers deliver at-least-once, so the same payment.failed can arrive three times and must fire one goal. Rate-limiting absorbs the flood when an upstream misbehaves.

Failure modes

  • Unverified webhooks. Attacker-submitted goals.
  • No dedup. One event firing three goals.
  • No rate-limit. An upstream flood becoming your outage.

Choose it when

  • External systems should drive agent actions.

03Data-change and IoT triggers#

PartialSourceImpl7/10Criticality6/10

Goals that fire when data changes or a sensor reports — a row inserted, a metric crossing a threshold, a geofence entered — with condition evaluation deciding whether the change warrants action.

Mechanism

Data-change triggers watch a source (a table, a stream) and fire when a condition matches. IoT triggers consume sensor and device signals — MQTT messages, geofence events, sensor thresholds. A condition evaluator decides whether a given change is significant enough to act on, so not every row insert or sensor reading becomes a goal. Monitoring triggers watch metrics and fire on threshold breaches.

In AgentVerse

  • app/triggers/data/consumers.pydata-change triggers
  • app/triggers/iot/mqtt.py, geofence.py, sensor.pyIoT sources
  • app/triggers/condition/evaluator.pycondition evaluation
  • app/triggers/monitoring/parsers.py, advanced/consumers.pymonitoring and advanced triggers

Worked example

data-change: a high-value order inserted
 condition: order.amount > ₹500,000 AND customer.risk = high → fire a
 fraud-review goal (most orders do not match → no goal)
IoT: a cold-storage sensor reports temperature > threshold for 5 min
 → fire an alert-and-remediate goal

At production scale

The condition evaluator is what keeps data and IoT triggers from firing constantly — the difference between "a goal per row insert" (unusable) and "a goal per significant change" (useful). Threshold and debounce logic (temperature over threshold for 5 minutes) prevents a flapping sensor from firing a hundred goals. These triggers make the platform reactive to the physical and data world.

Failure modes

  • Firing on every change. A goal per row insert.
  • Flapping sensors. No debounce, a hundred goals.
  • Missed significant changes. A condition too narrow.

Choose it when

  • Agents should react to data or physical-world changes.

04Dispatch, dead-letter, and trigger safety#

ShippedSafetyImpl8/10Criticality9/10

The controls that make autonomous triggers safe: re-check authorisation at fire time, rate-limit and bulkhead per tenant, quota-limit, and dead-letter failures — because a trigger acts without a human watching.

Mechanism

The dispatcher fires the goal but first applies the trigger-specific safety layer: re-check that the authorisation the trigger was created under is still valid (the user may have left), enforce per-tenant rate limits and bulkheads (a trigger must not stampede the fleet), enforce quotas, and dead-letter failures with backoff. A circuit breaker stops a repeatedly-failing trigger. State machines track trigger lifecycle; simulation lets a trigger be tested before it goes live.

In AgentVerse

  • app/triggers/dispatcher.py, state_machine.pydispatch and lifecycle
  • app/triggers/dlq.py, circuit_breaker.py, quota.pyDLQ, breaker, quota
  • app/triggers/rbac.py, events.py, metrics.pyauthorisation, events, metrics
  • app/triggers/simulation.py, consumers/hitl.py, consumers/chain.py, consumers/memory.pysimulation, HITL, chaining, memory consumers

Worked example

a scheduled trigger fires
 re-check auth: the creating user still has permission? → yes (or the
   trigger is disabled if they left)
 rate-limit + bulkhead: within the tenant's ceiling → proceed
 dispatch a normal governed goal
 [on repeated failure] → DLQ + backoff + breaker → stop retrying, alert

At production scale

The stale-authorisation check is the subtle, critical one: a trigger created by an employee who has since left must not keep acting on their authority — so authorisation is re-checked at fire time, not just at creation. Rate-limiting and bulkheading matter because an unbounded trigger is a self-inflicted load spike that no human requested. Simulation before go-live catches the trigger that would fire far more often than intended.

Failure modes

  • Stale authorisation. A trigger acting for a departed user.
  • Unbounded firing. A load spike nobody scheduled.
  • Unattended DLQ. Failed triggers silently dropped.
  • No simulation. A trigger that fires far too often, discovered live.

Choose it when

  • Always, for any trigger — this is the price of autonomy.

What is missing here

  • Trigger impact preview. Simulation tests behaviour, but a "this trigger would have fired N times last month" preview before activation is thin.
  • Cross-trigger coordination. Two triggers firing overlapping goals are not deduplicated at the goal level.
  • Prospective-memory integration. An agent setting its own future trigger (chapter 3) is a thinner path than externally-configured triggers.
  • Complex event processing. Conditions are per-event; correlating a pattern across multiple events over time is future work.

Reliability & QoS
CH 28VII · Not on the list

Reliability & QoS

Bulkheads, breakers, idempotency, backpressure, degraded mode.

Concepts
5
Mean impl
7.6
Mean criticality
9.2
Shipped
3
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

Reliability primitives appeared throughout the book as they were needed; this chapter assembles them as a system and adds the quality-of-service layer on top. The distinction: reliability keeps the platform correct under failure (idempotency, rollback, breakers); QoS keeps it fair and responsive under load (priority, backpressure, bulkheads, degraded mode).

The unifying idea is graceful degradation under both failure and load. A production agent platform never has the luxury of a clean environment — providers flap, tenants stampede, connectors die — so every primitive here answers "how do we stay correct and fair when something is wrong", and the answer is never "fall over" and never "silently do less without saying so".

Reliability and QoS

01Failure classification and recovery policy#

ShippedReliabilityImpl8/10Criticality10/10

Not all failures are equal: classify each — transient, rate-limited, auth, missing-input, invalid-plan, permanent — and map the class to a response, because retrying an auth failure is as wrong as escalating a timeout.

Mechanism

A failure classifier maps an error to a class; a recovery policy maps the class to an action; a retry strategy selector picks the backoff shape; an escalation policy decides when a human is involved. This is the recovery subsystem introduced in chapter 1, presented here as the platform's central failure-handling brain — every subsystem's failures flow through the same classification so responses are consistent.

In AgentVerse

  • app/recovery/failure_classifier.py, recovery_policy.pyclassify → respond
  • app/recovery/retry_strategy_selector.py, escalation_policy.pybackoff and escalation
  • app/recovery/recovery_trace.pywhat was tried and why

Worked example

failure                    class          response
timeout / 5xx              transient      retry, exp backoff + jitter
429                        rate-limited   retry after window; shed if repeated
403 / 401                  auth           no retry → escalate
"missing account id"       missing-input  clarification to a human
"step precondition false"  invalid-plan   replan with the failure as context
"unsupported operation"    permanent      fail; roll back side effects

At production scale

Consistent classification is what keeps failure handling sane across dozens of subsystems — the same timeout means the same thing whether it came from a tool, an embedder, or a database. The recovery trace is the audit of what was attempted, which is essential when a goal took nine iterations to fail: you can see it retried a permanent error four times because it was misclassified. Full treatment in chapter 1.

Failure modes

  • Misclassification. Retrying the permanent, escalating the transient.
  • Uniform retry. The same backoff for every failure class.

Choose it when

  • Always. Failure is the normal case in distributed systems.

02Idempotency and deduplication#

ShippedReliabilityImpl8/10Criticality10/10

In a system that retries constantly, safety means a repeated operation has the same effect as a single one — an idempotency key per write, dedup of repeated requests, so a retry never double-charges.

Mechanism

Every write carries an idempotency key derived from goal + step + argument hash, so the target (or the platform) recognises a retried call as the same call and does not repeat the side effect. Deduplication catches repeated requests earlier — the same goal submitted twice, the same webhook delivered twice — and returns the prior result. Together they make at-least-once delivery safe, which is the only delivery guarantee a distributed system can cheaply offer.

In AgentVerse

  • app/reliability/idempotency.pyidempotency keys
  • app/reliability/dedup.py, app/services/dedup.py, app/gateway/dedup_scheduler.pydeduplication
  • app/reliability/goal_lifecycle.pylifecycle state that dedup keys off

Worked example

goal retried after a worker crash mid-step-4 (create invoice)
 step 4's idempotency key = hash(goal, step 4, invoice args)
 the ERP recognises the key → returns the already-created invoice
 → the customer is billed once, not twice
without idempotency, the retry creates a second invoice

At production scale

Idempotency is non-negotiable for any agent that writes, because retries are constant — a worker crash, a timeout, a rebalance all trigger them. The key must be derived deterministically from the operation, not generated fresh, or the retry looks like a new operation. This is the primitive that lets you use at-least-once delivery (cheap and reliable) instead of exactly-once (expensive and often impossible).

Failure modes

  • Retry without idempotency. Duplicate side effects.
  • Non-deterministic keys. Retries not recognised as repeats.
  • Dedup window too short. A late retry treated as new.

Choose it when

  • Any write-capable agent — so any production agent.

03Bulkheads and circuit breakers#

ShippedIsolationImpl8/10Criticality9/10

Two isolation primitives: bulkheads cap per-tenant concurrency so one cannot starve the fleet, and breakers stop calling a failing dependency so its outage does not become yours.

Mechanism

A bulkhead is a concurrency ceiling per tenant (and per resource pool) — a fan-out that would exhaust the workers or connections queues instead. A circuit breaker fronts each flaky dependency: after repeated failures it opens and fails fast (or serves stale) until a probe confirms recovery. Breaker state is shared across replicas via Redis, so the whole fleet learns a dependency is down rather than each node discovering it independently.

In AgentVerse

  • app/reliability/bulkhead.pyper-tenant concurrency
  • app/reliability/circuit_breaker.py, redis_circuit_breaker.pybreakers, cross-replica state
  • app/providers/circuit_breaker.pyprovider breakers (chapter 16)
  • app/mcp/client.pybreaker + stale-cache on tool calls (chapter 19)

Worked example

bulkhead   acme capped at 50 concurrent tool calls → a 200-way fan-out
           queues; other tenants keep their capacity
breaker    the CRM connector fails 5× → open (shared via Redis, whole fleet
           stops calling it) → 60s later a probe → recovered → close

At production scale

The bulkhead is the ceiling that no amount of agent spawning (chapter 1) or trigger firing (chapter 27) can breach — it is what makes multi-tenancy survivable under load. Cross-replica breaker state is the detail that matters: without it, a hundred replicas each hammer a dead provider a hundred times before giving up. Together they turn "one thing is broken" into "one thing is isolated".

Failure modes

  • No bulkhead. One tenant's fan-out starving all.
  • Per-replica breakers. The fleet not learning collectively.
  • No stale fallback. A read failing when a cached answer would do.

Choose it when

  • Any multi-tenant system with external dependencies.

04Priority, backpressure, and queue policy#

PartialQoSImpl7/10Criticality8/10

Under load, decide what runs now, what waits, and what is shed — priority for what matters, backpressure to slow intake before the system tips over, and a queue policy that is fair by design.

Mechanism

A QoS layer over the queue: priority policy ranks work (an interactive goal over a batch one, a paying tenant's over a free one); backpressure signals upstream to slow down when the system is saturated, rather than accepting work it cannot serve; a queue policy governs fairness so no class is starved. A scheduler applies these. The goal is to degrade predictably under load — the right work still runs, the rest waits or is shed with a clear signal.

In AgentVerse

  • app/qos/priority_policy.py, queue_policy.py, scheduler.pypriority, fairness, scheduling
  • app/qos/backpressure.py, qos_trace.pybackpressure and its trace
  • app/scaling/priority_queue.py, celery_app.pythe queues it governs (chapter 20)

Worked example

load spike: 10,000 goals arrive in a minute
 priority: interactive + enterprise goals run first
 backpressure: intake slows, upstream told to retry later (not silently dropped)
 fairness: free tier still gets its guaranteed share, not zero
 result: predictable degradation — the important work is unaffected

At production scale

Backpressure is the primitive that separates a system that degrades gracefully from one that collapses: accepting work faster than you can serve it just moves the failure downstream and makes it worse. Priority is how you honour SLAs under contention — the enterprise tenant you promised 4-second latency should not queue behind a free tenant's backfill (chapter 20). QoS is where fairness stops being an aspiration and becomes a policy.

Failure modes

  • No backpressure. Accepting more than you can serve, then collapsing.
  • Priority without fairness. Low-priority work starved entirely.
  • Silent shedding. Dropping work without telling the caller.

Choose it when

  • Any system that experiences load spikes — so any real one.

05Degraded mode and readiness gates#

PartialResilienceImpl7/10Criticality9/10

When a dependency is down, run with less rather than failing entirely — lexical search without the embedder, deterministic guardrails without the toxicity model — and refuse to serve only what genuinely cannot run safely.

Mechanism

A degraded-mode policy defines what the platform does when a dependency is unavailable: fall back to the lexical retrieval path if the embedder is down (chapter 7), run deterministic guardrails if the toxicity model is down (chapter 12), delegate to a ready RAG strategy if one is unavailable (chapter 2). A readiness gate refuses to serve only what cannot run safely in degraded mode — a fail-closed control (chapter 12) must not degrade to fail-open. Dependency health drives both.

In AgentVerse

  • app/runtime_readiness/degraded_mode_policy.py, readiness_gate.py, dependency_health.pydegraded mode and readiness
  • app/rag/gateway.pystrategy delegation (chapter 2)
  • app/observability/health.py, app/api/public_status.pyhealth and status

Worked example

embedder provider down
 degraded mode: retrieval falls back to BM25 + trigram, flagged degraded
 guardrails: deterministic checks still run; toxicity model unavailable →
   for high-risk channels, BLOCK (never fail-open)
 status page: "semantic search degraded" — announced, not silent
 readiness gate: refuses only the operations that cannot run safely

At production scale

Degraded mode is the difference between a partial outage and a total one — most of the platform keeps working when one dependency fails, and the reduction is announced rather than silent. The one inviolable rule: fail-closed controls never degrade to fail-open. A toxicity model being down is a reason to run stricter deterministic checks, never a reason to skip safety. Announce degradation on the status page so users know why quality changed.

Failure modes

  • All-or-nothing. One dependency down taking everything down.
  • Fail-closed degrading to fail-open. Skipping safety when a model is down.
  • Silent degradation. Users blaming the product.

Choose it when

  • Any platform with external dependencies that can fail independently.

What is missing here

  • Adaptive concurrency limits. Bulkheads are configured, not learned from observed latency and error rates under load.
  • Chaos testing. The primitives exist; systematic fault injection to verify they work together under failure is thin (chapter 31).
  • Cross-region failover. Degraded mode handles dependency failure; regional failover for the datastores themselves is future work (chapter 32).
  • Predictive backpressure. Backpressure reacts to saturation; anticipating a spike from leading indicators would smooth degradation.

Cost & capacity engineering

Unit economics of an agent, and how to make them survive scale.

Concepts
4
Mean impl
7.8
Mean criticality
8.8
Shipped
3
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

An agent has unit economics, and if you do not understand them you will discover them on an invoice. The cost of a goal is not a mystery — it decomposes cleanly — and the levers to reduce it are known and ordered. This chapter is the economics of running agents at scale: what a goal costs, why, and how to make those numbers survive growth.

The core formula is worth memorising: cost per goal ≈ iterations × (tokens per iteration × price) + tool cost + compute cost. Every optimisation targets one factor, and they must be attacked in the right order, because the tempting lever (a cheaper model) is usually not the biggest one (fewer iterations, fewer tokens).

Cost and capacity

01The unit economics of a goal#

ShippedEconomicsImpl8/10Criticality10/10

Cost per goal decomposes into iterations, tokens per iteration, price, tool cost, and compute — measure each, attribute it (including sub-agents), and you can explain and control the bill.

Mechanism

The cost tracker accumulates real spend per run across every component and attributes it to the goal, including descendants of spawned agents. The breakdown by component (planner, executor, verifier, embeddings, reranker, tools, code execution) is what makes cost actionable — "this goal cost $0.42" is not useful; "51% of it was executor tokens, 38% of which were tool schemas" points at the fix.

In AgentVerse

  • app/intelligence/cost_tracker.py, cost_optimizer.pyper-run accumulation and analysis
  • app/observability/cost_breakdown.py, cost_breakdown_api.pythe breakdown
  • app/governance/cost.py, pricing.pythe controller and price table (chapter 13)
  • app/tenancy/billing.pytenant accounting

Worked example

goal class "invoice reconciliation", cost breakdown
 executor 51% (tool schemas 38% of that) · tools 15% · planner 15%
 verifier 11% · code exec 6% · embeddings+rerank 2%
 total $0.42/goal
the breakdown says: narrow the tool schemas first — biggest, easiest win

At production scale

Attribute descendant spend to the parent, or multi-agent goals look cheap and your per-goal costs do not reconcile with the provider invoice — the moment finance stops trusting the numbers. Publish cost per goal class to the teams that own those goals; visibility changes behaviour faster than any optimiser. The breakdown is what turns the recurring "just use a bigger model" argument into a specific, non-model fix.

Failure modes

  • Unattributed sub-agent spend. Costs that do not reconcile.
  • Total without breakdown. A number nobody can act on.
  • Model tokens only. Missing tool and compute cost.

Choose it when

  • From the first production goal.

02The cost levers, in order#

ShippedOptimisationImpl8/10Criticality9/10

Attack cost in the order that pays: iterations first (better planning, lessons, stall detection), then tokens (narrow schemas, tighter retrieval, caching), then price (per-role routing) — never price first.

Mechanism

The levers, ordered by impact and by how quality-neutral they are. Iterations: better planning, recalled lessons, stall detection, and cheap replans cut the multiplier that dominates cost. Tokens per iteration: narrowing tool schemas (often 30–40% of the prompt), tighter retrieval, prompt compression, and caching. Price: per-role model routing, shadow-tested downgrades. Starting with price risks quality for the smallest gain; starting with iterations and tokens is usually quality-neutral or positive.

In AgentVerse

  • app/optimization/token_optimizer.py, cache_optimizer.py, cost_optimizer.py, model_optimizer.py, latency_optimizer.pythe optimisers
  • app/agent/tool_selector.pyschema narrowing (the biggest lever)
  • app/rag/semantic_cache.py, app/mcp/tool_cache.pythe two caches that matter most
  • app/agent/prompt_compressor.pytoken reduction

Worked example

baseline $0.42/goal, quality 0.87
1 narrow tool schemas 34→9      −$0.11  (also improves selection → fewer iters)
2 semantic cache (31% hit)      −$0.06
3 stall detection tuning        −$0.07  (−0.6 iterations)
4 verifier model large→mid      −$0.09  (shadow-tested, quality held)
result $0.09/goal, quality 0.88 — 79% cheaper, quality unchanged

At production scale

The order matters because the levers interact: narrowing tool schemas cuts tokens and improves selection accuracy and thereby reduces iterations — one change, three factors. Model downgrades, the most tempting lever, come last and only after shadow testing (chapter 16) confirms quality holds. Report every optimisation with its quality delta; a cost win that lowers success is a loss.

Failure modes

  • Price first. Quality risk for the smallest gain.
  • Cost without quality. Optimising a proxy.
  • Caching personalised answers. A correctness bug sold as a saving.

Choose it when

  • As soon as volume is real.

03Capacity planning under variance#

PartialCapacityImpl7/10Criticality8/10

Agent workloads have enormous variance — a 200ms lookup and a four-hour audit run on the same platform — so capacity is planned against a distribution of goal shapes, not a single mean.

Mechanism

Because per-goal graph assembly (chapter 1) makes cost and duration vary by orders of magnitude, capacity planning uses the distribution: p50, p95, p99 of iterations, tokens, and duration per goal class, plus the mix of classes. Provision workers per plan queue (chapter 20) to meet each tier's SLA at its p95, and use autoscaling metrics that reflect agent work (queue depth, in-flight goals) rather than CPU alone.

In AgentVerse

  • app/scaling/celery_app.py, parallel_executor.py, priority_queue.pyworker pools and parallelism
  • app/observability/metrics.py, slo_tracker.pythe distribution metrics
  • agent-verse-frontend/src/features/observabilityautoscale metrics surface (the "Scaling & Autoscale" community)

Worked example

goal class distribution (per day)
 simple lookups   70% · p95 0.8s · $0.01
 standard goals   25% · p95 40s  · $0.40
 expert audits     5% · p95 25min · $6.00
capacity: provision enterprise-queue workers for the audit p95, not the mean
autoscale on queue depth + in-flight goals, not CPU

At production scale

Planning against the mean is the classic capacity mistake for agents — the mean is meaningless when the distribution spans four orders of magnitude. Provision for the p95 of each class on its own queue, and scale on queue depth: an agent worker waiting on a slow tool shows low CPU while being fully occupied, so CPU-based autoscaling under-provisions exactly when you need capacity.

Failure modes

  • Planning against the mean. Under-provisioned for the tail.
  • CPU-based autoscaling. Blind to IO-bound agent work.
  • One pool for all classes. The audit starving the lookups.

Choose it when

  • Any workload with variance — which agent workloads always have.

04The economics of caching#

ShippedOptimisationImpl8/10Criticality8/10

Caching is the highest-return cost lever on repetitive workloads — semantic cache on retrieval, tool-result cache, embedding cache — but each has a correctness boundary that, crossed, turns a saving into a bug.

Mechanism

Three caches with three risk profiles. The semantic cache (chapter 2) serves a repeated question's answer by embedding match — highest return on FAQ/support, but a loose threshold serves the wrong answer. The tool-result cache serves a repeated read — safe for idempotent reads, wrong for anything time-sensitive. The embedding cache (chapter 7) serves a repeated text's vector — safe as long as the model is in the key. Each must be tenant-scoped and invalidated on the underlying change.

In AgentVerse

  • app/rag/semantic_cache.py, llm_response_cache.py, vector_cache_backend.pysemantic and response caches
  • app/mcp/tool_cache.pyToolResultCache
  • app/optimization/cache_optimizer.pyhit-rate vs risk tuning

Worked example

support workload
 semantic cache: 31% hit → 31% of pipelines skipped → largest single saving
 tool cache: repeated reads within a goal served from cache
 embedding cache: repeated queries' vectors reused
boundaries: tenant in every key · invalidate on ingest · never cache
 personalised or time-sensitive answers

At production scale

On repetitive workloads (support, FAQ) semantic caching commonly removes 25–40% of pipeline executions — the single largest cost reduction available. But the correctness boundaries are unforgiving: a cross-tenant cache hit is a data leak, a stale cache after ingest is a wrong answer, and a cached personalised answer is a privacy bug. Tune hit-rate against these risks deliberately (chapter 2's semantic cache concept).

Failure modes

  • Cross-tenant hit. A data leak.
  • Stale after ingest. A wrong answer served fast.
  • Cached personalised content. A privacy bug.

Choose it when

  • Repetitive query distributions — the common case in support and FAQ.

What is missing here

  • Predictive cost estimation. Cost is measured after the fact and plans are estimated (chapter 1), but a learned per-goal-class cost predictor for admission control is thin.
  • Cost-anomaly detection. Spend is attributed but a per-tenant anomaly alarm is not wired (chapter 11).
  • Autoscaling on agent-native signals. Queue-depth scaling exists; a richer model using goal-class mix and predicted duration is future work.
  • Spot/preemptible execution. No use of cheaper preemptible capacity for interruptible batch goals, which the checkpointing (chapter 1) would make safe.

Data lifecycle & provenance

Classification, residency, retention, legal hold, export, deletion.

Concepts
4
Mean impl
8.0
Mean criticality
9.2
Shipped
4
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

An agent platform accumulates data everywhere — documents, chunks, embeddings, memory, traces, screenshots, transcripts, audit — and most of it describes real people. The data lifecycle is the discipline of knowing what you hold, why, where, for how long, and being able to prove you deleted it. It is where the platform meets the law, and where "we'll add compliance later" becomes a re-architecture.

The organising idea is classification drives everything downstream. Once a piece of data is classified — public, internal, confidential, restricted — its handling, retention, residency, and deletion follow automatically. Classify at ingestion and the rest of the lifecycle is enforcement; skip it and every later obligation becomes a manual hunt.

The lifecycle

01Data classification#

ShippedFoundationImpl8/10Criticality10/10

Every datum is tagged — public, internal, confidential, restricted — at creation, and that tag drives handling, retention, residency, and deletion for the rest of its life.

Mechanism

A classifier assigns a data class from content and context: PII detectors, source, and domain rules. The class is stored as metadata on the datum (chunk, memory row, document) and consulted at every boundary — retrieval filters by allowed classes (chapter 14), redaction acts on sensitive classes (chapter 12), retention and residency policies key off the class. Classifying at creation is what makes the rest automatic.

In AgentVerse

  • app/data_classification/classifier.py, schema.pyclassification and the taxonomy
  • app/data_classification/redaction.pyacting on the class
  • app/memory/contracts.pyClassification on every memory row (chapter 3)
  • app/ingestion/pipeline.pyclassification at stage 4 (chapter 5)

Worked example

an ingested invoice
 classifier → confidential (contains vendor bank details, PII)
 stored as metadata on every chunk
 → retrieval excludes it for principals below confidential
 → redaction applies before external tool calls
 → retention: 7 years (regulatory) · residency: tenant region
one classification, five downstream behaviours

At production scale

Classification at creation is the difference between compliance-by-design and a permanent manual burden. Get it right at ingestion and a data-subject request or an audit is a query; skip it and both become a hunt across every store. The four-level taxonomy is deliberately simple — enough to drive behaviour, few enough that classification is reliable.

Failure modes

  • Unclassified data. Every downstream obligation becomes manual.
  • Classification only in one store. Copies losing their class.
  • Over-classification. Everything restricted, nothing usable.

Choose it when

  • Always, at creation, before the data spreads.

02Provenance#

ShippedProvenanceImpl8/10Criticality8/10

Every datum knows where it came from — which source, which document, which revision, which extraction — so a claim can be traced to evidence and a data-subject request can find every derived copy.

Mechanism

Provenance records the origin chain: a chunk cites its document and source revision (chapter 4), a memory cites its evidence (chapter 3), a claim cites the chunk that supports it (chapter 18). A source reference is the canonical pointer; a claim trace links an assertion back through the chain to its origin. This is both a grounding mechanism (verify a claim) and a compliance mechanism (find everything derived from a subject's data).

In AgentVerse

  • app/provenance/source_ref.py, claim_trace.py, ledger.pysource references and claim traces
  • app/provenance/provenance_verifier.py, export.pyverification and WORM export
  • app/ingestion/provenance_builder.pybuilding provenance at ingestion

Worked example

a data-subject request for "j.patel"
 provenance finds: 3 documents mentioning them → 41 derived chunks →
 their embeddings → 4 memory rows citing those chunks → 2 cache entries
without provenance, finding the derived copies is a manual search that
misses things — and missing a copy is a compliance failure

At production scale

Provenance is what makes both grounding and deletion tractable. For grounding, it is the chain from a claim to its evidence (chapter 18); for compliance, it is the map that a deletion cascade follows. The two uses share the same records, which is why building provenance at ingestion pays twice. WORM export preserves the chain even against tampering.

Failure modes

  • Broken chains. Derived data that cannot be traced to its origin.
  • Provenance not built at ingestion. Retrofitting it is nearly impossible.

Choose it when

  • Any data that must be verifiable or deletable.

03Retention and residency#

ShippedPolicyImpl8/10Criticality9/10

Data has a lifespan and a location: retention policies expire it when its purpose ends, residency policies keep it in the region the tenant requires — both driven by classification and compliance regime.

Mechanism

A retention policy sets an expiry per data class and regime (a HIPAA record 6 years, a raw screenshot 7 days); an archive policy moves cold data to cheaper storage before expiry; an export policy governs what may leave. Residency pins where data may live — enforced at storage and at the connector, so an EU tenant's data neither rests nor transits outside its region. Both key off the classification and the compliance bundle (chapter 13).

In AgentVerse

  • app/lifecycle/retention_policy.py, archive_policy.py, export_policy.pyretention, archival, export
  • app/governance/compliance_bundles.pyregime-driven retention (chapter 13)
  • app/scaling/memory_tasks.pythe jobs that expire and archive

Worked example

data class          retention        residency
raw screenshot      7 days           tenant region
invoice (financial) 7 years          tenant region
chat transcript     90 days          tenant region
audit entry         7 years, WORM    tenant region
an EU tenant: connectors and storage refuse to place data outside the EU

At production scale

Retention is both a compliance requirement and a cost control — data that lives forever is a growing liability and a growing bill. Residency is a hard requirement for regulated tenants and must be enforced at every layer, including the connectors that could egress data out of region and the model providers whose regions matter. Default retention to a policy, never to infinite; the row nobody set a policy on is the one an auditor finds.

Failure modes

  • Infinite retention by default. A growing liability.
  • Residency only in storage. A connector egressing out of region.
  • Retention without archival. Hot storage for cold data.

Choose it when

  • Any data about people, or any regulated tenant.

04Deletion, cascade, and legal hold#

ShippedDeletionImpl8/10Criticality10/10

Real deletion is a cascade across every store a datum was copied into — rows, embeddings, caches, traces, screenshots — provable, and suspended by legal hold where the law requires the data kept.

Mechanism

A deletion orchestrator, given a subject or a datum, uses provenance to find every derived copy and removes each: the source row, its chunks and embeddings, cache entries, memory rows, artifacts, and (per policy) trace data — producing a deletion receipt that is itself audited. Legal hold is the exception: it suspends deletion for named subjects or matters, because destroying data under hold is a worse offence than retaining it. The hold's application is audited too.

In AgentVerse

  • app/lifecycle/deletion_orchestrator.pythe cascade
  • app/lifecycle/legal_hold_policy.py, app/governance/legal_holds.pylegal hold
  • app/api/dpdp.pydata-subject request surface
  • app/memory/postgres_repository.pymemory deletion (chapter 3)

Worked example

deletion request: subject "j.patel@example"
 legal hold check → none active for this subject
 provenance → 3 docs, 41 chunks, 41 embeddings, 4 memories, 2 cache entries,
   2 screenshots
 orchestrator deletes all → deletion receipt (counts, timestamps) → audited
if a hold were active: deletion SUSPENDED, the requester informed, the hold
 recorded

At production scale

Deletion is much harder than it looks because a datum has been copied into six or seven stores, and missing one is a compliance failure that surfaces at the worst time. Design the cascade on day one — retrofitting a deletion path across every store is a quarter of work, and provenance is what makes it possible at all. Legal hold is the correct exception mechanism: it must be able to override deletion, and its own application must be audited. Full memory-deletion treatment in chapter 3.

Failure modes

  • Orphaned embeddings. The row deleted, the vector still retrievable.
  • Cached content. A deleted datum served from cache.
  • Deletion during hold. Destroying evidence under legal hold.
  • No proof. Deletion you cannot demonstrate.

Choose it when

  • Always. Any system holding data about people needs this before the first row.

What is missing here

  • Automated classification accuracy monitoring. Classification drives everything, but its accuracy is not continuously measured against human-corrected samples.
  • Deletion verification. The cascade produces a receipt; an independent verification pass that confirms nothing survived is thin.
  • Cross-region data movement audit. Residency is enforced; a continuous audit that no datum crossed a region boundary is future work.
  • Consent lineage. Provenance tracks data origin; linking each datum to the consent that permits its processing is not first-class.

CH 31VII · Not on the list

Testing & certification

Simulation, red team, golden datasets, readiness gates, replay.

Concepts
4
Mean impl
7.2
Mean criticality
8.5
Shipped
1
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

You cannot test an agent the way you test a function, because its output is non-deterministic and its actions touch real systems. This chapter is how you gain confidence anyway: simulate before you execute, attack before an attacker does, measure against golden data, gate on readiness, and replay what happened.

The unifying principle is prove it in a sandbox before it touches production. Every technique here is a way to exercise an agent's behaviour — under mock tools, adversarial inputs, or replayed history — without the cost of a real mistake, so that when it does act for real, it has already been shown to behave.

Testing and certification

01Simulation and mock-tool sandboxes#

PartialTestingImpl7/10Criticality8/10

Run an agent against mock tools that return realistic results but have no real effects — so a goal that would file a return or send a payment can be exercised end-to-end, safely, thousands of times.

Mechanism

A simulation environment provides mock implementations of tools that return plausible results without side effects. An agent runs its full loop — plan, execute, verify — against these, so you observe its behaviour, its tool choices, and its failures without touching a real system. This is the substrate for evals (chapter 10), for certifying code-capable strategies (chapter 25), and for testing goals that are too dangerous to run for real during development.

In AgentVerse

  • app/enterprise/simulation.pythe mock-tool sandbox
  • app/sandbox_runtime/simulation_runner.py, sandbox_trace.pyrunning and tracing simulations
  • app/testing/harness.pythe test harness
  • app/api/simulation · frontend features/simulationthe surface

Worked example

test a "file GST amendment" goal
 mock tools: gst.fetch_filed returns a realistic filed return; gst.file_return
   records the call but files nothing
 the agent runs its full loop → observe: correct plan? right tools? gate hit?
 run 500 variations → measure behaviour distribution
no real filing, no real risk, full-loop confidence

At production scale

Simulation is what lets you develop and test dangerous goals at all — you cannot iterate on a payment-filing agent by filing real payments. It is also the engine under offline evals and strategy certification. The one risk is mock fidelity: mocks that diverge from real tool behaviour pass in simulation and fail in production, so mocks must be kept realistic and cross-checked against live behaviour periodically.

Failure modes

  • Unrealistic mocks. Passing simulation, failing live.
  • Simulation only for happy paths. Untested failure behaviour.

Choose it when

  • Any dangerous goal, and as the substrate for evals and certification.

02Red teaming#

ShippedSecurityImpl8/10Criticality10/10

Attack the agent before an attacker does: a growing corpus of injection, exfiltration, jailbreak, and abuse attempts, replayed on every change, with zero tolerance for a new pass.

Mechanism

A red-team corpus of adversarial cases — direct and indirect injection, encoded payloads, exfiltration attempts, dangerous-command generation, jailbreaks, cross-tenant probing — each asserting the control that should stop it. It runs as a safety eval (chapter 10) on every prompt, model, and guardrail change. The corpus only grows: every real incident and near-miss becomes a permanent case, so the platform can never regress on an attack it has seen.

In AgentVerse

  • app/enterprise/red_team.py, red_team_corpus.pythe red-team engine and corpus
  • app/evals/safety_score.pysafety scoring (chapter 10)
  • app/intelligence/indirect_injection.py, encoding_attacks.pythe detectors under test (chapter 12)
  • app/api/red-team · frontend features/red-teamthe operator surface

Worked example

red-team run on a prompt change
 190 cases across 8 attack categories
 189 blocked by the asserted control · 1 new pass (indirect injection)
 → BLOCKED: zero tolerance → the change cannot ship until fixed
the one that got through becomes a permanent regression case

At production scale

Red teaming is the safety net that makes fast iteration safe — prompt changes are the most common cause of safety regressions, and running the corpus on every change catches them before they ship. The ratchet is the point: the corpus never shrinks, so the platform's security monotonically improves. Asserting the specific control (not just the outcome) tells you not only that an attack was blocked but by what, so a regression is diagnosable. Full treatment in chapter 10.

Failure modes

  • Stale corpus. Yesterday's attacks only.
  • Tolerance for a new pass. One relaxed case becoming policy.
  • Testing only direct injection. Missing the harder indirect vector.

Choose it when

  • Always, before any external exposure.

03Golden datasets and regression gates#

PartialTestingImpl7/10Criticality8/10

A curated set of cases with known-good outcomes, built from real production runs, against which every change is measured — and a gate that blocks a change that regresses a protected dimension.

Mechanism

Golden datasets are curated cases (inputs plus expected outcomes or rubrics) drawn from real production — especially failures, which become permanent regression cases (chapter 10). A regression baseline records the incumbent's scores; a regression gate compares a candidate and blocks on a regression beyond tolerance in a protected dimension (safety and grounding at zero tolerance). This is the mechanism that makes rapid iteration safe: nothing ships that regresses what mattered.

In AgentVerse

  • app/api/golden_datasets.py, app/evals/dataset_builder.pycurated sets, built from production
  • app/evals/regression_baseline.py, regression_gate.pybaseline and gate
  • app/evals/certification_policy.pywhat must pass (chapter 10)

Worked example

golden set: 420 cases, half from real failures
 candidate prompt change → run the set
 goal 0.89 (was 0.87) · grounding 0.82 (was 0.82) · safety 0.98 (was 1.00)
 → BLOCKED on safety (zero tolerance) → fix or named override
the failures that built this set can never recur silently

At production scale

Golden datasets built from real failures are worth far more than synthetic ones — they encode the actual ways the system has been wrong, and the gate ensures it is never wrong that way again. The discipline is to feed every production failure back into the set (chapter 10's online-to-offline bridge), so the safety net tightens over time. Keep safety and grounding at zero tolerance; everything else can trade.

Failure modes

  • Synthetic-only sets. Easier than reality, flattering every change.
  • No gate. Regressions found by customers.
  • Auto-updating baseline. Drift with nothing to compare against.

Choose it when

  • Before the first automated change ships.

04Readiness gates, certification, and replay#

PartialOperationsImpl7/10Criticality8/10

Before anything serves production traffic it must pass a readiness gate and be certified against evidence; after it runs, replay lets you reconstruct exactly what happened for debugging or audit.

Mechanism

A readiness gate refuses to serve if a required control or dependency is unavailable (chapter 28). Certification binds a version to eval evidence — this agent, strategy, or connector passed these suites at these scores, approved by this person (chapter 10) — and uncertified configurations stay in the lab. Replay reconstructs a past goal from its recorded events and prompt recipes (chapter 11), so an incident is reconstruction, not archaeology, and a fix can be tested against the exact failing run.

In AgentVerse

  • app/runtime_readiness/readiness_gate.py, dependency_health.pyreadiness
  • app/orchestration/strategy_certification.py, app/rag/certification.py, app/mcp/certification.pycertification (chapter 10)
  • app/api/replay.py, app/coordination/replay.pyreplay
  • app/observability/runtime_decision_trace.pythe record replay reconstructs from (chapter 11)

Worked example

promote agent fin-ops@v13
 readiness gate: all required controls available? → yes
 certification: passed goal/retrieval/grounding/safety suites, approved → yes
 → serves production
incident on an earlier run: replay g-8891 from its events + prompt recipes
 → reproduce exactly → test the fix against the real failing case

At production scale

Certification is how you safely offer a large catalogue of agents, strategies, and connectors — each proven against evidence before it serves real tenants, and certificates expiring on model changes (chapter 10). Replay is the incident-response superpower: with recorded events and prompt recipes (stored, not full prompts, for cost and privacy — chapter 8), you reconstruct any run exactly and test a fix against it, turning speculative debugging into deterministic reproduction.

Failure modes

  • Uncertified paths reachable. The gate bypassable.
  • Certificates without expiry. Outliving the models they were measured against.
  • Replay impossible. Mutable sources or missing recipes.

Choose it when

  • Any multi-configuration platform, and before any incident.

What is missing here

  • Chaos and fault injection. Reliability primitives (chapter 28) exist; systematic fault injection to verify they hold together under failure is thin.
  • Mock-fidelity monitoring. Simulation mocks can drift from real tool behaviour with no continuous cross-check.
  • Automated red-team generation. The corpus grows from incidents; a generator that produces novel attacks to probe for unknown weaknesses is future work.
  • Property-based testing for agents. Cases are enumerated; testing invariants ("never calls a forbidden tool") across generated inputs is not first-class.

Scale playbook

Deployment topology and the numbers at 10, 10k, and 10M goals/day.

Concepts
4
Mean impl
7.5
Mean criticality
8.0
Shipped
3
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

Everything in this book changes character at scale. A pattern that is elegant at 10 goals/day is a cost incident at 10M; a control that is thorough is a bottleneck; a shortcut that is harmless becomes the outage. This chapter is the playbook for what changes, and when, presented as three regimes — 10, 10k, and 10M goals per day — because the right architecture is different at each.

The single most useful framing: at every scale the binding constraint moves. At small scale it is capability (can it do the task at all); at medium scale it is reliability and cost (does it stay up and stay affordable); at large scale it is isolation and tail behaviour (does one tenant's spike hurt another, and what happens at the p99). Design for the constraint you have, and know which one comes next.

The playbook

01Deployment topology#

ShippedTopologyImpl8/10Criticality9/10

The physical shape: API replicas, a worker fleet split by plan queue, Postgres with pgvector, Redis for state and messaging, and the optional full stack (pgbouncer, Keycloak, object store, observability).

Mechanism

The minimum production topology: stateless API replicas behind a load balancer, a Celery worker fleet with pools per plan queue, Postgres+pgvector as the datastore, and Redis for pub/sub, cache, locks, and checkpoints. The full stack adds pgbouncer (connection pooling), Keycloak (identity), an object store (artifacts, screenshots), an observability stack (OTel collector, tracing backend), a search backend, and mail. Workers and API are stateless because state lives in Postgres and Redis — so both scale horizontally.

In AgentVerse

  • infra/docker-compose.ymlthe full stack (postgres, redis, pgbouncer, keycloak, celery worker+beat, minio, mailpit, otel, jaeger, searxng, frontend)
  • app/main.pythe API app (stateless, replica-safe)
  • app/scaling/celery_app.pythe worker fleet
  • app/core/pools.pyconnection pooling

Worked example

minimum prod       API ×3 · workers (per-queue pools) · Postgres+pgvector · Redis
full stack adds    pgbouncer · Keycloak · MinIO · OTel+Jaeger · SearXNG · mail
scaling            add API replicas for request load; add workers per queue
                   for goal load; both stateless, state in Postgres/Redis

At production scale

Statelessness is the property that makes horizontal scaling work — because agent state lives in Redis checkpoints and Postgres, any worker can pick up any goal and any replica can serve any request. pgbouncer becomes essential once worker count grows, or connection exhaustion caps you before compute does. The full stack's components map to chapters throughout this book — each is infrastructure for a capability, not optional decoration.

Failure modes

  • Stateful workers. Losing horizontal scalability.
  • No connection pooling. Connection exhaustion under fan-out.
  • One worker pool. No per-plan isolation.

Choose it when

  • Any production deployment.

02The 10/day regime: get it right#

ShippedRegimeImpl8/10Criticality6/10

At small scale the constraint is capability, not scale — a single process, in-memory services, one queue and one database are fine, and the effort belongs in correctness, not distribution.

Mechanism

At tens of goals a day, run the in-memory service path (the pre-swap phase of chapter 19), a single worker, one Postgres, and optionally one Redis. Skip per-plan queues, sharding, and read replicas — they solve problems you do not have. Spend the effort on getting the agent loop, the patterns, the retrieval, and the guardrails right, because at this scale a wrong answer matters more than a slow one.

In AgentVerse

  • app/main.pycreate_app(manage_pools=False) — the in-memory path (chapter 19)
  • app/providers/fake.pyno keys needed to develop
  • infra/docker-compose.ymlpostgres + redis is the minimum (per CLAUDE.md)

Worked example

a pilot deployment
 single API + worker, one Postgres, one Redis
 in-memory services, real providers from env keys
 no per-plan queues, no sharding, no replicas
 all effort on: does the agent do the task correctly?

At production scale

The mistake at this regime is premature distribution — building sharding and multi-region for a pilot that serves ten goals a day. The correctness work (patterns, retrieval, guardrails, evals) transfers to every later regime; the distribution work does not exist yet as a need. Build the capability right, and add scale machinery when the constraint actually moves.

Failure modes

  • Premature distribution. Complexity solving non-problems.
  • Neglecting correctness. A fast wrong answer.

Choose it when

  • Pilots, early products, internal tools.

03The 10k/day regime: reliability and cost#

ShippedRegimeImpl8/10Criticality9/10

The constraint becomes staying up and staying affordable — the DB/Redis-backed swap, per-plan queues, breakers, idempotency, budgets, and caches all become load-bearing here.

Mechanism

At thousands of goals a day, real tenants and real money arrive. The DB/Redis-backed service path (the lifespan swap of chapter 19) is now essential for cross-replica state; per-plan queues (chapter 20) isolate tenants; circuit breakers (chapter 28) handle provider flakiness; idempotency (chapter 28) makes the constant retries safe; Redis-backed budgets (chapter 13) keep cost accurate across replicas; and caches (chapter 29) become the dominant cost lever. This is where the platform's reliability and cost machinery earns its place.

In AgentVerse

  • app/main.pythe lifespan swap to DB/Redis-backed services (chapter 19)
  • app/scaling/celery_app.pyper-plan queues (chapter 20)
  • app/reliability/*, app/governance/cost.pybreakers, idempotency, budgets (chapters 28, 13)
  • app/rag/semantic_cache.py, app/mcp/tool_cache.pycaches (chapter 29)

Worked example

growth to 10k/day
 enable the DB/Redis swap → cross-replica state, durable checkpoints
 split queues by plan → the enterprise SLA survives a free-tier backfill
 breakers + idempotency → provider flakiness and retries stop hurting
 budgets + caches → cost per goal understood and controlled
the machinery that was optional at 10/day is load-bearing here

At production scale

This is the regime most production platforms live in, and the one where the reliability and cost chapters of this book pay off. The failure mode is arriving here with the 10/day architecture — in-memory services that lose state on restart, one queue that lets one tenant starve another, no idempotency so retries double-charge. The transition is not one change but the activation of a dozen mechanisms that were dormant.

Failure modes

  • 10/day architecture at 10k. State loss, noisy neighbours, double-charges.
  • No cost controls. A surprise invoice.
  • No breakers. Provider outages becoming yours.

Choose it when

  • Real tenants, real money, thousands of goals a day.

04The 10M/day regime: isolation and the tail#

PartialRegimeImpl6/10Criticality8/10

At the largest scale the constraint is isolation and tail behaviour — bulkheads, backpressure, sharding, read replicas, and regional residency, with the p99 (not the mean) as the number that matters.

Mechanism

At millions of goals a day, the constraints are one tenant's spike not hurting another (bulkheads and backpressure, chapter 28), the database not being a single bottleneck (sharding by tenant, read replicas for retrieval), and the tail latency being acceptable (the p99, since at this volume the tail is a large absolute number of unhappy users). Regional residency (chapter 30) becomes a topology concern — data and compute pinned per region. Much of this — cross-region active-active, tenant sharding — is where the platform's current implementation thins out, which the rating reflects.

In AgentVerse

  • app/reliability/bulkhead.py, app/qos/backpressure.pyisolation under load (chapter 28)
  • app/core/pools.pyconnection pooling (pgbouncer)
  • app/db/rls.pytenant isolation that sharding would build on
  • app/lifecycle/*residency for regional topology (chapter 30)

Worked example

at 10M/day the numbers that matter
 p99 latency, not mean — the tail is millions of requests
 per-tenant bulkheads — one tenant's spike is invisible to others
 sharding by tenant + read replicas — the DB is not one bottleneck
 regional topology — EU data and compute stay in the EU
this regime's machinery is where the platform is thinnest (see the rating)

At production scale

Rated 6 on implementation deliberately: bulkheads, backpressure, and RLS-based isolation exist, but tenant sharding, cross-region active-active, and the operational maturity for 10M/day are where the platform would need investment. The honest position is that the architecture is sound to this regime's door — stateless workers, per-plan queues, Redis-backed coordination — but the last mile (sharding, multi-region, p99 engineering) is future work, which is exactly the kind of gap this manual is meant to name.

Failure modes

  • Optimising the mean. A p99 that is unusable for millions.
  • Single database. The bottleneck at the top.
  • No regional topology. Residency and latency both failing.

Choose it when

  • Genuinely large scale — and expect to build the last mile.

What is missing here

  • Tenant sharding. RLS isolates logically; physical sharding of the datastore by tenant for the largest scale is future work.
  • Cross-region active-active. Regional residency is enforced; multi-region failover and active-active operation are not built.
  • p99 engineering. Latency is measured per percentile (chapter 10) but systematic tail-latency reduction is thin.
  • Load-test harness at scale. No documented harness for validating the 10M/day regime before reaching it.

Workflow engine
