Workflow engine

Deterministic workflows, chat, and collaboration alongside the agent loop.

Concepts
5
Mean impl
7.8
Mean criticality
7.4
Shipped
4
Thin / missing
0

Orientation

The autonomous agent loop (chapter 1) is the platform's headline, but it is not the only execution model. Alongside it runs a deterministic workflow engine: a versioned DSL of typed steps that executes exactly as authored, with no model deciding control flow. The two are complementary — the agent loop for open-ended goals where the path is unknown, the workflow engine for known processes that must run the same way every time.

The distinction is the whole point. A goal like "investigate this incident" wants an agent; a process like "on every invoice: validate, screen for fraud, route for approval, file" wants a workflow — auditable, testable, versioned, and identical on run one and run ten thousand. A world-class platform needs both, and needs them to compose: workflow steps that invoke agents, agents that trigger workflows.

The engine

01The workflow DSL and definition#

ShippedDefinitionImpl8/10Criticality8/10

A workflow is authored as a versioned definition — a DAG of typed steps with a variable context — not written in code, so it can be created, reviewed, and changed without a deploy.

Mechanism

A WorkflowDefinition declares steps, their types, their inputs (including ${step.output} references resolved by an expression engine), and their dependencies. It is data — YAML or a stored definition — so a workflow is a configuration object with a version, not a function. That makes it reviewable by non-engineers, diffable across versions, and changeable at runtime.

In AgentVerse

  • app/workflow/dsl.pyWorkflowDefinition, StepDefinition
  • app/workflow/expression_engine.py, variables.py, context.pyvariable references and context
  • app/workflow/registry.pyStepTypeRegistry
  • app/db/models/workflow.pythe persisted Workflow model

Worked example

workflow "invoice-processing" v3
  steps
    parse:     tool  document_parser(input: ${trigger.file})
    validate:  code  check_totals(${parse.output})
    fraud:     rag   screen(${parse.output.vendor})       deps [validate]
    approve:   hitl  "approve payment ${parse.output.total}?"  deps [fraud]
    file:      tool  erp.create_payment(...)               deps [approve]
authored as data, versioned, reviewable — no code deploy to change it

At production scale

A DSL is what lets a compliance or operations team own a process without owning code. The variable context with explicit ${step.output} references is the detail that makes workflows composable and testable — every data flow is declared, so the compiler can validate it and a reviewer can read it. Versioning is non-negotiable: a running process must not change under a live run, and an audit must show which version executed.

Failure modes

  • Workflows as code. Every change a deploy, unreviewable by process owners.
  • Unversioned definitions. A process that changed mid-run, unauditable.
  • Implicit data flow. Undeclared dependencies the compiler cannot validate.

Choose it when

  • A process is known, repeatable, and must run identically every time.
  • Not for open-ended goals where the path is unknown — that is the agent loop.

02Compilation and testing#

ShippedValidationImpl8/10Criticality7/10

Before a workflow runs it is compiled — the DAG validated, variable references resolved, step types checked — and can be dry-run against test inputs, so a broken workflow fails at authoring, not at 3 a.m.

Mechanism

The compiler turns a definition into an executable form, validating that the DAG is acyclic, that every ${...} reference resolves to a real upstream output, that step types exist, and that required inputs are present. A test runner executes the compiled workflow against sample inputs with mocked side effects — the simulation discipline of chapter 31 applied to workflows — so it can be proven before it goes live.

In AgentVerse

  • app/workflow/compiler.pyWorkflowCompiler
  • app/workflow/test_runner.pydry-run against test inputs
  • app/workflow/security.pysecurity validation of a definition
  • app/workflow/state.py, storage.pycompiled state and storage

Worked example

compile "invoice-processing" v4
  DAG acyclic?            yes
  ${fraud.output.risk}    references a real fraud-step output?  yes
  step type "code"        registered?  yes
  approve step gated?     yes (hitl)
test run against 3 sample invoices (mocked ERP) → all pass → cleared to
publish; a v5 that referenced a deleted step would fail compilation

At production scale

Compilation catches the errors that would otherwise surface mid-run against real systems — a dangling reference, a cycle, a missing input. The test runner is the workflow equivalent of the certification gate (chapter 10): a workflow that touches money or files a return must be proven against sample data before it is allowed to run live. Security validation matters because a workflow with an http or code step is an execution surface.

Failure modes

  • No compile-time validation. A dangling reference discovered at runtime.
  • No dry-run. A workflow's first real run is its first test.
  • Unvalidated code/http steps. An execution surface with no security check.

Choose it when

  • Always, before a workflow serves production.

03Typed steps and the runner#

ShippedExecutionImpl8/10Criticality8/10

Fifteen step types — tool, LLM, RAG, HTTP, code, conditional, parallel, foreach, wait, set-var, transform, emit-event, HITL, sub-workflow, org — each a first-class auditable unit the runner executes against the variable context.

Mechanism

The runner walks the compiled DAG, executing each step by type: tool and http call out, llm and rag invoke the model and retrieval, code runs in the sandbox (chapter 25), conditional/parallel/foreach are control flow, hitl pauses for approval, sub-workflow composes, set-var/transform/emit-event manipulate state. Each step's execution is audited. The llm and agent-invoking steps are where determinism meets autonomy — a mostly-fixed process with one judgement step.

In AgentVerse

  • app/workflow/runner.pyWorkflowRunner (wired in create_app)
  • app/workflow/steps/*.pytool, llm, rag, http, code, conditional, parallel, foreach, wait, set_variable, transform, emit_event, hitl, sub_workflow, org steps
  • app/workflow/celery_tasks.pyexecute_workflow_run
  • app/workflow/audit_middleware.pyAutoAuditMiddleware — audits each step

Worked example

runner executes invoice-processing
  parse (tool)      → invoice fields                    audited
  validate (code)   → sandbox, totals consistent        audited
  fraud (rag)       → risk score 0.2                     audited
  approve (hitl)    → pause → human approves → resume    audited
  file (tool)       → ERP payment created                audited
foreach variant: process 200 invoices, parallel-bounded, one workflow run

At production scale

Typed steps are what make a workflow both expressive and governable — each step type has its own risk profile, audit shape, and failure handling, so the platform's controls (tool risk, sandbox, HITL, rollback) apply per step. The foreach and parallel steps bring the wave-execution benefit (chapter 1) to deterministic processes. The llm step is the seam that lets a workflow stay mostly deterministic while delegating the one genuinely-judgement step to a model or a full agent.

Failure modes

  • Untyped steps. Controls that cannot apply per step.
  • Unbounded foreach. A 10,000-item fan-out exhausting the pool (chapter 28).
  • Unaudited steps. A process no one can reconstruct.

Choose it when

  • Any repeatable multi-step process — the more regulated, the more this beats an agent.

04Versioning, HITL, and runs#

ShippedLifecycleImpl8/10Criticality8/10

Every workflow is versioned, every run records which version it executed, HITL steps pause durably like the agent loop, and templates ship proven processes (AML screening, KYC, invoice processing) ready to instantiate.

Mechanism

A workflow has versions; a run pins the version it executed, so an audit shows exactly what ran. HITL steps use the same durable-pause machinery as the agent loop (chapter 1) — the run checkpoints, releases its worker, and resumes on approval via callback. Templates package proven workflows with their steps, gates, and validation, so a tenant instantiates AML screening or invoice processing rather than authoring it. Runs are observable and replayable (chapter 11).

In AgentVerse

  • app/workflow/router_versions.py, router_runs.py, router_templates.py, router_hitl.pyversions, runs, templates, HITL routing
  • app/workflow/hitl_extension.py, steps/hitl_step.pyHITLWorkflowGateway — durable pause
  • app/workflow/template_store.py, templates/*.yamlaml-screening, kyc-automation, invoice-processing
  • app/workflow/nl_trigger.py, service.py, otel.pyNL triggering, service, tracing

Worked example

tenant instantiates the "kyc-automation" template
  comes with: document parse, identity extraction (OCR ch 21), sanctions
  screen, risk scoring, HITL gate for high-risk, audit on every step
run r-4471 pins workflow v3 → HITL pause at the high-risk gate → analyst
approves → resumes → completes; the audit shows v3 ran, who approved, when

At production scale

Versioning plus per-run version pinning is what makes workflows defensible to a regulator — "this exact process, this version, ran, and here is the audit". Templates are how vertical processes (KYC, AML, invoicing) become instantly available with governance baked in (chapter 20). The shared HITL machinery means a workflow's approval gate has the same durability and argument-hashing guarantees as an agent's (chapter 1). Together they make the deterministic engine as production-grade as the agent loop.

Failure modes

  • Runs not pinned to a version. An audit that cannot say what executed.
  • HITL blocking a worker. Use the durable pause, not a held thread (chapter 1).
  • Uncertified templates. A shared process that never passed its test runner.

Choose it when

  • Regulated, repeatable processes — and start from a template where one exists.

05Conversational and collaborative execution#

PartialAdjacentImpl7/10Criticality6/10

Two adjacent execution surfaces: a chat layer that runs goals conversationally with intent detection and streaming, and a collaboration runtime for multiple humans steering shared work in real time.

Mechanism

The chat layer wraps the agent loop in a conversation: it detects intent (a question, a command, a goal), maintains conversational context and session memory (chapter 3), and streams responses — the same goal engine, a conversational front door. The collaboration runtime adds real-time multi-human coordination over a WebSocket (chapter 23): shared goal views, clarification capture, human decision traces, and preference capture, so several operators can steer one piece of work.

In AgentVerse

  • app/chat/service.py, intent.py, execution.py, context.py, stream.pythe conversational layer
  • app/chat/memory_api.py, search.py, templates.pychat memory, search, templates
  • app/collab/agent_collab.py, store.pyagent collaboration
  • app/collaboration_runtime/clarification.py, human_decision_trace.py, preference_capture.py, missing_input_request.pyhuman-in-the-loop collaboration

Worked example

chat: "reconcile March payouts, then tell me the variance"
  intent → goal → agent loop runs → streams progress → answers in the thread
  follow-up "and file the amendment" → continues the session with context

collab: two analysts watch a KYC review; one requests clarification, the
  other approves the gate; both decisions recorded in the human decision trace

At production scale

The chat layer is how most users actually reach the platform — a conversation, not an API call — so it inherits every control (auth, scope, guardrails) while adding conversational context management, which is where multi-turn constraint persistence matters (chapter 10). The collaboration runtime is thinner (rated 7): real-time multi-operator steering with presence and conflict handling is an area a world-class platform would deepen — which is exactly the kind of gap the upgrade plan targets.

Failure modes

  • Chat losing constraints across turns. A stated constraint forgotten (chapter 10).
  • Collaboration without decision traces. No record of who steered what.
  • Session memory unbounded. Context overflow on long conversations (chapter 3).

Choose it when

  • Users interact conversationally, or multiple humans steer shared work.

What is missing here

  • Agent ⇄ workflow composition as first-class. An llm/agent step invokes an agent and an agent can trigger a workflow, but a seamless "escalate from deterministic to autonomous mid-process and back" is not fully first-class.
  • Workflow eval and certification parity. The test runner exists; a required certification gate for workflows matching the agent-side one (chapter 10) is thinner.
  • Real-time collaboration depth. Multi-operator steering with presence, cursors, and conflict resolution is early (chapter 23).
  • Conversational constraint persistence. Extracting stated constraints from chat into durable state, rather than trusting the transcript, is not fully wired (chapter 10).

Frontier & gaps

Orientation

Every chapter ended with a "what is missing" section. This chapter gathers those gaps into a coherent picture of the frontier — not a list of bugs, but the honest boundary of what this architecture, and agentic AI generally, cannot yet do well. A field manual that only described what works would be a sales brochure; the gaps are where the interesting work is.

The gaps cluster into five themes. Each is a place where the current answer is "hand-tuned rules" or "not yet built", and where the next generation of agent platforms will differentiate.

The frontier

01Learned decisions replacing hand-tuned rules#

ThinFrontierImpl4/10Criticality8/10

The platform is full of hand-written rule tables — pattern assembly, RAG strategy selection, model routing, retention. The frontier is replacing them with decisions learned from measured outcomes.

Mechanism

Today's decision points use ordered rule tables that a human wrote and tunes: the pattern assembler (chapter 1), adaptive RAG selection (chapter 2), per-role model routing (chapter 16). These are auditable and predictable, which is why they exist — but they are also static and hand-tuned. The frontier is a bandit or learned policy over each, optimising measured success-per-dollar per goal class, with the eval and experiment machinery (chapters 9–10) providing the training signal. The tension is auditability: a learned policy is harder to explain to a regulator than a rule table.

Where it would attach

  • app/agent/pattern_assembler.pylearned pattern selection
  • app/rag/agentic/retrieval_policy.pylearned RAG strategy selection
  • app/ai_router/role_policy.pylearned model routing
  • app/intelligence/experiment_registry.pythe training signal (chapter 9)

The gap

today   the assembler applies a hand-written rule table (chapter 1)
frontier a bandit over pattern sets, learning which combination gives the
         best success-per-dollar for each goal class, from measured outcomes
blocker  the eval/experiment machinery exists but is not wired to decisions;
         and learned policies are harder to audit than rule tables

Why it matters

Rated 4/8 — barely implemented, highly valuable. Hand-tuned rules are where a lot of the platform's remaining cost and quality sits: the assembler over-provisions patterns "to be safe", routing is conservative, retrieval selection is coarse. Learned decisions would close that gap, and the infrastructure to train them already exists. The open question is governance — how to keep a learned policy explainable enough for a regulated deployment.

The risk

  • Unexplainable decisions. A learned policy a regulator cannot audit.
  • Reward hacking. Optimising a proxy (cost) against quality.

The path

  • Wire evals to decisions, start with the lowest-risk (model routing), keep a rule-table fallback.

02Privacy-preserving cross-tenant learning#

ThinFrontierImpl3/10Criticality7/10

Every tenant learns alone. The frontier is aggregating lessons, failure modes, and attack patterns across tenants without leaking any tenant's data — the largest unrealised value in the platform.

Mechanism

Memory, reflexion lessons, red-team findings, and retrieval quality all improve per tenant in isolation (chapters 3, 9, 12) — which means common failure modes are rediscovered independently by every tenant. The frontier is privacy-preserving aggregation: federated learning, differential privacy, or careful anonymisation that lets the platform learn "this class of goal often fails this way" or "this injection pattern is circulating" across the fleet without any tenant's data reaching another. The hard part is proving the privacy guarantee.

Where it would attach

  • app/memory/*cross-tenant lesson aggregation (chapter 3)
  • app/enterprise/red_team_corpus.pyshared attack intelligence (chapter 12)
  • app/evals/dataset_builder.pyshared failure patterns (chapter 10)

The gap

today   tenant A discovers an injection pattern; tenants B-Z stay vulnerable
        until each is attacked independently
frontier the pattern hardens the detectors for everyone, without A's data
         leaving A
blocker  the privacy guarantee must be provable, not hoped

Why it matters

Rated 3/7 — essentially unbuilt, genuinely valuable. Security is the clearest case: an attack seen once should protect everyone, immediately. But the same applies to failure modes and retrieval quality. The reason it is unbuilt is that the privacy bar is high and the failure is catastrophic — a cross-tenant leak dressed as learning ends contracts. It is a frontier precisely because the value is large and the safety requirement is absolute.

The risk

  • Cross-tenant leakage. The catastrophic failure this must never cause.
  • Weak anonymisation. Re-identification from aggregated lessons.

The path

  • Start with the safest signal (attack patterns, which are not tenant data), prove the guarantee, then expand.

03Native multimodal and richer perception#

ThinFrontierImpl4/10Criticality5/10

Multimodal is extract-to-text today. The frontier is native reasoning over pixels, audio, and video — and the joint embeddings, cross-modal grounding, and speech-to-speech that come with it.

Mechanism

The current path captions images, transcribes audio, and reduces everything to text (chapter 15) — pragmatic, citable, governable, and lossy. The frontier is native multimodal: joint image/text embeddings for visual search (chapter 7), cross-modal grounding (verifying a claim against a chart, chapter 18), speech-to-speech voice without the STT/TTS round-trip (chapter 26), and true document understanding where layout is meaning. Each is more capable and harder to cite and govern, which is why the production path stays extract-to-text.

Where it would attach

  • app/embedding/router.pynative joint embeddings (chapter 7)
  • app/perception/multimodal.pynative perception (chapter 15)
  • app/voice/*speech-to-speech (chapter 26)

The gap

today   a diagram → caption + OCR → text → retrieve/reason (lossy)
frontier reason over the diagram's pixels directly, cite the region, ground
         a claim against a chart
blocker  citation and governance are harder for native modalities than for
         extracted text

Why it matters

Rated 4/5 — the production path (extraction) is sound and the frontier is genuinely better only for specific uses (visual search, document understanding, low-latency voice). It is a real frontier but a narrower one than the others — for most workloads, extract-to-text will remain the right, governable choice. The interesting cases are where layout or visual detail is the information, and extraction demonstrably loses it.

The risk

  • Uncitable claims. Native reasoning without a verifiable source.
  • Ungovernable modalities. Audio/video harder to scan and redact.

The path

  • Adopt where extraction demonstrably loses information; keep extraction as the governable default.

04Formal guarantees and verifiable safety#

ThinFrontierImpl3/10Criticality6/10

Safety today is enforced by controls and measured by evals. The frontier is provable guarantees — checkable arguments that a loop terminates, that a scope cannot leak, that a control cannot be bypassed.

Mechanism

The platform enforces safety through deterministic controls (chapter 12), scope composition (chapter 14), and append-only invariants (chapter 1), and measures it through evals and red teaming (chapters 10, 31). These are strong but empirical — they show safety holds on the cases tested. The frontier is formal: a checkable proof that the agent loop must terminate, that the scope intersection cannot leak, that a fail-closed control cannot degrade to fail-open under any path. Formal methods for AI systems are early, but the highest-risk autonomous flows are where they would matter most.

Where it would attach

  • app/agent/patterns/loop_engineering.pytermination proofs (chapter 1)
  • app/orchestration/runtime_profile_builder.pyscope-composition proofs (chapter 14)
  • app/policy_runtime/compiler.pyprovable policy invariants (chapter 13)

The gap

today   iteration caps enforce termination numerically; tests show scopes
        don't leak on the cases tried
frontier a checkable argument that the loop MUST terminate, that a tenant-A
         request CANNOT return a tenant-B row under any path
blocker  formal methods for non-deterministic AI systems are immature

Why it matters

Rated 3/6 — unbuilt, and valuable specifically for the highest-risk autonomous flows. For most goals, empirical safety (controls plus evals) is proportionate. But for an agent that can move money or delete data autonomously, a proof that a control cannot be bypassed is worth more than a thousand passing tests. This is the longest-horizon frontier, gated on the maturity of formal methods for AI, but it is where the ceiling of trustworthy autonomy ultimately sits.

The risk

  • False confidence. A proof of the wrong property.
  • Proving the model, not the system. Guarantees that do not cover the LLM's behaviour.

The path

  • Start with the deterministic parts (loop termination, scope composition) where proofs are tractable.

05The state of the art, honestly#

PartialSynthesisImpl6/10Criticality9/10

This platform is a genuinely complete production agent system — and it is complete in the way a first-generation system is: the capabilities exist, the hard problems have real answers, and the next generation of work is optimisation, learning, and formal rigour on top.

The assessment

Across 33 chapters and 300+ concepts, the pattern is consistent: the capabilities are shipped and governed (agent loop, retrieval, memory, guardrails, governance, observability all rate high), while the intelligence that would make those capabilities self-improving is where the gaps cluster (learned decisions, cross-tenant learning, formal guarantees all rate low). That is the honest shape of the current state of the art in production agentic AI: we know how to build agents that plan, retrieve, act, verify, and stay governed and safe; we are still learning how to make them get better on their own without giving up the auditability that makes them deployable.

The evidence

  • graphify-out/21,585 nodes, 1,165 communities, 45 subsystems — the map this manual is drawn from
  • The ratings across all chaptershigh on capability, low on learned intelligence — the shape of the frontier

The shape

rated high (shipped, governed)   the agent loop, RAG, memory tiers, guardrails,
                                 governance, scopes, observability, MCP, cost
rated low (frontier)             learned pattern/RAG/model selection,
                                 cross-tenant learning, native multimodal,
                                 formal guarantees, 10M/day topology
the capabilities are built; the self-improving intelligence on top is next

What to take from this

If you are building an agent platform, this book is a map of the problems you will face and real answers to most of them — the capability layer is well-understood and this system implements it thoroughly. If you are researching, the low-rated concepts are the open problems worth your time. And if you are an architect deciding whether to build or buy: the hard, unglamorous 80% (isolation, idempotency, rollback, audit, cost control, degraded mode) is exactly what separates a demo from a platform, and it is exactly what a first survey underestimates. That 80% is most of this book.

The honest caveat

  • Ratings are one engineer's reading of the code as it stands, not a benchmark.
  • The frontier moves. Today's low-rated concept is next year's table stakes.

Where to go next

  • Builders: the capability chapters (1–20). Researchers: the low-rated concepts. Architects: the reliability, governance, and scale chapters (13, 28–32).

Ratings matrix

Every rated concept in one sortable table.

How to read the ratings

Every concept in this manual carries two independent scores. Keeping them separate is the whole point: a concept can be beautifully implemented and barely matter, or crudely implemented and absolutely load-bearing. Reading them together is how you decide where to spend effort.

Impl — implementation depth

9–10 wired into the live path, governed, tested, exposed. 7–8 real and on the live path, one dimension short. 5–6 works but opt-in or narrowly wired. 3–4 adapter or scaffold. 1–2 named but effectively absent.

Criticality — does production need it?

9–10 ship without it and you get an incident, a breach, or an unexplained bill. 7–8 needed once you have real tenants. 5–6 materially improves quality or cost. 3–4 situational. 1–2 research interest.

On honesty

These are one engineer's readings of the code as it stands, not a vendor scorecard or a benchmark. The low scores are the most useful entries in the book — they are the work that is left. Read the frontier chapter (33) for the pattern the low scores form.

How to use the matrix below. Glossary
CH BAppendix

Glossary

The vocabulary, defined once.

The vocabulary, defined once

The terms this manual uses in its own specific senses. Where a term has a chapter, that is where it is developed in full.

TermDefinition
Agent loopThe checkpointed state machine (initialize → retrieve → plan → execute → verify → route) that runs one goal. The substrate, not an option. (Ch 1)
Agent patternA control-flow shape: the rule deciding what the model is asked next. ReAct, plan-execute, reflection, and the rest are answers to that one question. (Ch 1)
AssemblerThe rule table that maps a goal's classified properties to a pattern config, appending safety patterns it can never remove. (Ch 1)
BulkheadA per-tenant concurrency ceiling, so one tenant's fan-out cannot starve the shared pool. (Ch 20, 28)
ChunkThe atom of retrieval: a span of a document with a stable id, embedded, scored, cited, and deleted as a unit. (Ch 4, 17)
Circuit breakerA guard that stops calling a failing dependency after repeated failures, failing fast or serving stale until it recovers. (Ch 16, 28)
ClassificationA datum's tag — public/internal/confidential/restricted — assigned at creation, driving handling, retention, residency, and deletion. (Ch 30)
CollectionThe unit of authorisation, embedding model, and lifecycle for knowledge — not a folder. (Ch 4)
Consensus verificationUp to three independent verifiers (primary, cross-model, judge) for high-stakes goals; disagreement escalates to a human. (Ch 1)
Decision traceThe record of every runtime decision (pattern, model, tools, policy) with its reason — the agent-specific observability signal. (Ch 11)
Degraded modeRunning with less when a dependency is down — lexical search without the embedder — rather than failing, and never fail-open on a fail-closed control. (Ch 28)
Fail closedWhen a check errors or is uncertain, block rather than proceed. The principle that makes guardrails trustworthy. (Ch 12)
GoalThe process abstraction: a natural-language objective the platform plans, executes, verifies, and completes. (Ch 19)
GroundingChecking that every factual claim in an output is supported by the evidence — deterministically first, then by entailment. (Ch 18)
GuardrailA deterministic check that can block input, tool calls, or output independent of the model's cooperation. (Ch 12)
HITLHuman-in-the-loop: a durable pause where a goal checkpoints, releases its worker, and waits for a human decision. (Ch 1, 23)
Hybrid retrievalVector + lexical (BM25) + trigram search merged by rank fusion — the correct default for enterprise corpora with identifiers. (Ch 2, 6)
Idempotency keyA key derived from goal + step + arguments so a retried write is recognised as the same write, not a new one. (Ch 28)
Ingestion pipelineThe 13-stage path (receive → … → PII redact → … → embed → index → emit) every document takes, hash-gated at stage 3. (Ch 5)
MCPModel Context Protocol: the device-driver layer where tools live in their own processes behind a uniform, per-tenant protocol. (Ch 19, 20)
Memory tierOne of seven stores (execution, reflexion, long-term, episodic, procedural, knowledge-graph, prospective), each with its own lifetime and trust. (Ch 3)
Poisoned memoryAn attacker-authored lesson written to memory and recalled into future prompts; prevented by provenance, quarantine, and untrusted treatment. (Ch 3)
Prompt recipeThe reconstructable record of a prompt — variant ids, context item ids, budget, model — stored instead of the full prompt. (Ch 8)
ProvenanceThe origin chain of a datum — source, revision, extraction — used for both grounding and deletion. (Ch 30)
ReflexionReflection that outlives the run: a durable, scoped lesson extracted from failure and recalled for similar future goals. (Ch 1, 3)
RLSRow-level security: Postgres filtering every row by app.tenant_id, the independent database backstop to app-level tenant isolation. (Ch 13, 14)
RollbackApplying registered inverses in LIFO order to undo a failed goal's side effects, so failure leaves no half-built state. (Ch 1, 20)
ScopeOne of nine nested boundaries (tenant → API key → agent → collection → connector → tool → memory → policy → runtime) AND-ed to prevent leakage. (Ch 14)
Semantic cacheServing a repeated question's answer by embedding match rather than exact string — the largest cost lever on repetitive workloads. (Ch 2, 29)
Stall detectionHashing results to detect no progress across iterations, deterministic and resumable, so a loop cannot spin silently. (Ch 1)
Strategy readinessThe gateway checking whether a RAG strategy can actually run given the tenant's capabilities, delegating to a ready one rather than failing. (Ch 2)
TenantContextThe immutable, per-request identity that flows through everything and sets the RLS boundary — a top hub of the whole system. (Ch 13)
Tool risk classread / write_low / write_high / destructive — the classification that drives approval, rollback, and audit for a tool call. (Ch 1, 13)
Two-phase wiringThe app built once with in-memory services, then swapped to DB/Redis-backed ones in the lifespan — the source of most "works in tests, not in prod" bugs. (Ch 19)
VerifierThe only node with authority to end a run; judges the step against evidence, never against the actor's own reasoning. (Ch 1, 8, 18)

End of the manual. The 342 rated concepts across 33 chapters are indexed in the hub; the full ratings matrix is in Appendix A. Everything here is grounded in one real system's code — treat the file paths as navigation anchors, the ratings as an informed reading, and the gaps as the interesting work.
